lessons.title: What Is a Microprocessor?
lessons.content:
Picture a busy tea stall near a bus stop in Mirpur. One man takes the orders, boils the water, pours the tea, adds sugar, takes the money and gives change. He does one small job after another, very fast, all day long. He does not think about the whole day at once. He just repeats: hear the next order, understand it, do it. A microprocessor is that tea stall man inside every computer, phone, washing machine and car. It is a tiny chip that reads one small instruction, understands it, does it, and then moves to the next one, millions or billions of times every second.

What it is: A microprocessor is a complete CPU (Central Processing Unit) built on a single chip of silicon. The CPU is the part of a computer that actually follows instructions: it adds numbers, compares them, moves data around and decides what to do next. The word "micro" just means it is small enough to fit on one chip. Before microprocessors, a CPU was built from many separate boards full of chips and wires.

The problem it solved: In the 1950s and 1960s, computers filled whole rooms. A CPU was made of thousands of separate transistors or many small chips soldered onto boards. That made computers huge, expensive, hot and hard to repair. Only governments, universities and big companies could own one. Engineers wanted to put all the CPU parts together on one chip so that it would be cheap, small and reliable.

Before and after: In 1971 Intel released the 4004, usually called the first commercial microprocessor. It was a 4-bit CPU made for a calculator company. Suddenly the "brain" of a machine was one small chip that could be mass-produced. That one idea led to pocket calculators, personal computers, game consoles, mobile phones and almost every smart device today. Today a single phone chip holds billions of transistors.

The three big parts inside: Every microprocessor, simple or modern, has three main parts. The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does the actual maths and logic, like 5 + 3 or "is A equal to B?". The control unit is the manager: it reads each instruction, decides what it means and sends signals telling the other parts what to do. The registers are tiny, super-fast storage boxes inside the chip, each holding one number that the CPU is working on right now. Think of registers as the few things you keep in your hand while cooking, while memory is the fridge across the room.

Microprocessor vs memory: A microprocessor does not hold your whole program or your photos. Those live in memory (RAM) and storage. The microprocessor fetches instructions and data from memory, works on them in its registers, and writes results back. This back-and-forth happens through sets of wires called buses, which we will study in lesson 3. So a microprocessor alone is not a computer. It needs memory, input and output devices and a clock to become a working system.

Microprocessor vs microcontroller: These two words sound similar but they are different. A microprocessor is mainly the CPU; memory and input/output chips sit outside it on the board. A microcontroller puts a CPU, some RAM, some ROM (or flash) and input/output pins all on one chip. A laptop uses a microprocessor because it needs huge outside memory and flexibility. A microwave oven, a TV remote or a digital weighing scale uses a microcontroller because it needs a small, cheap, all-in-one chip that does one job. Arduino boards, for example, are built around microcontrollers.

How it works, the cycle: A microprocessor works in a loop called the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Step 1, fetch: the CPU looks at a special register that holds the address of the next instruction, sends that address to memory and reads the instruction bytes. Step 2, decode: the control unit figures out what the instruction means, for example "add the number in register BX to register AX". Step 3, execute: the ALU or other parts do the job and the result is stored. Then the address register moves to the next instruction and the loop starts again. Your Computer Architecture course covers this cycle in general; here we will see exactly how the Intel 8086 does it.

A tiny trace: Suppose memory holds three instructions: put 7 into AX, put 5 into BX, add BX into AX. Fetch first: AX becomes 7. Fetch second: BX becomes 5. Fetch third: the ALU adds 7 and 5 and AX becomes 12. Three tiny steps, and the processor has done 7 + 5. Every app on your phone, even a video call on Imo or WhatsApp, is built from billions of tiny steps like these.

The clock: How fast does the loop run? A crystal on the board produces a steady beat called the clock. Each beat is one clock cycle. A 1 GHz clock beats one billion times per second. Simple instructions may take one or a few cycles; on the old 8086 many instructions took several cycles. The original 8086 ran at 5 to 10 MHz, which means 5 to 10 million beats per second. A modern phone chip runs at about 2 to 3 GHz and can also do several instructions at the same time.

Machine code: The CPU does not understand English words or even letters. It only understands patterns of bits, 0s and 1s, stored as bytes. For example, on the 8086 the bytes B8 07 00 (written in hexadecimal) mean "put 7 into AX". This is called machine code. It is the only language the chip truly speaks. Writing programs directly in machine code is possible but painful: one wrong bit and the program does something totally different.

Assembly language: To make life easier, engineers gave each machine instruction a short name called a mnemonic. Instead of B8 07 00 we write MOV AX, 7. Instead of 01 D8 we write ADD AX, BX. This human-readable form is called assembly language. A program called an assembler translates assembly into machine code. The key idea: one assembly line usually becomes exactly one machine instruction. That is why assembly is called a low-level language. You see and control every single step the processor takes.

High-level languages: C, Python and Java are high-level languages. One line like total = a + b * c may become several machine instructions. A compiler (for C) or an interpreter (for Python) does that translation for you. High-level code is easier to write, read and move between different CPUs. Assembly is tied to one processor family: 8086 assembly will not run on an ARM chip in your phone without being rewritten.

A side-by-side view: Imagine the same job, "add two numbers", at three levels. High-level C: x = a + b. Assembly: MOV AX, a then ADD AX, b then MOV x, AX. Machine code: a list of hex bytes like A1 .. .. 03 06 .. .. A3 .. .. (the dots are memory addresses). Going down the ladder, each level is closer to the hardware, faster to run in theory, and harder for humans to write.

Why learn assembly today: Nobody writes a full mobile app in assembly. So why study it? First, it shows you what really happens inside the machine: where your variables live, how a loop really repeats, how a function call returns. Second, some jobs still need it: the first code that runs when a device powers on (boot code), tiny embedded devices with very little memory, device drivers, and speed-critical parts of programs. Third, security experts read assembly every day when they analyse viruses or crack open how a program works (reverse engineering). Fourth, compiler writers and operating system developers must understand it.

When not to use assembly: If you just need to build a website, an app or a data analysis script, assembly is the wrong tool. It takes many more lines, it is easy to make mistakes, it is hard for teammates to read and it only works on one CPU family. Modern compilers usually produce very good machine code anyway. The smart approach is: write in a high-level language, and drop to assembly only for the small part where you truly need it, or simply to understand and debug.

Why the 8086: Universities across Bangladesh, and around the world, usually teach this course with the Intel 8086, a 16-bit processor from 1978. Why such an old chip? Because it is simple enough to understand fully, yet it is the direct ancestor of the x86 processors in most desktop and laptop computers today. Modern Intel and AMD chips can still run 8086-style instructions. Learning the 8086 is like learning to drive in a simple manual car before driving a modern one: the basic controls are the same.

Real life example 1, a bKash payment: When you pay with bKash on your phone, you tap a button. Behind it, the app's high-level code (written by programmers in a high-level language) has been turned into machine code for the phone's ARM processor. The processor fetches instructions to read your tap, check your PIN, prepare the message, encrypt it and send it over the network. Each of those steps is thousands of fetch-decode-execute cycles, finished in a fraction of a second. You never see assembly, but it is there, one level below everything.

Real life example 2, a digital weighing scale at the bazar: The shopkeeper places one kilo of potatoes on a digital scale. A load sensor makes a tiny voltage, a converter turns it into a number, and a small microcontroller runs a short program: read the number, subtract the empty-tray weight, multiply by the price per kilo, show the result on the display. That program is small and must run on a cheap chip, so parts of such firmware have often been written in C, and sometimes in assembly. This is exactly the kind of system you will be able to understand by the end of this course.

Course map: Here is the journey. First the foundation: history of microprocessors, buses, the inside of the 8086, its registers and memory segmentation, and its pins and bus timing. Then programming: writing your first program, addressing modes, data movement, arithmetic, logic, jumps, loops, the stack, procedures, string instructions and DOS services. Then the hardware side: interrupts, the 8259 interrupt controller, connecting memory and I/O chips, the 8255, timers, DMA and serial communication. We finish with how modern x86 grew from the 8086.

Common mistakes: Beginners often think the microprocessor stores files; it does not, memory and storage do. Some think assembly is the same as machine code; it is not, assembly is the readable text and machine code is the bytes. Many mix up microprocessor and microcontroller. Others believe assembly is always faster than C; a careless assembly program can be slower than good compiler output. Also, assembly is not one language: each processor family (x86, ARM, AVR) has its own.

What exams ask: Define a microprocessor and list its main parts. Differentiate microprocessor and microcontroller. Explain the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Differentiate machine language, assembly language and high-level language, with advantages and disadvantages of assembly. Explain the role of an assembler.

Recap: A microprocessor is a CPU on one chip with an ALU, a control unit and registers. It runs a never-ending fetch-decode-execute loop, paced by a clock. It only understands machine code; assembly gives each machine instruction a readable name, and an assembler translates it. Use high-level languages for most work and assembly when you need full control or deep understanding. Next lesson: how microprocessors grew from the 4-bit 4004 to today's 64-bit chips.
key_points: A microprocessor is a complete CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) on one chip.
It needs memory, I/O devices, buses and a clock to become a working computer.
A microcontroller puts CPU, RAM, ROM/flash and I/O on one chip for small dedicated jobs.
Every instruction goes through fetch, decode and execute, paced by the clock.
Machine code is bytes the CPU runs; assembly gives each instruction a readable mnemonic; an assembler translates it.
Assembly is tied to one processor family; high-level languages are portable.
Learn assembly to see what really happens inside, and for boot code, embedded systems, drivers and security work.
The 8086 is taught because it is simple and is the ancestor of today's x86 chips.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a new instruction, ask three questions: what goes in, what comes out, and which register or flag changes. That habit makes assembly easy.
lessons.task: Look at three devices at home (fan regulator, microwave, phone, TV remote, calculator). For each, write whether it likely uses a microprocessor or a microcontroller and why.

quiz.q: What is a microprocessor?
options: A memory chip that stores programs
A complete CPU built on a single chip
A device that only does input and output
quiz.explain: A microprocessor is the whole CPU, ALU plus control unit plus registers, on one chip.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of a microcontroller?
options: A large chip used only in servers
A chip with CPU, memory and I/O together for dedicated jobs
quiz.explain: A microcontroller includes CPU, RAM, ROM/flash and I/O pins on one chip.

quiz.q: What does an assembler do?
options: Translates assembly language into machine code
quiz.explain: It converts mnemonics like MOV AX, 7 into the machine code bytes.

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU does the actual arithmetic?
quiz.explain: The Arithmetic Logic Unit does maths and logic operations.

quiz.q: Why is assembly language less portable than C?
options: It has no instructions for addition
It is tied to one processor family's instruction set
It can only run on phones
It must be interpreted line by line
quiz.explain: 8086 assembly only works on x86-family processors; C can be recompiled for other CPUs.

lessons.title: History of Microprocessors: From 4004 to x86-64
lessons.content:
Think of how mobile phones changed in Bangladesh. First came big button phones that could only call and send SMS. Then came phones with small colour screens and Snake games. Then smartphones with cameras, Facebook and bKash. Each new phone did not throw away the old ideas; it kept calling and SMS and added more. Microprocessors grew the same way. Each new chip kept the old abilities and added more power. Knowing this family story explains why a 2026 laptop can still understand instructions designed in 1978.

Why history matters here: In this course you will meet terms like 8-bit, 16-bit, real mode, protected mode, 8086 and x86. They only make sense when you see where they came from. History is not about memorising years. It is about seeing which problem each new chip solved: more memory, more speed, more safety. Once you see the problems, the features feel natural instead of random.

First, a few words we need: Word size is the number of bits the processor naturally works on in one go, mostly the width of its registers and ALU. An 8-bit processor adds two 8-bit numbers in one step; a 16-bit processor adds two 16-bit numbers in one step. The data bus width is how many bits travel between the CPU and memory at once. The address bus width decides how much memory the CPU can reach: with n address lines it can name 2 to the power n different byte locations. Clock speed is how many beats per second the processor runs at, measured in hertz.

A quick memory calculation: With 16 address lines, the CPU can name 2^16 = 65,536 locations, which is 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes). With 20 lines, 2^20 = 1,048,576 locations, which is 1 MB. With 32 lines, 2^32 bytes = 4 GB. Notice how each extra address line doubles the memory. This simple rule explains a lot of the history below, because "we need more memory" was a constant pressure.

Intel 4004 (1971): The first commercial single-chip microprocessor. It was 4-bit, had around 2,300 transistors and was designed for a Japanese calculator company called Busicom. Four bits are enough for one decimal digit (0 to 9 fits in 4 bits), which is perfect for a calculator but very weak for general computing.

Intel 8008 (1972) and 8080 (1974): The 8008 was Intel's first 8-bit processor. The 8080 improved it a lot and had a 16-bit address bus, so it could reach 64 KB of memory. The 8080 powered some of the earliest personal computers, such as the Altair 8800, which hobbyists built and programmed with switches. Competitors appeared too: the Zilog Z80, which could run 8080 programs, became very popular.

Intel 8085 (1976): An improved 8-bit chip that needed only a single +5 volt power supply, which made boards simpler and cheaper. It still had a 64 KB address space. The 8085 is still taught in many universities and diploma courses as a first microprocessor, and you may see 8085 trainer kits in some Bangladeshi labs.

The problem that led to the 8086: By the late 1970s, 64 KB of memory was too small, and 8-bit arithmetic was slow for bigger numbers. Adding two 16-bit numbers on an 8-bit chip took several instructions. Intel needed a chip that worked on 16 bits at once and could reach far more memory, while still being friendly to people who knew the 8080.

Intel 8086 (1978): The solution was a 16-bit processor with 16-bit registers, a 16-bit data bus and a 20-bit address bus, so it could reach 1 MB of memory. It had about 29,000 transistors and ran at 5 to 10 MHz in its different versions. To reach 1 MB using 16-bit registers, it used a trick called segmentation, which you will learn in lesson 6. The 8086 started the family name "x86", because later chips were named 80186, 80286, 80386 and so on.

8085 vs 8086 side by side: Data width: the 8085 handles 8 bits at once, the 8086 handles 16. Address bus: 16 lines (64 KB) versus 20 lines (1 MB). Speed trick: the 8086 fetches the next instructions while the current one is still executing, using a small queue inside the chip; the 8085 does not. Multiplication: the 8086 has MUL and DIV instructions; on the 8085 you had to build multiplication from loops of additions. A simple comparison like this is a favourite exam question, so read it as a story of problems solved: more bits, more memory, more speed, more built-in maths.

What "compatible" really means: The 8086 was not able to run 8080 machine code directly; the bytes were different. Intel instead made the instructions and registers similar enough that 8080 assembly programs could be translated to 8086 assembly mostly automatically. From the 8086 onward, however, each new x86 chip could run the previous chips' machine code directly. That is a stronger kind of compatibility, and it is why the x86 family became so long-lived.

Intel 8088 (1979) and the IBM PC: The 8088 is an 8086 inside, with the same 16-bit registers, but its external data bus is only 8 bits wide. That let computer makers use cheaper 8-bit memory and support chips. IBM chose the 8088 for its first Personal Computer in 1981. That decision made x86 the standard for PCs. So the 8086 family became famous partly because of a business choice, not only technical brilliance.

Intel 80286 (1982): Still 16-bit, but with a 24-bit address bus, so 16 MB of memory. Its big new idea was protected mode, which lets an operating system keep programs from damaging each other's memory. The old 8086 way of working was kept as real mode, so old programs still ran. This was the start of a pattern: always keep backward compatibility.

Intel 80386 (1985): The first 32-bit x86 processor. Registers grew to 32 bits (AX became part of EAX), the address bus became 32 bits wide (4 GB of memory), and it added paging, a way to manage memory in fixed-size pages that modern operating systems like Windows and Linux depend on. It also added virtual 8086 mode, so old DOS programs could run safely under a newer system.

Intel 80486 (1989) and Pentium (1993): The 486 put a floating-point unit (for decimal-point maths) and a small cache memory on the same chip in its DX versions, and used pipelining heavily so that most simple instructions finished in about one clock cycle. The Pentium was superscalar: it had two pipelines, so it could sometimes execute two instructions in the same clock cycle. How pipelines and caches work in general is covered in Computer Architecture; just note that the x86 family kept adding speed tricks while running the same old instructions.

x86-64 (2003 onward): AMD extended x86 to 64 bits, first in its Opteron and Athlon 64 processors. Registers grew to 64 bits (RAX) and eight more general registers were added. Intel later adopted the same extension. Today almost every Windows laptop and most servers run x86-64 processors, and inside them the old 16-bit AX register still exists as the lowest part of RAX.

The register family tree as a diagram: think of nested boxes. RAX (64 bits) contains EAX (lower 32 bits), which contains AX (lower 16 bits), which is split into AH (high 8 bits) and AL (low 8 bits). Written in one line: RAX > EAX > AX > AH and AL. When you learn AX on the 8086, you are learning the core of every modern x86 register.

Other families: x86 is not alone. Motorola's 68000 (1979) powered the first Apple Macintosh (1984) and many game machines. ARM, first designed in Britain in the mid-1980s, focused on simple instructions and low power use. Today ARM chips run almost every smartphone, including the ones from Samsung, Xiaomi and Apple, and Apple moved its Mac computers to its own ARM-based chips starting in 2020. Microcontroller families like AVR (used in many Arduino boards) and PIC power small devices.

Moore's law: Gordon Moore, a co-founder of Intel, observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling at a steady rate, roughly every two years. From about 2,300 transistors in the 4004 to billions today, this trend held for decades. It is an observation about industry progress, not a law of physics, and it has slowed in recent years as transistors approach atomic sizes.

Clock speed is not everything: A 3 GHz chip from today is not just 300 times faster than a 10 MHz 8086. It is far, far faster, because it also finishes several instructions per clock cycle, has big caches, has multiple cores, and works on 64 bits at once. So when comparing processors, look at the whole design, not only the MHz or GHz number printed on the box.

Trade-offs in this story: Backward compatibility is x86's superpower and its burden. The good side: decades of software still runs. The bad side: the chip must still carry old, complicated features, which costs design effort and chip area. ARM's simpler design made it better for battery-powered phones. There is no single "best" processor; there is the best one for a job.

Real life example 1, a computer shop at IDB Bhaban (BCS Computer City), Dhaka: When a shopkeeper says "this laptop has a Core i5" or "a Ryzen 5", both are x86-64 processors. If you installed DOSBox on it, you could run an 8086 program written by a student in 1990 and it would still work. That is backward compatibility you can actually test.

Real life example 2, your phone vs your laptop: Your Android phone almost certainly uses an ARM processor, and your Windows laptop almost certainly uses x86-64. An app compiled for one does not directly run on the other, because their machine codes are different. That is why app stores ship different builds for different processors, and why this course is specifically about the x86 family.

Common mistakes: Students sometimes say the 8088 is an 8-bit processor; internally it is 16-bit, only its external data bus is 8 bits. Another mistake is thinking a 32-bit processor can only use 32 MB; 32 address bits give 4 GB. Some think the 80286 was 32-bit; it was 16-bit with protected mode. And some confuse word size (register width) with address bus width; the 8086 has 16-bit words but a 20-bit address bus.

What exams ask: Trace the evolution of Intel microprocessors with word size, data bus and address bus. Calculate memory size from address lines. Differentiate 8086 and 8088. Explain why the 8086 was a major step over the 8085. Short notes on Moore's law and backward compatibility.

Recap: The 4004 was 4-bit; the 8080 and 8085 were 8-bit with 64 KB; the 8086 was 16-bit with 1 MB; the 80286 added protected mode; the 80386 went 32-bit with paging; the 486 and Pentium added on-chip cache, FPU and multiple pipelines; AMD's x86-64 went 64-bit. Memory reach = 2^(address lines). The 8086's ideas live inside every modern PC. Next lesson: the buses that connect the processor to memory and devices.
key_points: Word size = bits processed at once; data bus = bits moved at once; address bus = how much memory can be named.
Memory reachable = 2^(number of address lines): 16 lines = 64 KB, 20 = 1 MB, 32 = 4 GB.
8086 (1978): 16-bit registers and data bus, 20-bit address bus, 1 MB; 8088 has an 8-bit external data bus.
80286 added protected mode; 80386 was the first 32-bit x86 with paging.
486 and Pentium added on-chip cache, FPU and multiple pipelines; AMD created x86-64.
RAX contains EAX, which contains AX (AH and AL).
x86 keeps backward compatibility; ARM dominates phones with a simpler low-power design.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with columns: chip, year, word size, address lines, max memory. Filling it once by hand fixes the whole history in your head without memorising.
lessons.task: Find the processor name of any laptop or desktop near you (on Windows: Settings > System > About). Search whether it is x86-64 or ARM, and write how many address bits would be needed for 16 GB of RAM (hint: 16 GB = 2^34 bytes).

It is an observation that transistor counts doubled roughly every two years

lessons.title: Buses: How the CPU Talks to Memory and Devices
lessons.content:
Imagine a big apartment building in Dhanmondi with 64 flats and one delivery man from a food app. To deliver a parcel he needs three things: the flat number (where), the parcel itself (what), and an instruction from the guard: "deliver" or "pick up" (which action). A microprocessor talks to memory and devices in exactly this way. It sends an address (where), moves data (what), and sends control signals (which action). The sets of wires that carry these three things are called buses.

What a bus is: A bus is a group of parallel wires shared by several chips, used to carry one kind of information. Each wire carries one bit at a time: high voltage for 1, low voltage for 0. A 16-wire bus carries 16 bits at once. Instead of connecting every chip to every other chip with its own private wires, all chips hang on the same shared bus, like all the flats in a building sharing one staircase.

The problem buses solve: Suppose a CPU had to talk to 10 memory chips and 5 device chips using private wires to each. That is 15 separate sets of 16 or 20 wires coming out of the CPU, which is impossible on a small chip with a limited number of pins. A shared bus uses one set of wires for all of them. The price is that only one chip can talk on the bus at a time, so there must be rules about who talks and when.

The three buses: A typical microprocessor system has an address bus, a data bus and a control bus. Together they are called the system bus. A simple text diagram: CPU on the left, and to its right three horizontal lines labelled ADDRESS, DATA and CONTROL, with memory chips and I/O chips hanging below these lines like clothes on a washing line. Every chip listens to the address and control lines; only the selected chip uses the data lines.

The address bus: The CPU puts a number on the address bus to say which memory location or which device it wants. It is one-way (unidirectional): only the CPU drives it, others listen. On the 8086 the address bus has 20 lines, named A0 to A19. With n lines the CPU can produce 2^n different addresses, so 20 lines give 2^20 = 1,048,576 addresses, which is 1 MB, because each address points to one byte.

Worked example on address width: A small system needs 32 KB of memory. How many address lines are needed? 32 KB = 32 x 1024 = 32,768 = 2^15, so 15 lines. If someone says a chip has 13 address lines, it holds 2^13 = 8,192 locations, which is 8 KB if each location is one byte. You will use this calculation again and again in memory interfacing (lesson 22).

The data bus: This bus carries the actual data: an instruction being fetched, a number being read, or a result being written. It is two-way (bidirectional): the CPU sends data on it during a write and receives data on it during a read. The 8086 has a 16-bit data bus, D0 to D15, so it can move one 16-bit word or one byte at a time. The 8088 has the same insides but only 8 external data lines.

The control bus: These lines tell everyone what kind of operation is happening and when. Important ones on the 8086 include RD (read, active low, meaning the signal is "on" when it is 0), WR (write, active low), M/IO (is this a memory access or an I/O access?), ALE (address latch enable, explained in lesson 7), READY (lets slow memory ask the CPU to wait), plus inputs like RESET, CLK (clock), INTR and NMI (interrupt requests). Unlike the other two buses, the control lines are a mixed group: some go out of the CPU, some come in.

Active low, a quick note: Many control signals work "upside down". A bar over the name, or a # or "bar" in writing, means the signal is active when the voltage is low. Why? Historically, with the logic chips of the time, pulling a line low was easier and more noise-resistant, and many chips share one line by pulling it low. Just remember: for RD-bar, 0 means "reading now", 1 means "not reading".

How a memory read works, step by step: Say the CPU wants the byte at address 01234h. Step 1: the CPU places 01234h on the address lines. Step 2: it sets M/IO to say "memory". Step 3: address decoding logic sees the address and enables the one memory chip that owns it; all others stay quiet. Step 4: the CPU pulls RD low. Step 5: the selected memory chip puts the stored byte on the data bus. Step 6: the CPU reads the data lines and stores the byte in a register. Step 7: the CPU releases RD, and the memory chip stops driving the data bus.

How a memory write works: Step 1: address on the address bus. Step 2: M/IO says memory. Step 3: the CPU itself drives the data bus with the value to store. Step 4: the CPU pulls WR low. Step 5: the selected memory chip copies the value from the data bus into the location. Step 6: WR goes high again. The only real differences from a read are who drives the data bus and which control line is used.

Who may talk, tri-state outputs: If two chips put different values on the same data wire at the same time, one pushes high and the other pushes low. That is called bus contention; the data becomes garbage and the chips can even overheat. The solution is tri-state outputs. Besides 0 and 1, a tri-state output has a third state, high impedance (often written Z), which is like being electrically disconnected. Every chip on the bus keeps its outputs in Z unless it has been selected and told to talk. So only one speaker at a time, like a classroom where only the student called by the teacher may answer.

Memory space and I/O space: The 8086 has two separate address spaces. The memory space is 1 MB, as we saw. The I/O space is for devices like keyboard controllers, timers and printer ports, and the 8086 can address up to 65,536 (64K) byte-wide I/O ports, using up to 16 address lines. The M/IO control line tells the system which space is meant. Special instructions IN and OUT are used for I/O ports, while MOV and friends are used for memory. Some systems instead place devices inside the memory space; that is called memory-mapped I/O, and lesson 23 compares the two.

Bus width and speed trade-offs: A wider data bus moves more bits per trip, so it is faster, but it needs more pins, more wires on the board and more cost. This is exactly why the 8088 existed: an 8-bit external data bus made IBM PC boards cheaper, at the cost of needing two trips to move one 16-bit word. A wider address bus reaches more memory but again needs more pins. Designers always balance speed, cost and size.

Why the 8086 shares pins: The 8086 package has only 40 pins. It needs 20 address lines, 16 data lines, power, ground, clock and many control lines, which is far more than 40. So the 8086 uses the same pins for the lower 16 address bits and the 16 data bits at different moments, called a multiplexed address/data bus (AD0 to AD15). First the pins carry the address, then the same pins carry data. Lesson 7 shows exactly how outside latches separate them. For now, just know the trick exists to save pins.

The full 8086 system, block by block: At the centre is the 8086 CPU. Around it: the 8284 clock generator, which supplies the clock and synchronises RESET and READY; address latches (such as the 74LS373) that hold the address steady; data bus transceivers (such as the 74LS245) that strengthen and direct the data signals; memory chips (ROM for start-up code, RAM for programs and data); and I/O chips like the 8255 for parallel ports, the 8253 timer and the 8259 interrupt controller. In larger systems the 8288 bus controller generates control signals. All of these sit on the shared buses.

What happens at power on: When the 8086 is reset, it sets CS to FFFFh and IP to 0000h, so the first instruction is fetched from physical address FFFF0h, 16 bytes below the top of the 1 MB space. That is why ROM containing start-up code (on PCs, the BIOS) is placed at the top of memory. You will see how the address FFFF0h comes from CS and IP in lesson 6.

Real life example 1, a load-shedding moment: When power returns after load-shedding and you switch on your desktop, the processor is reset. Its very first bus operation is a memory read at the top of the address space, where the BIOS ROM sits. Address on the address bus, RD goes low, ROM puts the first instruction bytes on the data bus. Every boot, every day, starts with that one bus read.

Real life example 2, a supermarket billing counter: The barcode scanner at a Shwapno or Agora checkout sends the code to the computer. The scanner's controller sits in the I/O space or on a serial line. The CPU uses I/O reads to collect the code, memory reads to look up the price table in RAM, and I/O writes to send the bill to the printer. Address bus says where, data bus carries the numbers, control bus says read or write, memory or I/O, all in microseconds.

When a bus design is not enough: A single shared bus becomes a bottleneck when many fast devices want it at the same time, because only one may talk. Modern PCs therefore use many separate, faster links (for example, a dedicated memory controller and point-to-point links like PCI Express) instead of one shared bus for everything. The 8086-style shared bus is still the right model for small embedded systems and for learning the basic idea.

Common mistakes: Saying the address bus is bidirectional; on a basic 8086 system the CPU drives it. Mixing up address bus width with data bus width when calculating memory size. Forgetting that each address names one byte, not one word. Forgetting that RD and WR are active low. Believing the data bus can carry two speakers at once; tri-state control exists precisely to stop that.

What exams ask: Define address, data and control buses, with direction. Calculate memory size from the number of address lines, or address lines from memory size. Explain the read and write operation sequence. Explain tri-state buffers and why they are needed. Explain the difference between memory space and I/O space in the 8086.

Recap: A bus is a shared set of wires. The address bus (A0-A19 on the 8086) says where and gives 1 MB of memory space; the data bus (D0-D15) carries the value in both directions; the control bus (RD, WR, M/IO, ALE, READY and others) says what and when. Tri-state outputs let only the selected chip talk. The 8086 has a separate 64K I/O port space used with IN and OUT, and it multiplexes address and data on the same pins. Next lesson: what is inside the 8086 chip itself.
key_points: A bus is a shared group of wires; each wire carries one bit.
Address bus says where, is driven by the CPU, and n lines give 2^n byte addresses (8086: 20 lines, 1 MB).
Data bus carries the value and is bidirectional (8086: 16 bits).
Control bus says what and when: RD, WR, M/IO, ALE, READY, RESET, CLK, INTR, NMI.
Read: address, M/IO, chip selected, RD low, chip drives data; write: CPU drives data, WR low.
Tri-state (high impedance) outputs prevent bus contention so only one chip talks at a time.
8086 has a separate 64K I/O port space accessed by IN/OUT.
8086 multiplexes AD0-AD15 to save pins; it starts at FFFF0h after reset.
lessons.tip: For every bus question, ask: who drives this line, who listens, and when. Directions and timing are where most exam marks are lost.
lessons.task: Draw the 8086 system block diagram on paper from memory: CPU, clock generator, latches, transceivers, ROM, RAM and three I/O chips on the three buses. Then label the direction of each bus with arrows.

Which bus is bidirectional in a basic 8086 system?
quiz.explain: Data flows into the CPU on reads and out of it on writes.

quiz.q: What problem do tri-state outputs solve?
options: Two chips driving the same bus line at once
quiz.explain: Unselected chips go to high impedance so only one chip drives the bus.

quiz.q: What does the M/IO signal tell the system?
options: Whether the bus cycle is a read or write
Whether the access is to memory or to an I/O port
quiz.explain: Read vs write is shown by RD/WR; M/IO picks memory space or I/O space.

options: To save pins on its 40-pin package
To make memory larger than 1 MB
quiz.explain: Sharing pins over time saves 16 pins.

lessons.title: Inside the 8086: BIU, EU and the Instruction Queue
lessons.content:
Think of a busy biryani shop in Old Dhaka. If the cook had to go to the bazar himself every time he needed rice or meat, cooking would stop again and again. So the shop has two people: a helper who keeps bringing ingredients from the store room and lines them up on a shelf, and a cook who just picks the next item from the shelf and cooks. While the cook is busy, the helper is already fetching the next things. The 8086 is built exactly like this shop, with two units working side by side.

What this lesson covers: In lesson 1 we said every CPU has an ALU, a control unit and registers. Now we open the 8086 and see how Intel arranged those parts. The 8086 is split into two units: the Bus Interface Unit (BIU), the helper who deals with the outside world, and the Execution Unit (EU), the cook who actually runs instructions. Between them sits a small shelf called the instruction queue.

The problem: In a simple processor such as the 8085, the CPU first fetches an instruction from memory, then executes it, then fetches the next one, then executes it. While it executes, the buses sit idle. While it fetches, the ALU sits idle. Memory access was slow compared with the CPU, so a lot of time was wasted waiting. Intel wanted the 8086 to keep both the buses and the ALU busy as much as possible.

The solution in one sentence: Let one unit fetch instructions ahead of time while the other unit executes the current instruction. This overlap of fetching and executing is a simple form of pipelining. Computer Architecture covers pipelines in depth; the 8086 only has this simple two-part overlap, but it was a big step for its time.

The Bus Interface Unit (BIU): The BIU handles every contact with the outside world through the buses. Its jobs are: fetch instruction bytes from memory, read and write data operands in memory or I/O when the EU asks, and calculate the 20-bit physical address. Inside the BIU are the four segment registers (CS, DS, SS, ES), the instruction pointer (IP), an address adder that forms 20-bit addresses, the instruction queue, and the bus control logic that drives the pins.

The address adder: The 8086's registers are 16 bits, but its addresses are 20 bits. The BIU contains a dedicated adder that shifts a segment value left by 4 bits (multiplying it by 16) and adds a 16-bit offset to it. For example, segment 2000h and offset 0010h give 20000h + 0010h = 20010h. Lesson 6 explains segmentation fully. Here, remember that this calculation happens inside the BIU, not in the main ALU, so it does not slow down the EU.

The instruction queue: The 8086 has a 6-byte first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue. The BIU keeps filling it with the next instruction bytes from memory. On the 8086, the BIU fetches whenever at least 2 bytes of the queue are empty, because it reads a 16-bit word at a time. The EU takes bytes from the front of the queue. The 8088, with its 8-bit external data bus, has a smaller 4-byte queue and fetches whenever 1 byte is empty.

Why the queue works: Most of the time, programs run straight down, one instruction after another. So the bytes coming next in memory are very likely the bytes that will be needed next. By the time the EU finishes one instruction, the next one is usually already waiting in the queue, and no time is spent on fetching. This guessing that "the next bytes are the ones we need" is called prefetching.

The Execution Unit (EU): The EU decodes and executes instructions. It contains the ALU (16-bit, for arithmetic and logic), the general registers AX, BX, CX and DX, the pointer and index registers SP, BP, SI and DI, the flags register, and the control circuitry and instruction decoder. Importantly, the EU has no direct connection to the system buses. If it needs data from memory, it asks the BIU to do the bus cycle.

Byte and word work in the ALU: The ALU is 16 bits wide, but it can also work on 8-bit values. ADD AL, BL adds two bytes and ADD AX, BX adds two words. The instruction itself carries a bit that tells the EU whether this is a byte or a word operation, so the same adder hardware serves both. This matters later when you see that MOV AL, 300 is an error: 300 does not fit in 8 bits (the largest 8-bit unsigned value is 255).

The decoder and control circuitry: When the EU takes the first byte of an instruction from the queue, the decoder works out what kind of instruction it is and how many more bytes belong to it. 8086 instructions vary from 1 to 6 bytes long. The control circuitry then generates the internal steps: which register to read, what the ALU should do, where to store the result, and whether the BIU must be asked for a memory operand. The 8086 implements many of these steps using microcode, a small internal program stored inside the chip.

A text diagram of the whole chip: Picture two boxes side by side. The left box, labelled BIU, contains CS, DS, SS, ES, IP, the address adder and the 6-byte queue, and the external buses come out of its left side toward memory. An arrow from the queue goes right into the second box, labelled EU, which contains the decoder and control, AX, BX, CX, DX, SP, BP, SI, DI, the ALU and the flags. A 16-bit internal bus connects the two boxes so that data can pass both ways.

Step by step, an execution trace: Suppose memory holds MOV AX, 5 (3 bytes), ADD AX, BX (2 bytes) and MOV [2000h], AX (3 bytes). Time 1: the queue is empty, so the EU waits while the BIU fetches the first bytes. Time 2: the EU decodes and executes MOV AX, 5; meanwhile the BIU fetches the bytes of ADD AX, BX. Time 3: the EU executes ADD AX, BX straight from the queue; meanwhile the BIU fetches the next instruction. Time 4: the EU starts MOV [2000h], AX and needs to write to memory, so it hands the address and data to the BIU, which pauses prefetching, performs the write bus cycle, then goes back to filling the queue.

When the queue is thrown away: Prefetching assumes the program runs in a straight line. If the EU executes a jump, a call, a return or an interrupt, the program continues somewhere else. The bytes in the queue then belong to the wrong place. The 8086 simply discards (flushes) the queue, and the BIU starts fetching from the new address. Until the first new bytes arrive, the EU has to wait. That is why many jumps in a tight loop cost extra time on the 8086.

Who decides priority: The BIU has two kinds of work: prefetching instructions and doing data transfers requested by the EU. Data requests from the EU are given priority, because the EU is actually waiting for them. Prefetching fills the remaining free bus time. A good way to see it: the helper in the biryani shop stops refilling the shelf whenever the cook shouts "bring the yogurt now!".

How much speed it gives: The gain depends on the program. Code with long straight runs of simple instructions benefits most, because instruction fetches are almost fully hidden behind execution. Code with many jumps, or with many memory operands that keep the bus busy, benefits less. So the queue does not make the 8086 twice as fast in every case; it simply removes a lot of waiting in the common case.

The flags register's place: The flags register lives in the EU because flags are produced by the ALU after operations, for example the zero flag after a subtraction that gives 0. Conditional jumps read these flags. Lesson 5 explains each flag. Notice how the design follows the job: things produced by computation live with the ALU; things that touch memory addresses live with the bus unit.

When this design is a good idea: Splitting fetching from execution is useful whenever memory is slower than the processor and programs mostly run in order. That describes almost every computer, which is why modern processors use much deeper versions of the same idea, with many pipeline stages, caches and branch prediction to guess where jumps will go.

When it helps less: In code full of jumps, each jump flushes the queue. In code that constantly reads and writes memory operands, the bus is busy with data and has little time to prefetch. Also, the 8086 does not predict branches: it always prefetches the next sequential bytes, so every taken jump costs a refill.

Real life example 1, a garments factory line: In a Gazipur garments factory, one worker brings cut pieces from the cutting section and stacks them next to the sewing machine operator, while the operator stitches. The operator never walks to the cutting section. If the supervisor suddenly says "stop, switch to the other design", the stacked pieces are useless and must be cleared, and the operator waits until new pieces arrive. Stack = queue, carrier = BIU, operator = EU, design change = jump.

Real life example 2, watching a YouTube video: When you watch a video on a slow mobile connection, the app downloads a few seconds ahead (buffering) while you watch the current part. Normally playback is smooth. If you jump to a different minute in the video, the buffered part is thrown away and you see the loading circle until new data arrives. That is exactly the 8086 queue: prefetch ahead, and flush on a jump.

Where the analogy breaks: The YouTube buffer and the 8086 queue are similar in idea but not in size or timing. The queue holds only 6 bytes, which is just two or three instructions, and refilling it takes a few clock cycles, not seconds. Also the 8086 does not keep bytes it might need later; once flushed, they are gone.

Common mistakes: Saying the queue is in the EU; it is in the BIU. Saying the 8086 queue is 4 bytes; that is the 8088 (the 8086 has 6). Thinking the EU can access memory itself; it always goes through the BIU. Forgetting that the queue is flushed on jumps, calls, returns and interrupts. Thinking segment registers are in the EU; they are in the BIU because they are used to form addresses.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the internal architecture of the 8086 (BIU and EU). Explain the role of the instruction queue and how pipelining is achieved. List the registers in each unit. Explain what happens to the queue after a JMP. Compare the 8086 and 8088 queues.

Recap: The 8086 has two units. The BIU contains segment registers, IP, the address adder and the 6-byte queue, and does every bus operation. The EU contains the general, pointer and index registers, the ALU, flags and decoder, and executes instructions. While the EU executes, the BIU prefetches, which is a simple two-stage pipeline. A jump flushes the queue. Next lesson: every 8086 register and every flag, with examples.
key_points: The 8086 has two units: the Bus Interface Unit (BIU) and the Execution Unit (EU).
BIU: segment registers, IP, address adder, 6-byte instruction queue, bus control; does every bus cycle.
EU: ALU, AX/BX/CX/DX, SP/BP/SI/DI, flags, decoder and control; has no direct bus access.
The BIU prefetches while the EU executes, a simple two-stage pipeline.
The 8086 queue is 6 bytes and refills when 2 bytes are free; the 8088 queue is 4 bytes.
Jumps, calls, returns and interrupts flush the queue, costing time.
EU data requests get priority over prefetching.
lessons.tip: Draw the BIU and EU boxes from memory and write which register goes in which box. If you can explain why each register sits where it does, you will not forget it.
lessons.task: Write five instructions on paper in a column, including one JMP in the middle. Draw a time line showing what the EU and BIU do at each step, and mark the moment the queue is flushed.

quiz.explain: The BIU fills the queue; the EU reads from it.

quiz.q: What is the size of the 8086 instruction queue?
quiz.explain: The 8086 has 6 bytes; the 8088 has 4.

quiz.q: What happens to the queue when a JMP is executed?
options: It is flushed and refilled from the new address
It is saved on the stack
quiz.explain: The prefetched bytes are from the wrong place, so they are discarded.

quiz.q: Which unit calculates the 20-bit physical address?
quiz.explain: The BIU has its own adder for segment x 16 + offset.

quiz.q: Why does the EU not access memory directly?
options: All bus operations are handled by the BIU
quiz.explain: Only the BIU is connected to the external buses.

lessons.title: 8086 Registers and the Flags Register
lessons.content:
Think of a cashier at a busy medicine shop in Farmgate. On the counter in front of him are a few small trays: one for the current total, one for the customer's cash, one for counting items, one for change. He also has a little sticky note where he marks things like "this customer owes money" or "total was zero". He does not run to the back room for every number; the trays are right in front of him. The 8086's registers are those trays, and its flags register is that sticky note.

What a register is: A register is a tiny storage location inside the CPU itself. Reading or writing a register takes no bus cycle at all, so it is much faster than memory. The catch: there are very few of them. The 8086 has fourteen 16-bit registers in total. Learning what each one is for is the single most important step in learning 8086 assembly, because almost every instruction names at least one register.

The four groups: The 8086 registers fall into four groups. General-purpose (data) registers: AX, BX, CX, DX. Pointer and index registers: SP, BP, SI, DI. Segment registers: CS, DS, SS, ES. And two special ones: IP (instruction pointer) and the FLAGS register. Count them: 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14.

Splitting into halves: Each general-purpose register is 16 bits but can also be used as two 8-bit registers. AX splits into AH (high byte, bits 15 to 8) and AL (low byte, bits 7 to 0). Similarly BX into BH and BL, CX into CH and CL, DX into DH and DL. Example: if AX = 1234h, then AH = 12h and AL = 34h. If you then do MOV AL, 0FFh, AX becomes 12FFh. Changing a half changes the whole, because they are the same physical bits. SI, DI, SP, BP and the segment registers cannot be split.

AX, the accumulator: AX is the main worker for arithmetic. Some instructions use it automatically: MUL and DIV always use AX (and DX), and IN and OUT move data through AL or AX. Many instructions also have shorter machine code when they use AX, so programmers prefer it for heavy calculation.

BX, the base register: BX can hold a memory address. MOV AL, [BX] means "read the byte at the address stored in BX". Among AX, BX, CX and DX, only BX can be used inside square brackets to point at memory on the 8086. Think of BX as a finger pointing at a row in a table.

CX, the count register: CX is the counter. The LOOP instruction automatically decreases CX and repeats while it is not zero, and string instructions with REP repeat CX times. Shift and rotate instructions use CL as the count when shifting more than once, for example SHL AX, CL. If you want something done 10 times, you put 10 in CX.

DX, the data register: DX helps AX with big arithmetic. When you multiply two 16-bit numbers, the 32-bit answer is stored in DX:AX (DX holds the high half). When you divide a 32-bit number, the dividend is in DX:AX. DX also holds the port number in IN and OUT when the port is above 255, for example MOV DX, 3F8h then IN AL, DX.

SP and BP, the stack pointers: SP (stack pointer) always points to the top of the stack, an area of memory used for temporary storage and for function calls. PUSH and POP change SP automatically. BP (base pointer) is used to reach values inside the stack, such as function parameters, with addresses like [BP+4]. By default, addresses using BP or SP are in the stack segment. Lessons 16 and 17 go deep into both.

SI and DI, the index registers: SI (source index) and DI (destination index) are mainly used to walk through arrays and strings. String instructions read from DS:SI and write to ES:DI, moving SI and DI forward or backward automatically. They can also be used like BX inside brackets: MOV AL, [SI].

Segment registers and IP, briefly: CS (code segment), DS (data segment), SS (stack segment) and ES (extra segment) each hold the start of a 64 KB block of memory. IP holds the offset of the next instruction inside the code segment, so CS:IP together always point at the next instruction to fetch. You cannot write MOV IP, 100h; IP only changes through jumps, calls, returns and interrupts. Lesson 6 explains segments in full.

The FLAGS register: FLAGS is a 16-bit register, but the 8086 uses only 9 of its bits. Six are status flags that the ALU sets after an operation to describe the result: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF. Three are control flags that the programmer sets to change how the CPU behaves: TF, IF and DF. Bit positions: CF is bit 0, PF bit 2, AF bit 4, ZF bit 6, SF bit 7, TF bit 8, IF bit 9, DF bit 10, OF bit 11.

The status flags one by one: CF (carry flag) is 1 if an addition carried out of the top bit, or a subtraction needed a borrow; it is the overflow signal for unsigned numbers. PF (parity flag) is 1 if the low 8 bits of the result contain an even number of 1s. AF (auxiliary carry) is 1 if there was a carry or borrow between bit 3 and bit 4, used by BCD arithmetic. ZF (zero flag) is 1 if the result is exactly zero. SF (sign flag) copies the top bit of the result, which is 1 for a negative number in two's complement. OF (overflow flag) is 1 if the result is wrong when the numbers are treated as signed.

Worked example 1: MOV AL, 0FFh then ADD AL, 1. In binary, 1111 1111 + 0000 0001 = 1 0000 0000. AL keeps only 8 bits, so AL = 00h and the extra 1 goes out: CF = 1. The result is zero: ZF = 1. Top bit is 0: SF = 0. The low nibble F + 1 carried into bit 4: AF = 1. 00h has zero 1-bits, which is even: PF = 1. As signed numbers, -1 + 1 = 0 is correct: OF = 0. One instruction, six flags.

Worked example 2: MOV AL, 7Fh then ADD AL, 1. 0111 1111 + 1 = 1000 0000 = 80h. No carry out of bit 7: CF = 0. Not zero: ZF = 0. Top bit 1: SF = 1. Low nibble F + 1 carried: AF = 1. 80h has one 1-bit, odd: PF = 0. As signed numbers, 127 + 1 should be 128, but 8-bit signed numbers only go up to 127, and 80h means -128. The answer is wrong as signed: OF = 1.

Carry vs overflow, the key idea: CF and OF answer two different questions about the same bits. CF asks: "if these were unsigned numbers (0 to 255), did the answer fit?" OF asks: "if these were signed numbers (-128 to 127), did the answer fit?" The CPU does not know which kind you meant; it sets both, and you check the one that matches your data. A quick rule for OF in addition: it is set when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign.

Worked example 3, subtraction: MOV AL, 5 then SUB AL, 7. 5 - 7 = -2, stored as FEh (1111 1110). A borrow was needed: CF = 1. Not zero: ZF = 0. Top bit 1: SF = 1. As signed, 5 - 7 = -2 is correct: OF = 0. The low nibble 5 - 7 also needed a borrow: AF = 1. FEh has seven 1-bits, odd: PF = 0. This is how the CPU will later answer "is 5 below 7?": CF = 1 means yes for unsigned numbers.

The control flags: TF (trap flag) puts the CPU in single-step mode: after every instruction it raises an internal interrupt, which debuggers use to run your program one line at a time. IF (interrupt flag) decides whether the CPU accepts hardware interrupts on the INTR pin: STI sets it, CLI clears it. DF (direction flag) decides whether string instructions move forward (DF = 0, after CLD) or backward (DF = 1, after STD). CF can also be set by hand with STC, cleared with CLC and flipped with CMC.

Which instructions change flags: Arithmetic and logic instructions (ADD, SUB, CMP, AND, OR and so on) update the status flags. MOV, PUSH, POP (except POPF) and jumps do not change flags at all. This surprises beginners: after MOV AX, 0 the zero flag does not become 1. If you want to test whether AX is zero, use CMP AX, 0 or OR AX, AX.

Real life example 1, a mobile recharge shop: A shopkeeper's program adds up the day's recharges in AX. At some point the total goes past 65,535 taka, the largest unsigned 16-bit value. AX wraps around to a small number and CF becomes 1. A careful program checks CF after each ADD and carries the overflow into DX, building a 32-bit total. A careless one shows the shopkeeper a tiny total and a lot of confusion. That is exactly why the carry flag exists.

Real life example 2, a temperature controller in a cold storage: A cold storage for potatoes in Munshiganj keeps a temperature reading as a signed byte, for example -5 degrees stored as FBh. The controller subtracts the target from the reading and checks SF to see whether the room is colder (negative) or warmer (positive) than required, and ZF to see whether it is exactly on target. Here OF and SF matter, not CF, because the data is signed.

Common mistakes: Thinking MOV sets the zero flag. Using CF to check signed overflow (use OF). Forgetting that changing AL changes AX. Trying to split SI or BP into halves. Mixing up PF: it checks the number of 1-bits in the low byte, not whether the number is even. Writing MOV IP, value, which is not allowed. Forgetting that MUL and DIV silently use DX too, which destroys whatever you had stored there.

What exams ask: List the 8086 registers with their special uses. Draw the flags register with bit positions and explain each flag. Find the flag values after a given ADD or SUB (exactly like the worked examples). Differentiate carry and overflow. Explain the purpose of TF, IF and DF.

Recap: The 8086 has 14 registers: AX, BX, CX, DX (splittable into 8-bit halves), SP, BP, SI, DI, CS, DS, SS, ES, IP and FLAGS. AX does arithmetic and I/O, BX points to memory, CX counts, DX extends AX and holds port numbers. SI and DI walk through arrays, SP and BP manage the stack. Six status flags describe the last result; three control flags change CPU behaviour. CF is for unsigned overflow, OF for signed. Next lesson: how segment registers turn 16-bit values into 20-bit addresses.
key_points: 14 registers: AX, BX, CX, DX, SP, BP, SI, DI, CS, DS, SS, ES, IP, FLAGS.
AX, BX, CX, DX split into 8-bit halves (AH/AL and so on); changing a half changes the whole.
AX: accumulator for MUL/DIV and I/O; BX: base pointer to memory; CX: counter (LOOP, REP, CL for shifts); DX: high half of products and port numbers.
SP points to the stack top, BP reaches stack data, SI/DI index arrays and strings.
Status flags: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF; control flags: TF, IF, DF.
CF signals unsigned overflow; OF signals signed overflow.
MOV, PUSH, POP and jumps do not change flags.
CS:IP always points at the next instruction; IP changes only through jumps, calls, returns and interrupts.
lessons.tip: For flag questions, always write the operation in binary first. Then read off CF from the carry out, ZF from zero, SF from the top bit, PF by counting 1s in the low byte, AF from bit 3 to bit 4, and OF from the signs.
lessons.task: On paper, compute all six status flags for: ADD AL, BL with AL = 64h and BL = 9Ch, and SUB AL, BL with AL = 30h and BL = 30h. Then check each answer by explaining it in one sentence.

quiz.q: If AX = 1234h and you execute MOV AL, 0FFh, what is AX?
quiz.explain: Only the low byte changes; AH stays 12h.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 7Fh and ADD AL, 1, which flag shows a signed error?
quiz.explain: 127 + 1 does not fit in a signed byte, so OF = 1.

quiz.q: Which register is automatically used as the counter by LOOP?
quiz.explain: LOOP decrements CX and jumps while it is not zero.

quiz.q: Which instruction does NOT change any flags?
quiz.explain: MOV only copies; it never updates flags.

quiz.q: What does DF = 1 do?
options: Makes string instructions move backward through memory
quiz.explain: DF controls the direction of string instructions; STD sets it.

lessons.title: Memory Segmentation: Segment, Offset and Physical Address
lessons.content:
Imagine a huge apartment area in Mirpur with one million flats. Every flat has a number from 0 to 999,999. Now imagine the postman is only allowed to carry slips that hold four digits, so the biggest number he can write is 9,999. How will he ever deliver a letter to flat 523,417? One clever trick: write the address in two parts, "Block 52, flat 3,417". The block tells him roughly where to go, the flat number tells him exactly which door. The Intel 8086 faced exactly this problem, and the trick it used is called memory segmentation.

The problem in numbers: The 8086 has a 20-bit address bus. With 20 wires, each 0 or 1, it can name 2^20 = 1,048,576 different bytes, which is 1 MB. In hex those addresses go from 00000h to FFFFFh. But every register inside the 8086 is only 16 bits wide. A 16-bit number can only count from 0000h to FFFFh, which is 65,536 values, or 64 KB. So no single register can hold a full 20-bit address. The CPU can talk to 1 MB, but its own pockets can only hold numbers up to 64 KB. Something has to bridge that gap.

How it was done before: The older 8080 and 8085 chips had 16-bit addresses and 16-bit pointer registers. Life was simple: one register held one full address, and memory was a flat 64 KB. But 64 KB was becoming too small by the late 1970s. Intel wanted more memory without making every register bigger, and without breaking the style of the older chips too much. Segmentation was the answer.

What a segment is: A segment is a window of memory up to 64 KB long. The 8086 keeps the starting point of four such windows in four segment registers: CS (code segment, where instructions live), DS (data segment, where normal variables live), SS (stack segment, where the stack lives) and ES (extra segment, often used as a second data area and for string destinations). Inside a window, a 16-bit offset tells how far from the start you are. So a full address is written as a pair, segment:offset, for example 2000:0150. This pair is called the logical address. The real 20-bit number that goes out on the address bus is called the physical address.

The magic formula: Physical address = segment x 16 + offset. Multiplying by 16 is the same as shifting the number left by 4 bits, which in hex simply means sticking a 0 on the right. So segment 2000h becomes 20000h. Then add the offset: 20000h + 0150h = 20150h. That is the physical address. The adder that does this lives in the Bus Interface Unit, and it does the job for every single memory access, so you never do it by hand in a real program, but you must be able to do it in exams.

Worked example 1: CS = 2000h and IP = 0150h. The next instruction is fetched from 20000h + 0150h = 20150h. Worked example 2: DS = 1234h and a variable is at offset 0022h. Shift: 12340h. Add: 12340h + 0022h = 12362h. Worked example 3: SS = 3000h, SP = FFFEh. Physical = 30000h + FFFEh = 3FFFEh. Notice how in example 2 the segment's last digit, 4, is not lost. It moves one place left and becomes part of the address. Students who forget the shift and simply add 1234h + 0022h = 1256h get a completely wrong answer.

Picture it like this: think of memory as a long ladder of 1,048,576 steps. A segment register points at one step, and only steps whose number is a multiple of 16 can be pointed at. These 16-byte boundaries are called paragraphs. From that starting step, the offset lets you climb up to 65,535 more steps. In a little text diagram: 00000h ... [ 20000h = start of segment 2000h ... 20150h = offset 0150h ... 2FFFFh = end of segment ] ... FFFFFh. So segment 2000h covers 20000h to 2FFFFh, exactly 64 KB.

Segments can overlap: Because a segment can start at any paragraph, two segments can easily cover the same bytes. Segment 1000h covers 10000h to 1FFFFh, and segment 1001h covers 10010h to 2000Fh. They share almost everything. This also means one physical address has many logical names. 1000:0020 gives 10000h + 0020h = 10020h. 1002:0000 gives 10020h + 0000h = 10020h. Same byte, two names. It is like saying "the third shop after the mosque" or "the first shop after the pharmacy" and both mean the same tea stall. In exams they sometimes ask how many segment:offset pairs can point to one address; for most addresses the answer is 4096, because the segment can be any of 4096 consecutive values whose window still reaches that byte.

Going backwards: Sometimes you know the physical address and the offset and need the segment. Example: physical 4A3F5h, offset 00F5h. Subtract: 4A3F5h - 00F5h = 4A300h. Remove the last hex 0 (divide by 16): segment = 4A30h. Check: 4A300h + 00F5h = 4A3F5h. Correct. If the subtraction does not end in 0, the offset cannot be paired with any segment for that address, because segments must start on a 16-byte boundary.

Default segment pairs: The CPU does not make you name the segment every time. Each kind of access has a default partner. Instructions are always fetched from CS:IP. Stack operations (PUSH, POP, CALL, RET) use SS:SP. Any memory operand that uses BP as its base also defaults to SS, because BP is meant for reading values on the stack. Ordinary data accesses using BX, SI, DI or a plain variable name default to DS. String instructions read their source from DS:SI and write their destination to ES:DI. A small table to remember: CS with IP, SS with SP and BP, DS with BX, SI, DI and direct addresses, ES with DI for strings.

Segment override: If the default is not what you want, you can put a segment override prefix in front of an operand. MOV AX, ES:[BX] reads from ES:BX instead of DS:BX. MOV AL, CS:[SI] reads a byte from the code segment, which is handy for a lookup table stored next to the code. The assembler turns the override into a one-byte prefix placed before the instruction, so it costs a little extra size and time. Some defaults cannot be overridden: instruction fetch is always CS:IP, stack push and pop are always SS:SP, and the destination of string instructions is always ES:DI.

Why segmentation was useful: First, it reached 1 MB with 16-bit registers. Second, it made programs easy to relocate. If a program only uses offsets inside its own segments, DOS can load it anywhere in memory and just set CS, DS and SS to the right values. The program never notices. Third, it separates code, data and stack cleanly, so a quick look at the registers tells you where each part lives. Fourth, inside one segment a pointer is just 16 bits, which saves space and time on a 16-bit machine.

The price you pay: No single object can be bigger than 64 KB without extra work, because an offset cannot go past FFFFh. Pointers come in two kinds: a near pointer is only an offset (16 bits, inside the current segment), and a far pointer is segment plus offset (32 bits). Mixing them caused many bugs in old DOS C programs, and compilers offered memory models such as small and large to choose how pointers behave. Also, because many logical addresses map to the same byte, comparing two far pointers is not as simple as comparing numbers.

The edge of the world: What about FFFF:0010? Shift: FFFF0h. Add 0010h: 100000h, which needs 21 bits. The 8086 only has 20 address lines, so the top bit simply falls off and the address wraps around to 00000h. Later chips with more address lines did not wrap, which became a famous compatibility headache in PCs, but that story belongs to later processors.

Little endian, how bytes sit inside memory: Memory is organised in bytes, but a word is 2 bytes. When the 8086 stores a word, it puts the low byte at the lower address and the high byte at the next address. This is called little endian. If DS = 2000h and you execute MOV WORD PTR [0100h], 1234h, then physical address 20100h gets 34h and 20101h gets 12h. When the CPU reads the word back, it puts them together again correctly as 1234h. Think of writing the taka amount 1234 on two sticky notes and sticking the "34" note first. Odd, but consistent.

Why little endian matters: If you look at a memory dump in a debugger and see bytes 34 12, you must read them as 1234h, not 3412h. A double word like 12345678h is stored as 78 56 34 12. Other machines, and network protocols, often use big endian, the opposite order, so programmers converting data between systems have to swap bytes. Getting this wrong gives numbers that look like garbage.

A typical program's layout: When DOS loads a small .EXE program, it might look like this. CS = 0B50h holds the code, DS = 0B60h holds the variables, SS = 0B70h holds the stack. Physical code start 0B500h, data start 0B600h, stack start 0B700h. Each segment only uses as much space as needed, and they sit one after another. Note that segments do not have to be a full 64 KB; 64 KB is just the maximum an offset can reach.

Real life example 1, the bus counter at Gabtoli: A ticket counter writes seat numbers as "coach number : seat number". Coach 12, seat 30. Coaches are the segments, seats are offsets. The same seat could also be described from a different coach number if coaches overlapped, which would confuse passengers, and that is exactly why programmers usually keep their segments separate. A conductor who knows only seat numbers inside his coach is like an instruction using only an offset; he relies on the coach (segment register) already being set.

Real life example 2, loading a game in an old cyber cafe: In the 1990s, DOS games in Dhaka cyber cafes were loaded at whatever free memory address was available. The same game file could run at segment 1A00h one day and 2300h the next, because DOS just set the segment registers differently. The game's code only used offsets, so it worked both times. That is relocation through segmentation in action.

When to use it, and when not: You use segment:offset thinking whenever you write 8086 real mode code, read DOS or BIOS documentation, or work with old embedded x86 boards. You do not use this style on modern 64-bit operating systems; there, programs see one big flat address space, and the operating system uses paging instead. Even 32-bit protected mode changed the meaning of segment registers, making them selectors into tables. So treat segment x 16 + offset as the rule of the 8086 world, not of every x86 machine.

Common mistakes: Adding segment and offset without shifting. Forgetting that hex digits go up to F, so carrying wrongly in hex addition. Thinking a segment is always exactly 64 KB in use. Forgetting that BP defaults to SS, not DS, so [BP+2] reads the stack. Writing words to memory and expecting the high byte first. And trying to load a segment register with an immediate value like MOV DS, 2000h, which is not allowed; you go through a general register: MOV AX, 2000h then MOV DS, AX.

What exams ask: Calculate the physical address for given segment and offset values. Find the range covered by a segment. Find a segment from a physical address and offset. Show that two logical addresses map to the same physical address. Name the default segment for an operand such as [BP+SI] (answer: SS) or [BX+DI] (answer: DS). Explain advantages and disadvantages of segmentation. Show how a word is stored in little endian.

Recap: The 8086 needs 20-bit addresses but has 16-bit registers. It solves this by combining a segment register and an offset: physical address = segment x 16 + offset. Segments start on 16-byte paragraphs and reach at most 64 KB. They can overlap, so many logical addresses can name one byte. Each kind of access has a default segment, and you can override it with a prefix. Words are stored low byte first. With this map in your head, the next lessons on pins and addressing modes will make much more sense.
key_points: The 8086 has a 20-bit address bus (1 MB) but 16-bit registers (64 KB each).
Physical address = segment x 16 + offset, e.g. 2000:0150 = 20150h.
Four segment registers: CS (code), DS (data), SS (stack), ES (extra).
Segments start on 16-byte paragraphs, are at most 64 KB and can overlap.
Defaults: CS:IP, SS:SP, SS:BP, DS:BX/SI/DI, ES:DI for string destinations.
A segment override prefix like ES:[BX] changes the default segment.
Little endian: the low byte of a word is stored at the lower address.
Segmentation made relocation easy but limited each object to 64 KB.
lessons.tip: For any physical address question, write the segment with an extra 0 on the right first, then add the offset in hex column by column. This one habit kills most mistakes.
lessons.task: On paper, compute the physical addresses for 1000:0020, 1002:0000 and 0FFF:0030. Then write the 4 bytes of the double word 12345678h as they would sit in memory from address 20100h upward.

quiz.q: What is the physical address of DS = 1234h, offset = 0022h?
quiz.explain: 12340h + 0022h = 12362h; the segment is shifted left by one hex digit first.

quiz.q: Which segment does MOV AX, [BP+4] use by default?
quiz.explain: BP-based operands default to the stack segment.

quiz.q: Which pair gives the same physical address as 1000:0020?
How is the word 1234h stored at address 20100h?
quiz.explain: Little endian: low byte at the lower address.

quiz.q: Why does a segment cover at most 64 KB?
quiz.explain: An offset goes from 0000h to FFFFh, which is 65,536 bytes.

lessons.title: 8086 Pins and Bus Cycles
lessons.content:
Think of a busy shop in Bongo Bazar with only one narrow door. In the morning, the shopkeeper uses the door to let in a delivery man who shouts the name of the shop where goods must go. A moment later the same door is used to pass the actual boxes. One door, two jobs, at different moments. The 8086 chip does something very similar with its pins. It has only 40 legs, but it needs to send out 20 address bits, move 16 data bits and control a whole system. To fit, some pins carry an address first and data a moment later. Understanding these pins and this timing is what lets you connect a real 8086 to memory and devices.

What a pin is and why the count matters: A chip talks to the outside world only through its metal legs, called pins. Each pin is one wire that is either high (around 5 volts for the 8086) or low (around 0 volts) at any moment. The 8086 came in a 40-pin package because that was a common, cheap package in 1978. Count what it needs: 20 address lines, 16 data lines, power, ground, clock, reset, interrupt lines and read/write control lines. That is far more than 40. So Intel had to share pins. This sharing is called multiplexing.

The multiplexed pins: AD0 to AD15 are sixteen pins that carry address bits A0 to A15 at the start of a bus cycle and data bits D0 to D15 later in the same cycle. A16/S3 to A19/S6 carry the top four address bits first, then status information. BHE/S7 carries the Bus High Enable signal first and a status bit later. The status bits S3 and S4 tell which segment register is being used for the access, and S5 shows the state of the interrupt flag.

The other important pins, briefly: VCC is the 5 volt supply and there are two GND pins. CLK is the clock input. RESET restarts the chip. READY lets slow memory ask the CPU to wait. INTR is the normal interrupt request, NMI the non-maskable interrupt, and INTA (in minimum mode) acknowledges an interrupt. TEST is checked by the WAIT instruction. HOLD and HLDA let another bus master, such as a DMA controller, borrow the bus. RD goes low when the CPU wants to read, WR goes low when it writes. M/IO tells whether the access is to memory (high) or to an I/O port (low). MN/MX picks the operating mode. Interrupts and DMA get their own lessons later, so here we focus on reading and writing.

The problem multiplexing creates: Memory chips need the address to stay steady during the whole read or write. But on AD0 to AD15 the address disappears after a moment because the same pins start carrying data. If nothing is done, the memory would see the address vanish halfway through. The solution is a latch: a small chip that grabs the address and holds it on its own output pins.

ALE, the address catcher: ALE stands for Address Latch Enable. The 8086 pulses ALE high at the beginning of each bus cycle, exactly while the address is on the pins. External latches, such as the 8282 or the common 74LS373, use this pulse to capture the address. When ALE falls, the latches hold the address steady for the rest of the cycle, even though the AD pins are now free to carry data. Three 8-bit latches are typically used to hold A0 to A19 plus BHE.

Transceivers for data: On the data side, the 8086 often uses bidirectional buffers called transceivers, like the 8286 or 74LS245. They strengthen the signals so many chips can be connected. Two CPU pins control them. DT/R (data transmit/receive) sets the direction: high means data flows out from the CPU (a write), low means data flows in (a read). DEN (data enable, active low) switches the transceivers on only during the data part of the cycle, so they do not fight with the address.

The demultiplexed system as a picture: 8086 AD0-AD15, A16-A19 ---> [latches, clocked by ALE] ---> stable address bus A0-A19 to memory and I/O. 8086 AD0-AD15 ---> [transceivers, direction by DT/R, enabled by DEN] <---> data bus D0-D15. 8086 RD, WR, M/IO ---> control bus. After this, the rest of the system sees three clean, separate buses, just like the textbook bus diagram.

BHE and A0, picking bytes: The 8086 data bus is 16 bits, but memory is addressed in bytes. Memory is split into two banks: the even bank holds even addresses and connects to D0-D7, the odd bank holds odd addresses and connects to D8-D15. A0 low selects the even bank. BHE low selects the odd bank. So BHE = 0, A0 = 0 means a whole word at an even address. BHE = 1, A0 = 0 means only the even byte. BHE = 0, A0 = 1 means only the odd byte. BHE = 1, A0 = 1 means no bank, which is not used for a normal transfer. Lesson 22 shows how banks are wired.

Aligned and unaligned words: If a word starts at an even address, both bytes come in one bus cycle. If it starts at an odd address, say 20101h, the low byte is in the odd bank at 20101h and the high byte in the even bank at 20102h. The 8086 must do two bus cycles. So keeping words at even addresses makes programs faster. Assemblers offer an EVEN directive to align data for this reason.

The clock and the 8284: Everything happens on clock ticks. The 8086 does not make its own clock. A helper chip, the 8284 clock generator, takes a crystal and divides its frequency by 3. A 15 MHz crystal gives a 5 MHz CPU clock, with a high time of one third of each period. The 8284 also cleans up the RESET and READY signals so they change at safe moments relative to the clock. Standard versions ran at 5 MHz (8086), 8 MHz (8086-2) and 10 MHz (8086-1). At 5 MHz one clock period is 200 nanoseconds.

The bus cycle, T1 to T4: A bus cycle is one complete memory or I/O read or write, and it takes at least four clock periods called T-states.
