T1: the CPU puts the address on AD0-AD15 and A16-A19, sets M/IO, sets DT/R for the direction, and pulses ALE so the latches catch the address. T2: the address is removed from the AD pins. For a read, the AD pins float (go into a high impedance, disconnected state) and RD goes low. For a write, the CPU puts the data on the pins and WR goes low. DEN goes active to turn on the transceivers. T3: the data travels; the memory or device has had time to respond. T4: RD or WR goes back high and the cycle closes. For a read, the CPU has taken in the data by this point.

A timeline you can draw: CLK: |T1|T2|T3|T4|. ALE: pulse in T1 only. AD pins: address in T1, then data from T2 to T4. RD (for a read): high in T1, low in T2 and T3, back high in T4. M/IO: set at T1 and steady for the whole cycle. Drawing this once with a pencil makes most timing questions easy.

Wait states, when memory is slow: Suppose a cheap ROM needs more time than T2 and T3 allow. The memory logic pulls READY low. The CPU then inserts extra clock periods called wait states (Tw) between T3 and T4, and keeps everything frozen until READY goes high again. Each wait state at 5 MHz adds 200 ns. So a cycle with one wait state takes 5 clocks, 1 microsecond. This is the trade-off: slower memory is cheaper but makes the whole system slower.

Idle states: When the instruction queue is full and the execution unit does not need the bus, the BIU simply does nothing. These clock periods are called idle states (Ti). They show that the bus is not busy every single moment.

Minimum mode: The MN/MX pin decides the mode. Tied high, it gives minimum mode, for a small system with just one 8086. In this mode the CPU itself produces all the control signals: M/IO, RD, WR, ALE, DT/R, DEN, INTA, HOLD/HLDA. This is perfect for a training kit or a simple controller, because it needs the fewest extra chips.

Maximum mode: Tied low, MN/MX gives maximum mode, used for bigger systems, for example with the 8087 math coprocessor. Eight pins (24 to 31) change meaning. Instead of direct control signals, the CPU outputs status bits S0, S1 and S2, and a separate chip, the 8288 bus controller, decodes them into memory read, memory write, I/O read, I/O write and interrupt acknowledge commands. The freed pins become QS0 and QS1 (showing the queue status so a coprocessor can follow the instruction stream), RQ/GT0 and RQ/GT1 (request/grant lines to share the bus) and LOCK (to keep other masters off the bus during a critical instruction). Trade-off: more chips and cost, but support for multiprocessor setups.

What happens on RESET: When RESET is held high for at least four clocks and then released, the 8086 clears its flags, sets DS, SS and ES to 0000h, empties the queue, and sets CS = FFFFh and IP = 0000h. So the very first instruction is fetched from physical address FFFF0h, just 16 bytes below the top of memory. That is why system ROM (the BIOS in a PC) is placed at the top of the address space, and the instruction there is usually a jump to the real start-up code.

The 8088 cousin: The 8088, used in the first IBM PC in 1981 at 4.77 MHz, is the same inside as the 8086 but with an 8-bit external data bus. Only AD0-AD7 are multiplexed; A8-A15 are plain address pins. It has a 4-byte queue instead of 6, no BHE pin (it has SS0 instead), and its memory/IO pin is reversed (IO/M). Every word transfer needs two bus cycles, so it is slower, but it was cheaper to build boards for, which is why IBM chose it.

Real life example 1, a training kit in a university lab: In many Bangladeshi university labs, students use 8086 trainer kits. If you look at the board, you can spot the 8086, the 8284 clock chip next to a crystal, a row of 74LS373 latches, 74LS245 transceivers, and ROM and RAM chips. Now each of those chips has a meaning: latches because of ALE and multiplexing, transceivers because of DT/R and DEN, the crystal at three times the CPU clock.

Real life example 2, a slow sign board controller: Imagine a shop sign in Gulshan run by an old 8086-based controller whose EPROM is slow. The designer adds a small circuit that pulls READY low for one clock whenever the EPROM is selected. Every instruction fetch from EPROM now takes 5 clocks instead of 4, but RAM accesses still take 4. The sign scrolls slightly slower, but it works reliably. Without the wait state, the CPU would read garbage before the EPROM finished.

Common mistakes: Thinking AD0-AD15 carry address and data at the same time; they take turns. Forgetting that without latches the address disappears. Mixing up DT/R polarity. Believing BHE is active high; it is active low. Thinking every bus cycle is exactly four clocks; wait states make it longer. And forgetting that maximum mode needs the 8288.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the read or write bus cycle. Explain why ALE and latches are needed. Explain minimum vs maximum mode with the role of the 8288. Give the BHE and A0 table. State CS and IP after reset and the first physical address fetched. Calculate the bus cycle time for a given clock and number of wait states. Compare 8086 and 8088.

Recap: The 8086 saves pins by multiplexing address and data on AD0-AD15. ALE tells latches to hold the address, DT/R and DEN steer transceivers for data. BHE and A0 choose the even, odd or both banks. A bus cycle takes T1 to T4, longer with wait states when READY is low. Minimum mode for small single-CPU systems, maximum mode with the 8288 for bigger ones. After reset, execution starts at FFFF0h. Next we finally write our first assembly program.
key_points: AD0-AD15 are multiplexed: address in T1, data later in the same bus cycle.
ALE pulses in T1 so external latches (74LS373/8282) hold the address steady.
DT/R sets transceiver direction and DEN enables them for the data phase.
BHE (active low) and A0 select the odd bank, even bank or both.
A bus cycle has T1-T4; READY low inserts wait states between T3 and T4.
Minimum mode: CPU makes control signals. Maximum mode: 8288 decodes S0-S2.
After RESET: CS = FFFFh, IP = 0000h, first fetch from FFFF0h.
The 8088 has an 8-bit external data bus and a 4-byte queue.
lessons.tip: Draw the T1-T4 timing diagram from memory once a day for a week: CLK, ALE, AD lines, RD, WR. Most pin questions become one quick sketch.
lessons.task: Calculate the time of one read bus cycle at 5 MHz with 0, 1 and 2 wait states. Then fill a 4-row table of BHE and A0 values and write what is transferred in each row.

quiz.q: Why does the 8086 need address latches?
options: Because AD pins stop carrying the address once data appears
To store data for the ALU
quiz.explain: Multiplexed pins switch to data, so the address must be held outside.

quiz.q: During which T-state does ALE pulse?
quiz.explain: The address is on the bus in T1, so ALE latches it then.

quiz.q: BHE = 0 and A0 = 0 means:
options: A word transfer on both banks
quiz.explain: Both banks enabled: a full 16-bit word at an even address.

quiz.q: What chip decodes S0-S2 in maximum mode?
quiz.explain: The 8288 bus controller generates the commands.

quiz.q: What is the first physical address fetched after RESET?
quiz.explain: CS = FFFFh and IP = 0000h give FFFF0h.

lessons.title: Your First Assembly Program
lessons.content:
Remember the first time you wrote "Hello World" in C? A few lines, one command, and the words appeared. In assembly, printing a message also takes only a handful of lines, but every line means something you can see happening inside the CPU. In this lesson we write, assemble, link and run our first 8086 program, and we understand every word in it. After this, assembly stops being a scary wall of letters.

What an assembly program really is: The CPU only understands machine code, which is just bytes. For example, the bytes B8 05 00 tell the 8086 to put 5 into AX. Nobody wants to write programs as raw bytes, so we write mnemonics like MOV AX, 5 instead. A program called an assembler translates each line into its bytes. Assembly is therefore a human friendly spelling of machine code: almost one line becomes one instruction, unlike C where one line may become many instructions.

The tools and the flow: The classic tools are MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler) or TASM (Turbo Assembler) plus a linker, LINK or TLINK. The flow is: you write hello.asm in a text editor. The assembler reads it and produces hello.obj, an object file with machine code and some unresolved names. The linker joins one or more object files, fixes addresses, and produces hello.exe. Then DOS loads and runs it. In a picture: hello.asm --assembler--> hello.obj --linker--> hello.exe --DOS loader--> running in memory. Today most students run these old tools inside DOSBox, or use emu8086, an emulator that combines editor, assembler and a step-by-step debugger, which is great for learning.

Why two passes: An assembler usually reads your file twice. In pass one it walks through every line, counts how many bytes each instruction and variable will need, and builds a symbol table: a list of every label and variable with its offset. In pass two it generates the actual bytes, now knowing where every label is, even ones defined later in the file. That is how a JMP to a label further down can be assembled. If you ask for a listing file (.LST), you can see each line next to its offset and machine code bytes.

The shape of a statement: Each line has up to four parts: name or label, mnemonic or directive, operands, and a comment. Example: AGAIN: ADD AX, BX ; add BX to AX. AGAIN is a label, ADD is the mnemonic, AX, BX are operands, and everything after the semicolon is a comment that the assembler ignores. Code labels end with a colon; variable names in the data area do not. MASM is not case sensitive, so mov and MOV are the same.

Instructions vs directives: An instruction, like MOV or ADD, becomes machine code that the CPU executes. A directive, like .DATA or END, is an order to the assembler itself. It tells the assembler how to organise the program but does not run on the CPU. Some directives, like DB, do put bytes into the file, but those bytes are data, not instructions. Mixing these two ideas is a common beginner confusion.

Our first program, the whole thing: Here it is, line by line as you would type it. .MODEL SMALL / .STACK 100H / .DATA / MSG DB 'Assalamu Alaikum, Dhaka!$' / .CODE / MAIN PROC / MOV AX, @DATA / MOV DS, AX / LEA DX, MSG / MOV AH, 09H / INT 21H / MOV AH, 4CH / INT 21H / MAIN ENDP / END MAIN. (The slashes here just separate lines.) Fifteen short lines. Now we go through them.

.MODEL SMALL: This chooses the memory model. SMALL means one code segment and one data segment, each up to 64 KB. Other models exist: TINY puts code and data together in one 64 KB segment (used for .COM files), MEDIUM allows many code segments with one data segment, COMPACT the opposite, and LARGE allows many of both. For learning, SMALL is nearly always enough.

.STACK 100H: This reserves 100h = 256 bytes for the stack. The stack is needed even if you never write PUSH, because interrupts and procedure calls use it. The loader sets SS and SP for you so they point to this area.

.DATA and the message: .DATA starts the data segment. MSG DB 'Assalamu Alaikum, Dhaka!$' defines a variable named MSG. DB means define byte: each character becomes one byte with its ASCII code, so 'A' becomes 41h. The dollar sign at the end is not printed; it is the end marker that DOS function 09h looks for. Forget it, and DOS keeps printing whatever bytes come next in memory until it happens to hit a $ somewhere, giving you a screen full of strange symbols.

More ways to define data: DW defines a word (2 bytes), DD a double word (4 bytes). NUM DB 25 makes one byte holding 25. TOTAL DW 0 makes a word holding 0. X DB ? reserves one byte without a chosen value. ARR DB 10 DUP(0) makes ten bytes, all 0; DUP means duplicate. MARKS DB 70, 85, 90 makes three bytes in a row. Numbers can be written in decimal (25), hex with an H (19H) or binary with a B (11001B). A hex number starting with a letter must get a leading 0, like 0FFH, otherwise the assembler thinks FFH is a name.

EQU, constants without memory: COUNT EQU 10 tells the assembler to replace the word COUNT with 10 everywhere. No memory is used, it is just a nickname. Compare with COUNT DB 10, which creates a real byte in memory that a program can change. Use EQU for fixed values like array sizes or port numbers, and DB or DW for values that live in memory.

.CODE and the procedure: .CODE starts the code segment. MAIN PROC and MAIN ENDP mark the start and end of a procedure named MAIN. For now think of it as the main function. The last line, END MAIN, tells the assembler that the source file ends here and that execution should start at MAIN. Without it, the linker would not know the entry point.

Loading DS, the line everyone forgets: MOV AX, @DATA puts the segment address of the data segment into AX. @DATA is a value that the loader fixes when the program is put in memory. MOV DS, AX then copies it into DS. Why two steps? Because the 8086 cannot move an immediate value directly into a segment register; MOV DS, @DATA is illegal. And why at all? When DOS starts an .EXE program, DS does not point to your data; it points to a 256-byte area called the PSP (program segment prefix). If you skip these two lines, LEA DX, MSG gives the right offset but in the wrong segment, and DOS prints garbage.

Printing the message: LEA DX, MSG loads the offset of MSG into DX. MOV AH, 09H chooses DOS function 9, "print a $-terminated string at DS:DX". INT 21H calls DOS. Think of INT 21H as ringing a bell at the DOS office, and AH as the token number saying which service you want. DOS reads AH, sees 9, takes the string from DS:DX, and prints until $.

Exiting properly: MOV AH, 4CH then INT 21H calls DOS function 4Ch, "terminate the program", and the value in AL becomes the return code. This line is essential. The CPU does not know that your program has ended; it just keeps fetching the next bytes from memory. Without the exit call, it would run into whatever random bytes follow your code, which can hang the computer.

An execution trace: Suppose DOS loads the program and the data segment ends up at 0B60h. Step 1, MOV AX, @DATA: AX = 0B60h. Step 2, MOV DS, AX: DS = 0B60h. Step 3, LEA DX, MSG: MSG is the first variable, so DX = 0000h. Step 4, MOV AH, 09H: AH = 09h. Step 5, INT 21H: DOS prints the text found at 0B60:0000. Step 6, MOV AH, 4CH: AH = 4Ch. Step 7, INT 21H: DOS frees the memory and returns to the prompt. In emu8086 you can single-step and watch these registers change exactly like this.

Building and running: With MASM in DOSBox you would type MASM HELLO; then LINK HELLO; then HELLO. With TASM it is TASM HELLO then TLINK HELLO. If the assembler finds a mistake, it prints the line number and an error message, such as an undefined symbol (you misspelled a name) or an operand type mismatch (you tried to put a word into a byte register). Read the line number first; it nearly always points straight at the problem.

.COM vs .EXE: There are two kinds of DOS programs. A .COM file is a plain memory image, at most about 64 KB, where code, data and stack all share one segment. DOS loads it at offset 100h, right after the 256-byte PSP, and sets CS, DS, ES and SS to the same value, so you need ORG 100H in the source and no DS setup. An .EXE file has a header with relocation information and can have separate segments for code, data and stack, so it can be bigger. Trade-off: .COM is tiny and simple, .EXE is flexible and is what most course programs use.

Other assemblers and syntax: NASM is a popular free assembler today. It uses slightly different syntax: square brackets are required whenever you access memory, so MOV AX, [NUM] reads memory while MOV AX, NUM loads the address. Linux tools often use AT&T syntax where operands are reversed (source first). The CPU is the same; only the spelling differs. This course uses MASM/TASM style because most Bangladeshi university labs and textbooks do.

Real life example 1, a shop receipt: Imagine a tiny program in an old cash machine at a Mohammadpur grocery that prints "Dhonnobad, abar ashben!$" after every sale. It is exactly our pattern: define the message with DB and a $, load DS, put the offset in DX, AH = 9, INT 21H. The shopkeeper never sees the registers, but they move just like in our trace.

Real life example 2, the lab exam: In many lab finals, the first question is "print your name and roll number on two lines". The trick is that a new line needs carriage return 0DH and line feed 0AH inside the string: LINE1 DB 'Rahim', 0DH, 0AH, 'Roll 23$'. Knowing what DB really stores lets you mix characters and byte values freely in one definition.

When to use assembly and when not: Use it to learn how the machine really works, to write tiny code where every byte or clock matters (boot code, some embedded routines), to read compiler output, or to debug at the lowest level. Do not use it for whole applications like a shopping website; C, Python or Java are much faster to write, safer and portable across machines. Assembly code for the 8086 will not run on an ARM phone without rewriting.

Common mistakes: Forgetting MOV AX, @DATA and MOV DS, AX. Forgetting the $ at the end of a string for function 09h. Forgetting the 4Ch exit. Writing FFH instead of 0FFH. Missing END MAIN. Trying MOV DS, 1234H directly. Putting data in the middle of code, so the CPU tries to execute your text as instructions.

What exams ask: Explain the difference between an assembler, linker and loader. Explain directives vs instructions with examples. Explain the role of .MODEL, .STACK, .DATA, .CODE, DB, DW, DUP and EQU. Write a program to print a string. Explain why DS must be initialised. Compare .COM and .EXE files. Describe the two-pass assembler.

Recap: An assembly program is a human readable list of machine instructions plus directives that organise it. The assembler turns it into an object file in two passes, the linker makes an executable, and DOS loads it. A standard SMALL program sets up DS, uses INT 21H for printing and must exit with function 4Ch. With this template in hand, the next lessons can focus on what really happens inside each instruction, starting with how operands are found: the addressing modes.
key_points: The assembler turns mnemonics into machine code; the linker builds the .EXE; DOS loads it.
A two-pass assembler builds a symbol table first, then generates bytes.
Directives (.MODEL, .DATA, DB, EQU, END) guide the assembler; instructions run on the CPU.
DB, DW and DD define bytes, words and double words; DUP repeats; EQU makes a constant with no memory.
MOV AX, @DATA then MOV DS, AX is needed because DS starts at the PSP and segments cannot take immediates.
INT 21H with AH = 09H prints a $-terminated string at DS:DX; AH = 4CH exits.
.COM files share one 64 KB segment starting at offset 100h; .EXE files have a header and separate segments.
Hex numbers starting with a letter need a leading 0, like 0FFH.
lessons.tip: Keep one working template file with .MODEL, .STACK, .DATA, .CODE, DS setup and the 4Ch exit. Start every new exercise by copying it, so you only think about the new part.
lessons.task: Write (on paper or in emu8086) a program that prints your name on one line and your university on the next, using 0DH, 0AH inside one DB string. Trace AX, DS, DX and AH after each line.

quiz.q: Why do we write MOV AX, @DATA then MOV DS, AX?
options: Because DS cannot be loaded with an immediate value and starts at the PSP
quiz.explain: Segment registers take values only from registers or memory, and DS initially points to the PSP.

quiz.q: What does the $ at the end of a string do for function 09h?
options: It marks the end of the string
quiz.explain: DOS prints characters until it finds $.

quiz.q: Which line ends the program and returns to DOS?
quiz.explain: Function 4Ch terminates; END MAIN is only a directive for the assembler.

quiz.q: COUNT EQU 10 does what?
options: Makes a constant name with no memory
quiz.explain: EQU is replaced by its value at assembly time.

quiz.q: Why must FFH be written as 0FFH?
options: Hex starting with a letter would be read as a name
quiz.explain: A leading digit tells the assembler it is a number.

lessons.title: Addressing Modes of the 8086
lessons.content:
Suppose your mother sends you to fetch something. She can say it in different ways. "Here, take this 50 taka note" (the thing is right in her hand). "It is in your pocket" (a place you carry). "It is in the third drawer" (a fixed place). "Look at the slip in your pocket, it says which drawer" (a place that points to another place). "It is the fifth item after the drawer the slip points to" (a pointer plus a step). Every instruction needs data, and the different ways an instruction says where that data is are called addressing modes. The 8086 has a small, very regular set of them, and once you see the pattern, you can read any operand.

What an operand is: Most instructions work on one or two operands. In MOV AX, BX the first operand AX is the destination and the second, BX, is the source. An operand can be a constant written inside the instruction, a register inside the CPU, or a location in memory. Registers are fastest because no bus cycle is needed. Memory operands are slower because the CPU must calculate an address and do a bus cycle. Constants are fetched along with the instruction itself.

Why so many modes: High-level programs use simple variables (x = 5), arrays (marks[i]), records (student.age), arrays of records (students[i].age) and pointers. Each of these maps naturally to one addressing mode. Without them, the programmer would have to calculate every address with extra ADD instructions, making code longer and slower. Before such rich modes, very early processors had only a few, and programmers did that arithmetic by hand.

Effective address and physical address: For a memory operand, the 8086 first computes the effective address (EA), which is the offset inside a segment. EA = base + index + displacement, where any part may be missing. The base is BX or BP, the index is SI or DI, and the displacement is a constant written in the instruction (8 or 16 bits). Then the Bus Interface Unit makes the physical address: PA = segment x 16 + EA, using the default segment (DS for most, SS when BP is used) unless you override it.

Mode 1, immediate: The data is a constant inside the instruction. MOV AX, 1234h puts 1234h into AX. MOV CL, 5 puts 5 into CL. The constant travels with the instruction bytes, so no extra memory read is needed. Rule: an immediate can only be a source, never a destination; MOV 5, AX makes no sense. Also, as you saw earlier, an immediate cannot go straight into a segment register.

Mode 2, register: Both operands are registers. MOV AX, BX copies BX into AX. ADD CL, DL adds DL into CL. This is the fastest mode. Rule: both must be the same size. MOV AX, BL is an error because AX is 16-bit and BL is 8-bit.

Mode 3, direct: The instruction contains the offset of the data. MOV AX, [1234h] reads the word at DS:1234h. More often you write a variable name: MOV AX, TOTAL, and the assembler puts TOTAL's offset into the instruction. Example: DS = 2000h, TOTAL is at offset 0050h. PA = 20000h + 0050h = 20050h. Good for simple global variables whose position never changes.

Mode 4, register indirect: A register holds the offset, like the slip in your pocket. MOV AL, [BX] reads the byte at DS:BX. Only BX, SI, DI and BP can be used this way; [AX], [CX] and [DX] are illegal on the 8086. Example: DS = 2000h, BX = 0300h. MOV AL, [BX] reads from 20300h. Why useful: change BX and the same instruction reads a different place, which is exactly what a loop over an array needs.

Mode 5, based: A base register plus a displacement: [BX + disp] or [BP + disp]. Think of a record. If BX points to the start of a student record and the age is 4 bytes in, MOV AL, [BX+4] reads the age. With BP the default segment is SS, so MOV AX, [BP+4] reads from the stack. This is how procedures read parameters, which you will see in the procedures lesson. Example: SS = 3000h, BP = 0FF0h, EA = 0FF0h + 4 = 0FF4h, PA = 30FF4h.

Mode 6, indexed: An index register plus a displacement: [SI + disp] or [DI + disp]. MASM also lets you write it like an array: MOV AL, ARR[SI] means [SI + offset of ARR]. Example: DS = 2000h, ARR at offset 0100h, SI = 0003h. EA = 0103h, PA = 20103h, which is ARR's fourth byte (index 3, counting from 0). Loop over the array by increasing SI.

Mode 7, based indexed: A base plus an index: [BX+SI], [BX+DI], [BP+SI], [BP+DI]. Useful when one register points to the start of an array and the other is the position. Example: DS = 2000h, BX = 0100h, SI = 0020h. MOV AL, [BX+SI] gives EA = 0120h, PA = 20120h.

Mode 8, based indexed with displacement: All three parts: [BX+SI+disp]. This fits a two-dimensional table or an array of records. Example: a class table where each row (one student) is 10 bytes and the third byte of a row is the math mark. BX = row start offset, SI = column, displacement = table start. If TABLE is at 0200h, BX = 20 (third row, 2 x 10 = 20 = 14h), SI = 2, then MOV AL, TABLE[BX+SI] gives EA = 0200h + 0014h + 0002h = 0216h.

The full legal list: The 8086 allows exactly these memory forms: [disp], [BX], [BP+disp] (plain [BP] is encoded as [BP+0]), [SI], [DI], [BX+disp], [SI+disp], [DI+disp], [BX+SI], [BX+DI], [BP+SI], [BP+DI], and each of those last four with a displacement. Not allowed: two bases ([BX+BP]), two indexes ([SI+DI]), any of AX, CX, DX, SP inside brackets, or scaling like [SI*2]. Remember the rule: at most one base (BX or BP) and at most one index (SI or DI).

How the CPU knows the mode: Inside the machine code, most instructions with operands have a byte after the opcode called the ModR/M byte. It has three fields: mod (2 bits), reg (3 bits) and r/m (3 bits). The reg field names one register operand. The r/m field, with 3 bits, picks one of 8 memory forms: [BX+SI], [BX+DI], [BP+SI], [BP+DI], [SI], [DI], [BP] and [BX]. The mod field says whether there is no displacement, an 8-bit one or a 16-bit one, or that r/m is actually a register. One special case: mod 00 with the [BP] code means a plain direct address instead, which is why [BP] alone is encoded as [BP+0]. This is also why the list of legal forms is so short: there are only 8 slots.

Default segment rule again: If BP appears in the address, the default segment is SS. Otherwise it is DS. So [BP+SI] uses SS, [BX+SI] uses DS, [BP+DI+6] uses SS. You can override: MOV AX, DS:[BP+2] forces DS. This tiny rule causes many lab bugs where students use BP as a general pointer to data and read the stack by accident.

Size problems and PTR: In MOV AL, [BX] the size is clear because AL is a byte. But in MOV [BX], 5 the assembler cannot tell whether to store a byte 05h or a word 0005h. You must say: MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 5 or MOV WORD PTR [BX], 5. The same is true for INC [SI] and similar instructions with only a memory operand. PTR simply tells the size; it does not change the address.

Word arrays: If an array holds words (DW), each element is 2 bytes. Element i is at offset start + 2i. So when you move to the next element, add 2 to SI, not 1. Forgetting this is one of the most common bugs: the program reads half of one number and half of the next.

One memory operand only: An 8086 instruction can have at most one memory operand. MOV [BX], [SI] is illegal. To copy memory to memory you go through a register: MOV AL, [SI] then MOV [BX], AL. (String instructions, covered later, are a special exception that moves memory to memory by themselves.)

Other modes you will meet: Some textbooks also list port addressing for IN and OUT (an 8-bit port number, or DX for a 16-bit port), relative addressing for jumps (the instruction stores a distance from the current IP), and implied addressing where the operand is fixed by the instruction, like CBW which always uses AL and AH. Each gets explained in its own lesson.

Cost of modes: Every memory mode needs the EA calculation plus a bus cycle. On the original 8086 this calculation took extra clock cycles, and the more parts the address had, the longer it took; for example [BX+SI+disp] was slower than [BX]. Modern x86 chips calculate addresses in dedicated hardware very quickly, but the idea that registers are faster than memory is still true everywhere.

Execution trace with an array sum preview: DATA: ARR DB 4, 7, 9. Code: LEA SI, ARR / MOV AL, 0 / ADD AL, [SI] / ADD AL, [SI+1] / ADD AL, [SI+2]. Suppose ARR is at offset 0010h. LEA SI, ARR: SI = 0010h. MOV AL, 0: AL = 0. ADD AL, [SI]: EA 0010h, reads 4, AL = 4. ADD AL, [SI+1]: EA 0011h, reads 7, AL = 11 (0Bh). ADD AL, [SI+2]: EA 0012h, reads 9, AL = 20 (14h). Later lessons turn this into a loop by increasing SI.

Real life example 1, a school marks table: A headmaster in Sylhet keeps marks of 40 students, each row 5 subjects, one byte each. To read student k's subject j he needs table + 5k + j. In assembly: put 5k in BX, j in SI, and use TABLE[BX+SI]. One instruction does the job that would otherwise need two additions.

Real life example 2, a bKash style transaction record: Imagine a record of 8 bytes: a 2-byte ID, a 4-byte amount and a 2-byte fee. If BX points to the record start, the fee is at [BX+6] and the amount's low word at [BX+2]. Moving BX by 8 jumps to the next record. That is based addressing used exactly the way a C struct is used.

When to use which: Use immediate for fixed constants, register for hot values in loops, direct for single global variables, register indirect or indexed for walking through arrays, based with BP for stack parameters and locals, and based indexed for tables. Don't use a complicated mode just because it exists; if a value is used many times, load it into a register once.

Common mistakes: Using [AX] or [DX]. Writing [SI+DI]. Forgetting BYTE PTR or WORD PTR. Forgetting that BP uses SS. Adding 1 instead of 2 for word arrays. Trying memory-to-memory moves. Confusing LEA SI, ARR (load the address) with MOV SI, ARR (load the value stored at ARR), which is covered in the next lesson.

What exams ask: Name the addressing mode of a given instruction. Compute EA and PA given register values. Identify illegal instructions and explain why. Explain the default segment for an operand. Write a short program accessing a 2-D array element.

Recap: Addressing modes describe where an operand lives: in the instruction (immediate), in a register, or in memory. For memory, EA = base (BX/BP) + index (SI/DI) + displacement, and PA = segment x 16 + EA. BP means SS by default; everything else means DS. Only one memory operand per instruction, and you must state size with PTR when it is unclear. With operands understood, the next lesson looks at the instructions that move data between all these places.
key_points: Operands can be immediate, register or memory; registers are fastest.
EA = base (BX or BP) + index (SI or DI) + displacement; PA = segment x 16 + EA.
Memory modes: direct, register indirect, based, indexed, based indexed, with displacement.
Any address using BP defaults to SS; others default to DS.
Illegal: [AX], [CX], [DX], [SI+DI], [BX+BP], two memory operands in one instruction.
Use BYTE PTR or WORD PTR when the size of a memory operand is unclear.
Word arrays step by 2 bytes per element.
Each mode matches a high-level idea: variable, array, record, table, stack parameter.
lessons.tip: For every bracket you see, ask three questions: which base, which index, which displacement. Then ask: is BP there? If yes, the segment is SS.
lessons.task: Given DS = 2000h, SS = 3000h, BX = 0100h, BP = 0200h, SI = 0010h, DI = 0020h, compute the physical address for [BX], [BX+SI+5], [BP+DI], [SI+40h] and [BP+4]. Then mark which of these is illegal: [CX], [BX+DI+2], [SI+DI].

quiz.q: What is the addressing mode of MOV AL, [BX+SI+4]?
quiz.explain: It uses a base, an index and a displacement.

quiz.q: DS = 2000h, BX = 0100h, SI = 0020h. PA of [BX+SI]?
Which is legal on the 8086?
quiz.explain: One base plus one index is allowed; the others break the rules.

quiz.q: Which segment does [BP+DI] use by default?
quiz.explain: Any address with BP defaults to SS.

quiz.q: Why write MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 5?
options: Because the size of the memory operand is otherwise unknown
PTR is needed for all MOVs
quiz.explain: With only memory and a constant, the assembler cannot guess byte or word.

lessons.title: Data Transfer Instructions
lessons.content:
Watch a busy kitchen before an Eid feast. Most of the work is not cooking at all. It is moving things: rice from the sack to the pot, onions from the basket to the chopping board, plates from the shelf to the table. Programs are the same. Studies of real programs show that a large share of all executed instructions just move data from one place to another. On the 8086, those are the data transfer instructions. They do no arithmetic, but without them nothing else can happen.

What data transfer means: A data transfer instruction copies a value from a source to a destination: register to register, memory to register, register to memory, a constant into a register or memory, or between the CPU and an I/O port. The source keeps its value. Almost none of these instructions change the flags, because nothing is being calculated. That is important: you can move data around between a CMP and a conditional jump without spoiling the result.

MOV, the workhorse: MOV destination, source copies source into destination. MOV AX, BX copies BX into AX; BX is unchanged. MOV AL, [SI] copies a byte from memory. MOV TOTAL, AX stores AX into the variable TOTAL. MOV CX, 10 loads a constant. The name "move" is misleading. Nothing moves away; it is a copy, like photocopying a page, not tearing it out.

The rules of MOV: First, both operands must be the same size: MOV AX, BL is illegal. Second, no memory-to-memory: MOV VAR1, VAR2 is illegal; go through a register. Third, no immediate into a segment register: MOV DS, 2000h is illegal. Fourth, no segment register to segment register: MOV ES, DS is illegal; use MOV AX, DS then MOV ES, AX. Fifth, CS cannot be a destination of MOV, because changing CS alone would jump to a random place; jumps and calls are the proper way. Sixth, IP is not an operand at all; you cannot MOV into or out of it. And of course the destination cannot be an immediate.

Bytes into words: Since MOV demands equal sizes, how do you put a byte value into a 16-bit register? Load the low half and clear the high half yourself: MOV AL, NUM / MOV AH, 0. Now AX holds the same value as a word. Writing to AL or AH never changes the other half, so AX = 1234h followed by MOV AL, 0FFh gives AX = 12FFh. For signed numbers, clearing AH is wrong for negative values; the arithmetic lesson shows CBW, which copies the sign bit instead.

Why these rules exist: They come from how instructions are encoded and how the hardware is built. An 8086 instruction has room for one memory address in its ModR/M byte, so two memory operands cannot be described. Segment registers have only a few special opcodes that load them from a general register or memory. The rules keep the chip simple and cheap. Later x86 chips kept the same rules for compatibility.

Loading SS safely: When you set up a stack yourself, you write MOV AX, STACKSEG / MOV SS, AX / MOV SP, 100h. What if an interrupt came between MOV SS and MOV SP? The CPU would push to a half-set-up stack. The 8086 protects you: after an instruction that loads a segment register, it does not accept an interrupt until the next instruction has finished. So always load SP immediately after SS.

XCHG, swapping in one go: XCHG AX, BX swaps the two values. If AX = 5 and BX = 9, afterwards AX = 9 and BX = 5. It works register with register or register with memory, but not with segment registers or constants, and not memory with memory. Without XCHG you would need a third temporary place, like swapping two glasses of juice using an empty third glass. A fun fact: the one-byte NOP instruction (opcode 90h) is actually XCHG AX, AX, which does nothing useful.

Swapping two variables: To swap memory variables A and B: MOV AX, A / XCHG AX, B / MOV A, AX. Trace with A = 3, B = 8: after MOV AX, A, AX = 3. After XCHG AX, B, AX = 8 and B = 3. After MOV A, AX, A = 8. Swapped in three instructions.

LEA, load effective address: LEA reg, memory computes the offset of the memory operand and puts that address, not the value stored there, into the register. LEA SI, ARR puts the offset of ARR into SI. LEA BX, [BX+SI+4] computes BX + SI + 4 and puts the result into BX. Think of it as writing down a house address instead of going into the house. LEA does not even touch memory, and it does not change flags.

LEA vs MOV with OFFSET: MOV SI, OFFSET ARR also loads the offset of ARR. The difference: OFFSET is calculated by the assembler at assembly time, so it works only for fixed addresses. LEA calculates at run time, so it works with registers inside the brackets: LEA DI, [BX+SI] has no OFFSET equivalent. For a plain variable, MOV with OFFSET is one byte shorter. And note MOV SI, ARR, without OFFSET, is completely different: it loads the value stored at ARR.

LEA as a calculator: Because LEA only computes base + index + displacement, programmers sometimes use it to add without touching flags: LEA AX, [BX+SI+10] gives AX = BX + SI + 10 in one instruction. It is a neat trick, but use it only when it makes code clearer.

LDS and LES, loading far pointers: A far pointer is 4 bytes: offset in the low word, segment in the high word. LDS SI, PTRVAR loads SI from the first word and DS from the second word in one instruction. LES DI, PTRVAR does the same with ES. Example: PTRVAR DD with bytes 00 01 00 30 in memory means offset 0100h, segment 3000h. After LDS SI, PTRVAR: SI = 0100h, DS = 3000h, so DS:SI points to 30100h. Useful when a function receives a pointer to data somewhere far away in memory.

XLAT, table lookup in one instruction: XLAT replaces AL with the byte at DS:[BX + AL]. You first point BX at a table of up to 256 bytes, put an index in AL, and XLAT gives you the table entry. Example: HEX DB '0123456789ABCDEF'. LEA BX, HEX / MOV AL, 0Ch / XLAT. EA = BX + 0Ch, the thirteenth character, so AL = 'C' (43h). This turns any small mapping into a single fast instruction, instead of a chain of compares.

XLAT for a seven-segment display: Digital displays on petrol pumps and shop scales light up 7 small bars to show a digit. Each digit needs a pattern byte. For a common cathode display with bits gfedcba, the patterns are 3Fh, 06h, 5Bh, 4Fh, 66h, 6Dh, 7Dh, 07h, 7Fh, 6Fh for digits 0 to 9. Store them as SEG DB 3Fh, 06h, 5Bh, 4Fh, 66h, 6Dh, 7Dh, 07h, 7Fh, 6Fh. To show the digit 7: LEA BX, SEG / MOV AL, 7 / XLAT gives AL = 07h, which you then send out to the display port. Lesson 23 wires this to real hardware.

LAHF and SAHF: LAHF copies the low byte of the flags register into AH. That byte holds SF (bit 7), ZF (bit 6), AF (bit 4), PF (bit 2) and CF (bit 0). SAHF does the reverse. They exist mainly for compatibility with the older 8080 and for moving flags around quickly. Note SAHF is one of the few transfer instructions that does change flags, because that is its whole job.

PUSH and POP, a preview: PUSH source puts a 16-bit word on the top of the stack, POP destination takes it off. On the 8086 they work only on words, never single bytes, and PUSH of a constant is not available (it arrived with the 80186). You cannot POP into CS. PUSHF and POPF save and restore the whole flags register. The stack lesson explains exactly how SP changes.

IN and OUT, a preview: Devices like keyboards and LED boards sit at I/O port addresses, separate from memory. IN AL, 60h reads a byte from port 60h. OUT 43h, AL writes AL to port 43h. For port numbers above FFh, put the number in DX: MOV DX, 3F8h / IN AL, DX. Only AL (byte) or AX (word) can hold the data. These come back in the I/O interfacing lessons.

A complete little example: Copy a 5-byte array SRC to DST. Without string instructions it goes: LEA SI, SRC / LEA DI, DST / then five times: MOV AL, [SI] / MOV [DI], AL / INC SI / INC DI. Each byte must pass through AL because memory-to-memory MOV is illegal. In the loops lesson this becomes a loop, and in the string lesson a single REP MOVSB will replace the whole thing.

Real life example 1, a cricket scoreboard: The scoreboard program at a district stadium in Chattogram keeps runs, wickets and overs in memory. When a new over starts, it copies the current bowler's figures into a table row, swaps the striker and non-striker with XCHG, and uses XLAT to turn each digit into a display pattern. No arithmetic in these steps at all, only moving data, yet without them the board would show nothing.

Real life example 2, a Daraz parcel label: A label printer gets a far pointer to the customer's address, stored somewhere in a big buffer. One LDS SI, ADDRPTR sets DS:SI to the start of the address, and the printer routine then reads byte after byte from there. This is exactly why LDS and LES exist: one instruction to set up both halves of a far address.

When to use what: Use MOV for almost everything. Use XCHG when you really need a swap. Use LEA when you need an address, especially one built from registers. Use LDS or LES for far pointers. Use XLAT for small lookup tables. Use PUSH and POP to save and restore. When not: don't use XLAT for a table larger than 256 entries, it cannot reach; don't use LEA where a simple MOV with OFFSET is clearer; and don't keep copying a value to memory and back in a tight loop when it could stay in a register.

Common mistakes: Thinking MOV erases the source. Writing MOV VAR1, VAR2. Writing MOV DS, 2000h or MOV ES, DS. Mixing up LEA SI, ARR with MOV SI, ARR. Forgetting that XLAT needs BX pointing at the table and uses DS. Using PUSH AL (only words can be pushed). Loading SS and then doing other work before SP.

What exams ask: List the rules of MOV and give illegal examples. Explain the difference between LEA and MOV with OFFSET. Show what LDS does with a given memory dump. Write a program using XLAT to convert a number to its hex character or seven-segment code. Write a program to swap two variables. State which of these instructions affect flags.

Recap: Data transfer instructions copy data between registers, memory and ports without doing arithmetic and, except SAHF and POPF, without touching flags. MOV has strict rules: same size, no memory-to-memory, no immediate or segment register into a segment register, never into CS. XCHG swaps, LEA loads an address, LDS and LES load far pointers, XLAT looks up a table, and PUSH, POP, IN and OUT are previews of the stack and I/O lessons. Next we start calculating with the arithmetic instructions.
key_points: Data transfer instructions copy data; the source keeps its value and flags usually stay unchanged.
MOV rules: same size, no memory-to-memory, no immediate or segment into a segment register, never into CS.
XCHG swaps register-register or register-memory in one instruction.
LEA computes an address at run time; MOV with OFFSET uses an assembly-time constant.
LDS and LES load a 4-byte far pointer into a register plus DS or ES.
XLAT sets AL = DS:[BX + AL], a one-instruction lookup in a table of up to 256 bytes.
PUSH and POP work on words only; IN and OUT use AL or AX with a port number or DX.
After loading SS, load SP in the very next instruction.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write a MOV, say it aloud as 'copy source into destination' and check the two operand sizes. Half of all assembler errors in the first weeks are size or memory-to-memory mistakes.
lessons.task: Write the instructions to swap two word variables X and Y, then trace them with X = 1234h and Y = 00FFh. Next, build an XLAT table for seven-segment codes and find AL after XLAT for AL = 3 and AL = 8.

quiz.q: Which instruction is legal?
quiz.explain: Copying a segment register into a general register is allowed.

quiz.q: LEA SI, [BX+DI+2] does what?
options: Loads SI with the value stored at BX+DI+2
Loads SI with the address BX+DI+2
quiz.explain: LEA puts the computed offset, not the memory contents, into SI.

quiz.q: BX points to '0123456789ABCDEF' and AL = 0Ah. After XLAT, AL = ?
quiz.explain: Index 10 in the table is 'A'.

quiz.q: Memory at PTRVAR holds 00 02 00 40. After LDS SI, PTRVAR:
quiz.explain: Low word 0200h goes to SI, high word 4000h goes to DS (little endian).

quiz.q: Which of these changes the flags?
quiz.explain: SAHF loads flags from AH; the others do not touch flags.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Instructions: ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV and the Flags
lessons.content:
Remember doing addition in school? You write 47 under 38, add the right column, 7 plus 8 is 15, write 5 and keep 1 in your hand for the next column. Your teacher called it the carry. The 8086 does exactly the same thing, only in binary, and it keeps the carry in a tiny box called the carry flag. In this lesson we learn the arithmetic instructions of the 8086: how it adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides, which registers it secretly uses, and which flags it changes after every sum.

What it is: Arithmetic instructions are the commands that do maths on numbers stored in registers or memory. The main group is ADD, ADC, SUB, SBB, INC, DEC, NEG and CMP for adding and subtracting, then MUL, IMUL, DIV and IDIV for multiplying and dividing, plus CBW and CWD for making a small signed number bigger. They work on 8-bit values (like AL, BL) or 16-bit values (like AX, BX). BCD and ASCII adjust instructions are a separate family that we keep for the next lesson.

The problem they solve: The ALU inside the CPU can only add, subtract and do logic on fixed-size boxes of bits. A program, on the other hand, wants to calculate a bKash balance, a cricket run rate or a shopkeeper's total. Arithmetic instructions are the bridge. Each one tells the ALU exactly what to do, where to take the inputs from, where to put the answer, and how to report what happened, using the flags. Without the flags, the program would have no way to know if the answer overflowed or was zero.

A quick flag refresher: After most arithmetic, six status flags are updated (lesson 05 covered them): CF for unsigned overflow (carry or borrow), ZF when the result is 0, SF copying the top bit, OF for signed overflow, PF for even parity of the low byte, and AF for a carry out of bit 3.

ADD, step by step: ADD destination, source means destination = destination + source. The destination can be a register or memory, the source can be a register, memory or an immediate number, but both cannot be memory, and both must be the same size. Example: MOV AL, 200 then ADD AL, 100. The true answer is 300, but AL holds only 8 bits, maximum 255. The ALU computes 300 minus 256 = 44, which is 2Ch, and sets CF = 1 to say the unsigned answer spilled over. Viewed as signed numbers, 200 in AL means -56, and -56 + 100 = 44 fits fine, so OF = 0.

The same ADD, a different story: MOV AL, 100 then ADD AL, 50 gives 150, which is 96h. Unsigned, 150 fits in 8 bits, so CF = 0. But signed 8-bit numbers only go from -128 to +127, and 150 does not fit. The top bit of 96h is 1, so the CPU would read it as -106. Two positive numbers gave a negative-looking answer, so the CPU sets OF = 1 and SF = 1. Key idea: the CPU does not know if you meant signed or unsigned. It sets both CF and OF, and you decide which flag to trust.

ADC, adding with carry: ADC destination, source means destination = destination + source + CF. Why would anyone want that? Because registers are only 16 bits, but sometimes you need bigger numbers, like a 32-bit total. You add the low halves with ADD, which may produce a carry, then add the high halves with ADC, which pulls that carry in, exactly like the hand-carry in school addition.

Worked 32-bit addition: Suppose the first number is 0001FFFFh and the second is 00000001h. Keep the low words in AX and BX and the high words in DX and CX. So AX = FFFFh, DX = 0001h, BX = 0001h, CX = 0000h. Step 1: ADD AX, BX gives FFFFh + 0001h = 10000h, which does not fit, so AX = 0000h and CF = 1. Step 2: ADC DX, CX gives 0001h + 0000h + 1 = 0002h. The final answer DX:AX = 0002:0000, which is 00020000h. Correct! If you had used ADD instead of ADC in step 2, you would get 00010000h, a silent wrong answer.

SUB and SBB: SUB destination, source means destination = destination - source. If the unsigned source was bigger, a borrow happens and CF = 1. Example: MOV AL, 5 then SUB AL, 7 gives FEh, which is -2 in signed form, with CF = 1 because 5 is less than 7 unsigned. SBB is subtract with borrow: destination = destination - source - CF. It is the partner of ADC for big numbers. Subtract low words with SUB, then high words with SBB, and the borrow travels across.

INC and DEC: INC adds 1 and DEC subtracts 1. They are shorter and handy for counters and pointers. One special detail many students miss: INC and DEC do not change the carry flag. They update ZF, SF, OF, AF and PF, but CF keeps its old value. Intel designed it this way so you can use INC on a pointer inside a loop that is chaining ADC operations, without destroying the carry you are carrying along. So if you want to test whether a register wrapped from FFFFh to 0000h after INC, check ZF, not CF.

NEG: NEG operand replaces the value with its two's complement, which means it flips the sign. If AL = 5 (00000101b), NEG AL gives FBh, which is -5. Internally the CPU computes 0 minus the operand. That is why CF becomes 1 for every value except 0, since subtracting anything nonzero from 0 needs a borrow. A cute trap: NEG on -128 (80h) gives 80h again, because +128 cannot fit in 8 signed bits, and OF = 1 tells you so.

CMP, the subtraction that throws away its answer: CMP destination, source does the same work as SUB, sets the same flags, but does not store the result. Both operands stay unchanged. It exists only to set flags for the jump instructions you will meet in lesson 14. Example: if AX = 10 and BX = 10, CMP AX, BX gives ZF = 1. If AX = 3 and BX = 10, the subtraction needs a borrow, so CF = 1 (AX is smaller as unsigned) and the sign of the result says it is smaller as signed too.

MUL, unsigned multiply: Multiplying two 8-bit numbers can give up to a 16-bit answer, since 255 times 255 = 65025. So MUL uses fixed, hidden registers. For a byte: MUL BL means AX = AL times BL. For a word: MUL BX means DX:AX = AX times BX, with the high 16 bits in DX and the low 16 bits in AX. You only name one operand, and it must be a register or memory. On the original 8086 you cannot write MUL 5 with an immediate number; you first put 5 in a register. After MUL, CF and OF are both 1 if the upper half (AH or DX) is not zero, so you can tell if the answer needed the extra space.

MUL traced: MOV AL, 20, MOV BL, 30, MUL BL. The product is 600, which is 0258h. So AX = 0258h, meaning AH = 02h and AL = 58h. Since AH is not zero, CF = OF = 1. If you only looked at AL you would see 58h, which is 88, and wonder where your 600 went. Lesson: after a byte MUL, read all of AX.

IMUL, signed multiply: Bits do not know if they are signed. FEh could be 254 or -2. Suppose AL = FEh and BL = 3. MUL BL treats them as unsigned: 254 times 3 = 762 = 02FAh. IMUL BL treats them as signed: -2 times 3 = -6 = FFFAh. Same bits, different instruction, different answer. That is why the 8086 has both. For IMUL, CF and OF become 1 when the upper half is not just a sign extension of the lower half, meaning the result really needed the bigger size.

DIV, unsigned divide: Division is multiply backwards, so it uses the same hidden registers. For a byte divisor: DIV BL divides AX by BL, the quotient goes to AL and the remainder goes to AH. For a word divisor: DIV BX divides the 32-bit DX:AX by BX, the quotient goes to AX and the remainder goes to DX. Example: MOV AX, 100, MOV BL, 7, DIV BL. 100 divided by 7 is 14 remainder 2, so AL = 14 (0Eh) and AH = 2. Think of sharing 100 mangoes among 7 friends: each gets 14, and 2 stay in the basket.

Divide error: What if the quotient does not fit? MOV AX, 1000, MOV BL, 2, DIV BL should give 500, but AL can only hold up to 255. The 8086 cannot store it, so it raises a type 0 interrupt, the divide error. The same happens if you divide by zero. In DOS, this usually prints a 'Divide overflow' message and kills the program. Fix: use a word divide instead, putting 1000 in AX, 0 in DX, 2 in BX, then DIV BX gives AX = 500, DX = 0.

The forgotten DX bug: In a word divide, DX is part of the dividend. If DX still holds some old value, say 0005h from an earlier MUL, then DIV BX divides 0005xxxxh, a huge number, and you get a wrong quotient or a divide error. Before an unsigned word DIV, always clear DX with MOV DX, 0 or XOR DX, DX. This single line saves more students in exams than any other.

IDIV, CBW and CWD: IDIV is the signed divide, using the same registers. The remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 divided by 2 gives quotient -3 and remainder -1. For signed division you cannot just clear AH or DX, because a negative number needs its upper half filled with 1s. CBW (convert byte to word) copies the sign bit of AL into all of AH. CWD (convert word to double) copies the sign bit of AX into all of DX. Example: AL = F9h (-7). CBW makes AX = FFF9h, still -7. Then MOV BL, 2 and IDIV BL gives AL = FDh (-3) and AH = FFh (-1).

When to use what: Use ADD and SUB for normal 8 or 16-bit maths. Use ADC and SBB when numbers are wider than 16 bits. Use INC and DEC for counters and pointers. Use CMP when you only want to decide something. Use MUL and DIV for unsigned values like prices, counts and addresses, and IMUL and IDIV for values that can be negative, like temperature or profit and loss. When not to use MUL or DIV: if you multiply or divide by 2, 4, 8 or another power of two, a shift instruction (lesson 13) does it far faster. On the 8086 a MUL takes dozens of clock cycles while an ADD or shift takes only a few.

Real-life example 1, a shop bill: A grocery in Mirpur sells rice at 68 taka per kg and a customer buys 12 kg. MOV AL, 68, MOV BL, 12, MUL BL gives AX = 816, which is 0330h. Notice it needed AH, because 816 is bigger than 255. Now the shop offers the bill split into 3 equal instalments: MOV DX, 0, MOV BX, 3, DIV BX gives AX = 272 taka per instalment and DX = 0 remainder. A digital cash register in a shop is doing this kind of work inside its processor.

Real-life example 2, a bigger total: A small business in Chattogram wants to add two monthly sales figures, 70,000 taka and 65,000 taka. Each fits in 16 bits (max 65,535)? No, 70,000 does not fit! So we store them as 32-bit numbers in two registers each: 70,000 = 0001:1170h and 65,000 = 0000:FDE8h. ADD the low words: 1170h + FDE8h = 10F58h, so the low word becomes 0F58h with CF = 1. ADC the high words: 0001h + 0000h + 1 = 0002h. Result 0002:0F58h = 135,000 taka. Correct, thanks to the carry riding along.

Common mistakes: Thinking MUL BL puts the answer in BL. It does not; the answer lives in AX. Forgetting to clear DX before a word DIV. Using CBW or CWD for unsigned numbers, which turns big positive values into wrong negative ones. Checking CF after INC. Writing MUL 10 with an immediate on the 8086. Mixing sizes like ADD AX, BL, which the assembler rejects. And trusting CF for signed numbers or OF for unsigned ones.

What exams ask: Find AX, CF and OF after a given ADD or MUL. Add two 32-bit numbers with ADC. Say where quotient and remainder go after byte and word DIV. Compare MUL and IMUL with an example. Explain divide overflow. Find the average of five numbers.

Recap: Arithmetic instructions make the ALU do maths and report through the flags. ADC and SBB carry across words for big numbers. MUL and DIV use AX and DX as hidden partners, and the signed versions need CBW or CWD first. Next, we will see how the 8086 handles decimal digits directly with BCD and ASCII arithmetic.
key_points: ADD/SUB set CF for unsigned overflow and OF for signed overflow; the CPU sets both, you choose which to read.
ADC adds the carry, SBB subtracts the borrow, letting you build 32-bit or bigger maths from 16-bit pieces.
INC and DEC do not change CF; NEG makes the two's complement; CMP subtracts only to set flags.
MUL byte: AX = AL x operand. MUL word: DX:AX = AX x operand. No immediate operand on the 8086.
DIV byte: AX / operand gives AL quotient, AH remainder. DIV word: DX:AX / operand gives AX quotient, DX remainder.
A quotient too big or a zero divisor raises a type 0 divide error interrupt.
Clear DX before an unsigned word DIV; use CBW or CWD before IDIV for signed values.
lessons.tip: For every arithmetic question, draw the registers as boxes (AH, AL, DX, AX) and write the hex value in each after every line. Most exam marks are lost by not tracking DX and AH.
lessons.task: On paper, trace MOV AX, 0FFFFh then ADD AX, 1 and write AX, CF, ZF, SF and OF. Then trace MOV AL, 9, MOV BL, 4, MUL BL, then DIV BL again and check you get back 9 with remainder 0. If you have emu8086 or DOSBox, run both and watch the flags.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 200 and ADD AL, 100, what is in AL and CF?
quiz.explain: 300 does not fit in 8 bits; 300 - 256 = 44 and the carry out sets CF.

quiz.q: Where does the 8086 put the result of MUL BX?
quiz.explain: A word multiply makes up to 32 bits: high word in DX, low word in AX.

quiz.q: After MOV AX, 100, MOV BL, 7, DIV BL, what are AL and AH?
quiz.explain: 100 / 7 = 14 remainder 2; quotient in AL, remainder in AH.

quiz.q: Which instruction does NOT change the carry flag?
quiz.explain: INC and DEC leave CF unchanged on purpose.

quiz.q: Why is ADC used when adding two 32-bit numbers on the 8086?
options: It adds the carry from the low-word addition into the high words
quiz.explain: ADD the low words, then ADC the high words so the carry is included.

lessons.title: BCD and ASCII Arithmetic: DAA, DAS, AAA, AAS, AAM, AAD
lessons.content:
Type 7 on a calculator, press plus, type 8, press equals. The screen shows 15, as two separate digits, a 1 and a 5. Inside the computer, though, 15 is normally stored as binary 00001111. To show it, the computer must split that binary value back into decimal digits, which needs division, and division is slow. What if the computer simply kept the number as decimal digits all along? That is the idea behind BCD, and the 8086 has special instructions to do arithmetic directly on decimal digits.

What BCD is: BCD means binary coded decimal. Each decimal digit 0 to 9 gets its own 4-bit pattern: 0 is 0000, 5 is 0101, 9 is 1001. The six patterns 1010 to 1111 (A to F in hex) are simply never used. So the decimal number 47 in BCD is 0100 0111, which written in hex looks exactly like 47h. That is the cute part: in BCD, the hex digits you see are the decimal digits you mean.

Packed vs unpacked: There are two ways to put BCD into bytes. Packed BCD squeezes two digits into one byte, one per nibble (a nibble is 4 bits). So 47 is stored as the single byte 47h. Unpacked BCD puts one digit per byte, in the low nibble, with the high nibble 0. So 47 becomes two bytes, 04h and 07h. Packed saves memory; unpacked is closer to how digits are typed and displayed.

Where ASCII comes in: When you press the 7 key, DOS gives your program the ASCII code of the character '7', which is 37h, not the number 7. The ASCII codes of '0' to '9' are 30h to 39h. Look carefully: the low nibble is already the digit, and the high nibble is just 3. So an ASCII digit is basically an unpacked BCD digit with a 3 stuck on top. To turn '7' into 7, do SUB AL, 30h or AND AL, 0Fh. To turn 7 back into '7' for printing, do ADD AL, 30h or OR AL, 30h.

The problem: The ALU only knows binary addition. If you add BCD 47h and 38h as plain binary, you get 7Fh. But 47 plus 38 in decimal is 85, and 7Fh is not even a valid BCD number, since F is not a decimal digit. Binary carries happen at 16, decimal carries happen at 10, and the difference between them is 6. That number 6 is the whole secret of BCD correction.

Before these instructions: Without help, a programmer would add the digits, then write extra code to check each nibble, compare it with 9, and fix it up manually. That is slow and easy to get wrong. Intel solved it with six adjust instructions. You first do a normal binary ADD, SUB, MUL or DIV, and then one adjust instruction repairs the answer into correct decimal. The adjust instructions work on AL (and sometimes AH), and they use the AF flag, the carry out of bit 3, to know whether the low digit already overflowed.

DAA, decimal adjust after addition: Use it right after adding two packed BCD bytes into AL. The rule has two parts. Part 1: if the low nibble of AL is more than 9, or AF = 1, add 06h to AL. Part 2: if the original AL was more than 99h, or CF = 1, add 60h to AL and set CF = 1. Adding 6 skips over the six unused patterns A to F so the digit wraps at 10, just like decimal.

DAA traced, example 1: MOV AL, 47h, ADD AL, 38h gives AL = 7Fh. Low nibble F is more than 9, so add 6: 7Fh + 6 = 85h. High nibble 8 is fine, CF = 0. AL = 85h, which reads as decimal 85. And 47 + 38 really is 85. The correction worked.

DAA traced, example 2: MOV AL, 59h, ADD AL, 48h. Binary: 59h + 48h = A1h. While adding, 9 + 8 = 17 caused a carry out of bit 3, so AF = 1. The low nibble 1 looks fine, but AF = 1 tells DAA the digit secretly overflowed, so add 6: A7h. Now the high nibble A is more than 9, so add 60h: A7h + 60h = 107h, which leaves AL = 07h with CF = 1. Read it as carry 1 and AL 07, which is 107. Check: 59 + 48 = 107. This is exactly why AF exists; without it, DAA could not catch that hidden overflow.

DAS, decimal adjust after subtraction: It is the mirror image of DAA. After SUB on packed BCD in AL: if the low nibble is more than 9 or AF = 1, subtract 6; if the original AL was more than 99h or CF = 1, subtract 60h and set CF = 1. Example: MOV AL, 85h, SUB AL, 38h gives 4Dh. Low nibble D is more than 9 (and 5 minus 8 also borrowed, so AF = 1), so subtract 6: 47h. Check: 85 - 38 = 47. Correct.

Adding big BCD numbers: Packed BCD numbers longer than two digits are stored as several bytes. You add them byte by byte from the lowest, using ADD and DAA for the first byte, then ADC and DAA for the rest, so the decimal carry rides along. Example: 1234 + 5678. Low bytes: 34h + 78h = ACh, DAA gives 12h with CF = 1. High bytes: 12h + 56h + 1 = 69h, DAA leaves 69h. Answer 6912. Check: 1234 + 5678 = 6912.

AAA, ASCII adjust after addition: This one works on unpacked digits and ASCII digits, and it uses both AL and AH. Rule: if the low nibble of AL is more than 9 or AF = 1, add 6 to AL, add 1 to AH, and set AF and CF to 1; otherwise clear AF and CF. In both cases it then clears the high nibble of AL. So after AAA, AL holds a single digit 0 to 9, and AH has been bumped if there was a decimal carry.

AAA traced: The user types '8' and '5'. MOV AH, 0, MOV AL, '8' (38h), ADD AL, '5' (35h) gives AL = 6Dh. Low nibble D is more than 9, so AL = 6Dh + 6 = 73h and AH = 1. Then the high nibble is cleared, AL = 03h. Now AX = 0103h, the unpacked digits 1 and 3, meaning 13. Check: 8 + 5 = 13. To print it, OR AX, 3030h gives 3133h, which is '1' in AH and '3' in AL. Notice we never subtracted 30h before adding; AAA ignored the 3s for us by clearing the high nibble.

AAS, ASCII adjust after subtraction: The mirror of AAA. If the low nibble of AL is more than 9 or AF = 1, subtract 6 from AL, subtract 1 from AH, set AF and CF; then clear the high nibble of AL. Example: AL = '3' (33h), SUB AL, '5' (35h) gives FEh with a borrow from the low nibble, so AF = 1. AAS makes AL = FEh - 6 = F8h, then 08h, AH decreases by 1, and CF = 1. The answer means 8 with a borrow from the tens place, like 13 - 5 = 8 in school subtraction.

AAM, ASCII adjust after multiply: Multiply two unpacked digits with a normal MUL, then AAM splits the binary answer into two digits. It does AH = AL divided by 10 and AL = AL mod 10. Example: MOV AL, 7, MOV BL, 8, MUL BL gives AX = 56 (38h). AAM gives AH = 5, AL = 6. Now OR AX, 3030h makes them printable '5' and '6'. Inside, AAM is really a small divide by 10, which is why it is also a handy trick to split any value from 0 to 99 in AL into two digits.

AAD, ASCII adjust before division: This one is special because you use it before the divide, not after. It turns two unpacked digits in AH and AL into one binary number: AL = AH times 10 plus AL, and AH = 0. Example: AX = 0705h means the digits 7 and 5, or 75. AAD makes AL = 75 (4Bh) and AH = 0. Now MOV BL, 5 and DIV BL gives AL = 15, AH = 0. Then AAM turns 15 into AH = 1, AL = 5. Why before? Because DIV needs a binary dividend, so the digits must be converted first.

A quick comparison: DAA and DAS work on packed BCD, two digits per byte, and only for addition and subtraction. AAA, AAS, AAM and AAD work on unpacked BCD, one digit per byte, and cover all four operations. There is no adjust for packed multiply or divide. All of them work on AL, and the unpacked ones also use AH.

When to use BCD: When numbers must be shown as decimal digits often, like on clocks, meters and 7-segment displays. When exact decimal values matter, like money, because binary fractions cannot store 0.1 exactly. Many real-time clock chips, including the classic PC CMOS clock, keep the time in BCD by default, so a time like 12:59 is stored as bytes 12h and 59h and can go straight to a display.

When not to use BCD: For general maths, plain binary is faster and smaller. A byte holds 0 to 255 in binary but only 0 to 99 in packed BCD. Also, these adjust instructions are legacy: in 64-bit mode on modern x86-64 processors, DAA, DAS, AAA, AAS, AAM and AAD are not valid instructions at all. Modern software usually stores money as integer poisha or uses decimal libraries instead.

Real-life example 1, a digital clock: Think of the clock above the counter of a bus company office in Gabtoli, showing 09:59. Store the minutes in packed BCD as 59h. One minute passes: MOV AL, 59h, ADD AL, 1 gives 5Ah. DAA sees low nibble A, adds 6: 60h. Now check if AL equals 60h; if yes, set minutes to 00h and add 1 to the hour byte the same way, so 09h becomes 10h. The display shows 10:00 without a single division, because each nibble already is a digit for the 7-segment display.

Real-life example 2, a simple calculator program: Your program reads two single-digit keys with DOS, say '9' and '6'. It puts '9' in AL and 0 in AH, adds '6', and does AAA: 39h + 36h = 6Fh, low nibble F is more than 9, so AL becomes 05h and AH becomes 1. OR AX, 3030h gives '1' and '5'. Print AH then AL, and the screen shows 15. That is a tiny model of what a shop calculator does.

Common mistakes: Using DAA after an INC or after a subtraction, when it is only for addition. Forgetting that DAA works only on AL, so ADD BL, CL followed by DAA fixes the wrong register. Forgetting to clear AH before AAA, so an old value in AH spoils the tens digit. Using AAD after the division instead of before. Treating ASCII '5' (35h) as the number 5. Thinking 10h in packed BCD is sixteen; it means ten.

What exams ask: Represent 1995 in packed and unpacked BCD. Trace ADD then DAA for given values and show AL, AF and CF. Explain why 6 is added in decimal adjustment. Write a program to add two ASCII digits and print the result. Explain AAM and AAD with an example and say why AAD comes before DIV. Add two 4-digit packed BCD numbers using ADC and DAA.

Recap: BCD stores each decimal digit in 4 bits, packed (two per byte) or unpacked (one per byte), and ASCII digits are unpacked digits plus 30h. The ALU still adds in binary, so a correction of 6 per digit is needed. DAA and DAS fix packed addition and subtraction, AAA and AAS fix unpacked addition and subtraction, AAM splits a product into two digits, and AAD joins two digits before a division. Next, we move from decimal digits down to single bits with logic, shift and rotate instructions.
key_points: BCD stores each decimal digit in 4 bits; packed puts two digits in a byte (47 = 47h), unpacked puts one (04h, 07h).
ASCII '0' to '9' are 30h to 39h; subtract or mask 30h to get the digit, add or OR 30h to print it.
Binary carries at 16, decimal at 10, so the adjust instructions add or subtract 6 per digit.
DAA/DAS fix packed BCD in AL after ADD/SUB, using AF and CF.
AAA/AAS fix unpacked digits after ADD/SUB, clear AL's high nibble and carry into or borrow from AH.
AAM after MUL: AH = AL / 10, AL = AL mod 10. AAD before DIV: AL = AH x 10 + AL, AH = 0.
BCD suits clocks, displays and money; binary is faster for general maths; these instructions are invalid in 64-bit mode.
lessons.tip: Remember the magic 6: every decimal adjust is just 'add or subtract 6 when a nibble passed 9 or AF says it overflowed'. Learn that one idea and all six instructions make sense.
lessons.task: On paper, add 2748 + 1596 in packed BCD byte by byte: low bytes with ADD then DAA, high bytes with ADC then DAA. Write AL, AF and CF after each step and check you get 4344.

quiz.q: How is decimal 47 stored in packed BCD?
quiz.explain: Packed BCD puts one digit per nibble, so 47 becomes the byte 47h.

quiz.q: After MOV AL, 47h and ADD AL, 38h, AL = 7Fh. What does DAA make AL?
quiz.explain: Low nibble F is more than 9, so DAA adds 6: 7Fh + 6 = 85h.

quiz.q: What does AAM do after MOV AL, 7, MOV BL, 8, MUL BL?
quiz.explain: AAM splits AL = 56 into AH = 56 / 10 = 5 and AL = 56 mod 10 = 6.

quiz.q: Which adjust instruction is used BEFORE the arithmetic operation?
quiz.explain: AAD converts two unpacked digits into binary before DIV.

quiz.q: What is the ASCII code of the character '7'?
quiz.explain: ASCII digits are 30h to 39h, so '7' is 37h.

lessons.title: Logic, Shift and Rotate Instructions
lessons.content:
Imagine a row of eight light switches on a wall in your house: fan, tube light, bulb, and so on. Sometimes you want to turn one switch off without touching the others. Sometimes you want to flip one. Sometimes you want to slide every switch's position one step to the left. A byte is exactly such a row of eight switches, and the 8086 has instructions that work on those switches one by one. In this lesson we meet the logic instructions AND, OR, XOR, NOT and TEST, and the shift and rotate instructions that slide bits left and right.

What they are: Logic instructions do bitwise operations. Bitwise means the CPU takes bit 0 of one operand with bit 0 of the other, bit 1 with bit 1, and so on, with no carries between columns. Shift instructions move all bits of a register or memory value left or right, dropping a bit out of one end and filling the other end. Rotate instructions do the same, but the bit falling out of one end comes back in at the other end, like a circle.

Why they matter: Hardware talks in bits. A keyboard controller reports a key press in one bit of a status byte. An I/O port drives eight LEDs with eight bits. A flag byte in a program may store eight yes or no answers. To read, set, clear or flip one bit without disturbing the others, you need logic instructions. Shifts give you super fast multiply and divide by powers of two, and they are the building blocks for printing numbers in binary, packing and unpacking BCD, and checksums.

The truth table refresher: AND gives 1 only if both bits are 1. OR gives 1 if at least one bit is 1. XOR gives 1 if the bits are different. NOT flips every bit. Example with AL = 1100 1010b and BL = 1010 0110b: AND AL, BL gives 1000 0010b. OR gives 1110 1110b. XOR gives 0110 1100b. NOT AL alone gives 0011 0101b. Do one column at a time and you cannot go wrong.

Flags after logic: AND, OR, XOR and TEST always clear CF and OF to 0, because there is no carry or overflow in bitwise work. They set ZF, SF and PF from the result, like arithmetic does. NOT is unusual: it changes no flags at all. This matters when you follow a logic instruction with a conditional jump, for example JZ after AND.

Masking with AND, clearing bits: A mask is a pattern that says which bits to keep. AND with 1 keeps a bit, AND with 0 forces it to 0. Example: to keep only the low nibble of AL, do AND AL, 0Fh. If AL = 37h (the ASCII code of '7'), AND AL, 0Fh gives 07h, the digit 7. This is the same trick you saw in the BCD lesson, and now you know why it works: 0Fh is 0000 1111b, so the top four bits are wiped and the bottom four survive.

Setting bits with OR: OR with 1 forces a bit to 1, OR with 0 leaves it alone. To turn on bit 7 of AL without touching others, do OR AL, 80h, since 80h is 1000 0000b. To make digit 5 printable, OR AL, 30h turns 05h into 35h, which is '5'.

Toggling with XOR: XOR with 1 flips a bit, XOR with 0 leaves it. Lowercase 'a' is 61h and uppercase 'A' is 41h; the only difference is bit 5 (20h). So XOR AL, 20h switches the case of a letter, AND AL, 0DFh forces uppercase, and OR AL, 20h forces lowercase. Another favourite: XOR AX, AX makes AX zero, because any bit XOR itself is 0. Programmers use it instead of MOV AX, 0 because the instruction is shorter, though note it also changes the flags while MOV does not.

TEST, checking without changing: TEST destination, source does an AND but throws the result away, keeping only the flags, just like CMP is a SUB that throws its result away. Example: to know if bit 0 of AL is set, which also tells you if the number is odd, write TEST AL, 01h. If bit 0 is 0, the AND result is 0 and ZF = 1. If bit 0 is 1, ZF = 0. Then a JZ or JNZ can decide. AL itself is untouched, which is the whole point.

Shifts, the idea: Think of a queue of eight people on a bench, and everyone slides one seat left. The person at the left end falls off, and an empty seat appears on the right. In the 8086, the bit that falls off goes into CF, so you can still check it. On the 8086 the shift count is either the number 1, written like SHL AL, 1, or the value in CL, written like SHL AL, CL. Writing SHL AL, 3 with an immediate count bigger than 1 only became legal on the 80186 and later, so for the 8086 put 3 in CL first.

SHL and SAL, shift left: Both names mean the same instruction. Every bit moves one place left, a 0 enters at bit 0, and the old bit 7 (or bit 15) goes into CF. Example: AL = 0001 0110b (22). SHL AL, 1 gives 0010 1100b (44), CF = 0. Shifting left once multiplies by 2, twice by 4, n times by 2 to the power n, as long as no 1 bit falls out. If AL = 1000 0001b, SHL AL, 1 gives 0000 0010b with CF = 1, and the answer is wrong as an unsigned number, which CF warns you about.

SHR, logical shift right: Every bit moves one place right, a 0 enters at the top, and the old bit 0 goes into CF. For unsigned numbers this divides by 2 and throws away the remainder, which lands in CF. Example: AL = 45 (0010 1101b). SHR AL, 1 gives 0001 0110b (22), CF = 1, meaning 45 / 2 = 22 remainder 1.

SAR, arithmetic shift right: For signed numbers, filling the top with 0 would turn a negative number positive. SAR instead copies the old sign bit back into the top, so the sign stays. Example: AL = F8h (1111 1000b, which is -8). SAR AL, 1 gives 1111 1100b (FCh, which is -4). Correct. One subtle point: for odd negative numbers SAR rounds toward minus infinity. -5 is FBh, SAR AL, 1 gives FDh, which is -3, while IDIV by 2 would give -2. So SAR is not always an exact replacement for IDIV.

Rotates: ROL rotates left: every bit moves left, and the old top bit goes into both bit 0 and CF. ROR rotates right: the old bit 0 goes to the top and into CF. Nothing is lost; after 8 rotates of a byte you get the original back. Example: AL = 1001 0011b. ROL AL, 1 gives 0010 0111b with CF = 1. A handy trick: MOV CL, 4 then ROL AL, CL swaps the two nibbles, turning 47h into 74h.

RCL and RCR, rotate through carry: These treat CF as an extra bit in the circle, making a 9-bit loop for a byte or a 17-bit loop for a word. RCL moves the top bit into CF and the old CF into bit 0. RCR does the mirror. Why bother? To shift a 32-bit number held in DX:AX left by one: SHL AX, 1 pushes AX's top bit into CF, then RCL DX, 1 pulls it into DX's bottom. Together they act like one 32-bit shift, the same team idea as ADD with ADC.

Flags after shifts and rotates: Shifts set CF to the last bit shifted out and update ZF, SF and PF from the result. Rotates change only CF and OF, leaving ZF and SF alone. For one-bit shifts, OF is set when the sign bit changed, which for SHL signals a signed overflow. For multi-bit counts OF is undefined, so do not rely on it.

Worked trick, multiply by 10 without MUL: 10x = 8x + 2x. MOV BX, AX, SHL AX, 1 (AX is now 2x), MOV CL, 3, SHL BX, CL (BX is now 8x), ADD AX, BX (AX is 10x). If AX started at 7: AX becomes 14, BX becomes 56, and the sum is 70. This is useful when reading a decimal number digit by digit, because each new digit means old value times 10 plus the digit. On the 8086 this short sequence beats MUL by a lot of clock cycles.

Worked trick, splitting packed BCD: AL = 59h holds the digits 5 and 9. MOV AH, AL, AND AL, 0Fh leaves AL = 09h. MOV CL, 4, SHR AH, CL leaves AH = 05h. Now AX = 0509h, two unpacked digits ready for printing with OR AX, 3030h.

Worked trick, counting 1 bits: To count the 1s in AX, repeat 16 times: SHL AX, 1, and if CF = 1 increase a counter. For AX = 00F1h (0000 0000 1111 0001b) you get 5. Using ROL instead of SHL has a bonus: after 16 rotates AX is back to its original value. The same pattern prints a number in binary: rotate left, look at CF, print '1' if set and '0' if not.

When to use, when not: Use AND, OR, XOR to read, set, clear or flip particular bits, and TEST when you only need the answer. Use SHL and SHR for unsigned multiply and divide by powers of two, and SAR for signed division only when rounding toward minus infinity is fine. Do not use shifts for multiplying by non-powers of two unless you combine them carefully, and do not use SHR on signed numbers. For readability in large programs, a clear MUL can be better than a clever shift chain; on modern CPUs the speed gap is much smaller than on the 8086.

Real-life example 1, an LED panel: A small factory in Gazipur uses an 8086 trainer board where an output port drives eight status LEDs, one per machine. The program keeps a copy of the port value in AL. Machine 3 starts: OR AL, 08h turns on bit 3. Machine 6 stops: AND AL, 0BFh clears bit 6 (0BFh is 1011 1111b). The alarm LED on bit 7 should blink: XOR AL, 80h each half second. Then OUT sends AL to the port. Every change touches one LED and leaves the rest exactly as they were.

Real-life example 2, attendance in bits: A class teacher in a Sylhet school wants to store attendance for 16 students in one word, one bit per student. Present means 1. Roll 4 arrives: OR AX, 0010h. To check if roll 9 is present: TEST AX, 0200h then JNZ PRESENT. To count how many came, use the shift-and-count loop. Sixteen yes or no answers fit in just 2 bytes instead of 16 bytes.

Common mistakes: Writing SHL AX, 4 on the 8086 instead of putting 4 in CL. Using SHR to halve a negative number. Expecting NOT to set ZF. Thinking XOR AX, AX keeps the flags like MOV does. Confusing ROL with RCL, so the old carry sneaks into the result. Forgetting that AND, OR and XOR clear CF, which can break a following JC. Writing the mask in decimal when you meant hex, like AND AL, 15 versus AND AL, 0Fh, which happen to be equal, but AND AL, 80 is not the same as 80h.

What exams ask: Give AL and the flags after an AND, OR, XOR or shift on given values. Explain the difference between SHR and SAR, and between ROL and RCL, with diagrams. Write code to convert a lowercase string to uppercase, count the 1s in a register, multiply by 10 using shifts, or print a number in binary. Explain masking with an example.

Recap: Logic instructions work on each bit separately: AND clears bits, OR sets them, XOR flips them, NOT inverts all, and TEST checks without changing.
