Shifts slide bits and drop one into CF: SHL multiplies by 2, SHR divides unsigned numbers by 2, SAR keeps the sign. Rotates go round in a circle, and RCL or RCR include CF to build bigger shifts. On the 8086 multi-bit counts go in CL. Next we use flags and CMP to make decisions with jumps.
key_points: AND clears bits (mask with 0), OR sets bits (mask with 1), XOR flips bits, NOT inverts everything.
AND, OR, XOR and TEST clear CF and OF and set ZF, SF, PF; NOT changes no flags.
TEST is an AND that keeps only the flags, used with JZ/JNZ to check bits.
SHL/SAL multiply by 2 per step, SHR divides unsigned by 2, SAR divides signed and keeps the sign.
The bit shifted out goes into CF; on the 8086 the count is 1 or CL.
ROL/ROR rotate in a circle; RCL/RCR rotate through CF to chain multiword shifts.
Shift tricks: x10 = x8 + x2, nibble swap with ROL by 4, counting or printing bits via CF.
lessons.tip: Always write values in binary on paper before a logic or shift question. Hex hides the bits; binary shows you exactly which switch moves where.
lessons.task: Take your roll number (or any number under 256), write it in binary, then work out by hand: AND with 0Fh, OR with 80h, XOR with FFh, SHL by 1, SHR by 1 and ROL by 4. Check the SHL and SHR answers by doubling and halving the decimal value.

quiz.q: AL = 37h. What does AND AL, 0Fh give?
quiz.explain: 0Fh keeps only the low nibble, so 37h becomes 07h.

quiz.q: Which instruction keeps the sign of a negative number while dividing by 2?
quiz.explain: SAR copies the sign bit into the top, so negatives stay negative.

quiz.q: What does TEST AL, 01h do?
options: Sets ZF from AL AND 01h without changing AL
quiz.explain: TEST is an AND that only updates flags.

quiz.q: On the 8086, how do you shift AX left by 3 places?
options: MOV CL, 3 then SHL AX, CL
MOV CX, AX then SHL CX
quiz.explain: The 8086 accepts a shift count of 1 or CL; immediate counts above 1 came with the 80186.

quiz.q: AL = 1001 0011b. What is AL after ROL AL, 1?
quiz.explain: Every bit moves left and the old top bit 1 wraps into bit 0.

lessons.title: Flow Control: Jumps, Conditions, if/else and while
lessons.content:
When you walk home from school, you make decisions all the time. If it is raining, take the rickshaw; otherwise walk. If the shop is open, buy a chocolate. In Python or C, you write such decisions with if, else and while. But the 8086 has no if and no while. It only has one simple trick: change the address of the next instruction. Every decision, every loop, every function call in every program on an x86 computer is built from that trick. This lesson shows you how.

What flow control is: Normally the CPU runs instructions one after another. The instruction pointer IP holds the offset of the next instruction, and after each one, IP moves forward by that instruction's length. A jump instruction breaks this straight line by loading a new value into IP (and sometimes CS). The next fetch then comes from the new place. A conditional jump does this only if certain flags are set; otherwise it does nothing and execution falls through to the next line.

The problem it solves: Without jumps, a program could only run top to bottom once, like reading a list. It could never repeat anything or choose between two paths. Jumps give a machine the power to decide and to repeat, which is what makes a computer more than a calculator.

Unconditional JMP: JMP label always jumps. The assembler turns the label into a number, and there are three kinds. A short jump stores a signed 8-bit displacement, so it can reach from 128 bytes back to 127 bytes forward. A near jump stores a 16-bit displacement and can go anywhere inside the same code segment, changing only IP. A far jump stores a new CS and a new IP, so it can go to a different segment. Short is 2 bytes, near is 3 bytes, far is 5 bytes, so assemblers pick short when the target is close.

How the displacement works, step by step: The displacement is measured from the instruction after the jump, because by the time the jump executes, IP already points there. Example: a 2-byte short JMP sits at offset 0100h, so the next instruction is at 0102h. The target is at 0110h. Displacement = 0110h - 0102h = 0Eh. The CPU adds 0Eh to IP = 0102h and gets 0110h. A backward jump just uses a negative displacement in two's complement. Because it is relative, the code still works if the whole program is loaded somewhere else in memory.

Indirect jumps: You can also jump to an address held in a register or memory, like JMP BX, which sets IP = BX. This is how jump tables work: put the addresses of several code blocks in a table, pick one with an index, and jump. It is the machine-level version of a switch statement.

What happens inside on a jump: In the 8086, the BIU has already prefetched the next few bytes into its instruction queue, assuming the code runs straight. When a jump is taken, those bytes are useless. The queue is flushed, and the BIU starts fetching from the new address, so the EU has to wait for fresh bytes. This is why taken jumps cost more clock cycles than not-taken ones, and why tight code avoids unnecessary jumps.

CMP plus conditional jump, the decision pair: A decision is usually two instructions. First CMP sets the flags by doing a hidden subtraction. Then a conditional jump reads the flags. Example: CMP AX, BX then JE SAME jumps to SAME only if AX equals BX, because equal values make the subtraction zero, so ZF = 1. Conditional jumps never change flags themselves, so you can test the same CMP result with two jumps in a row.

The equality jumps: JE (jump if equal) and JZ (jump if zero) are the same instruction, taken when ZF = 1. JNE and JNZ are taken when ZF = 0. Use the name that reads better: JE after CMP, JZ after DEC or AND.

Unsigned jumps, above and below: For unsigned numbers like counts, prices and addresses, Intel uses the words above and below. JA (jump if above) is taken when CF = 0 and ZF = 0. JAE (above or equal) when CF = 0. JB (below) when CF = 1. JBE (below or equal) when CF = 1 or ZF = 1. The logic: CMP does AX - BX; if AX is smaller as unsigned, the subtraction needs a borrow, so CF = 1.

Signed jumps, greater and less: For signed numbers, Intel uses greater and less. JG (greater) is taken when ZF = 0 and SF = OF. JGE when SF = OF. JL (less) when SF is not equal to OF. JLE when ZF = 1 or SF is not equal to OF. Why compare SF with OF? If the subtraction did not overflow, SF alone tells you if the result is negative, meaning AX is less. If it did overflow, the sign came out flipped, so SF lies, and OF = 1 corrects it. Example: AL = 100, BL = -100. CMP AL, BL computes 200, which overflows 8 bits to C8h, so SF = 1 and OF = 1. SF = OF, so JGE is taken, and indeed 100 is greater than -100.

Same bits, different answers: Let AL = FFh and BL = 01h, then CMP AL, BL. As unsigned, FFh is 255, bigger than 1, so JA is taken. As signed, FFh is -1, smaller than 1, so JG is not taken and JL is taken. The CMP was identical; only your choice of jump decided the meaning. This is the number one source of bugs in assembly decisions, so always ask: are these numbers signed or unsigned?

Single-flag jumps: Some jumps test one flag directly: JC and JNC for carry, JO and JNO for overflow, JS and JNS for sign, JP (also JPE) and JNP (also JPO) for parity. They are handy right after arithmetic, for example ADD AX, BX then JC TOO_BIG to catch an unsigned overflow.

The range limit of conditional jumps: On the 8086, every conditional jump is short only, so its target must be within -128 to +127 bytes. If the target is farther, the assembler gives an error like 'relative jump out of range'. The fix is to flip the condition and jump over a JMP: instead of JE FAR_AWAY, write JNE SKIP, JMP FAR_AWAY, SKIP:. Since the 80386, conditional jumps can also take a 16 or 32-bit displacement, so this problem mostly disappeared.

Building if-then: To write 'if AX equals 0 then BX = 1', jump around the body when the condition is false. CMP AX, 0, JNE END_IF, MOV BX, 1, END_IF:. Notice the trick: we test the opposite condition and skip, because the jump goes away from the body.

Building if-else: For signed 'if AX > BX then CX = 1 else CX = 2': CMP AX, BX, JLE ELSE_PART, MOV CX, 1, JMP END_IF, ELSE_PART: MOV CX, 2, END_IF:. Trace with AX = 5, BX = 3: CMP gives a positive result, JLE is not taken, CX = 1, then JMP skips the else. Trace with AX = 2, BX = 3: JLE is taken, CX = 2. The JMP after the then-part is essential; without it, the CPU would fall into the else-part and overwrite CX.

AND and OR conditions: For 'if AL >= 'A' and AL <= 'Z'', which checks an uppercase letter, any false part should skip the body: CMP AL, 'A', JB NOT_UPPER, CMP AL, 'Z', JA NOT_UPPER, then the body, then NOT_UPPER:. For an OR, any true part should enter the body: CMP AL, ' ', JE IS_SPACE, CMP AL, 13, JE IS_SPACE. Character codes are unsigned, so we use JB and JA, not JL and JG.

Building while and do-while: A while loop tests first: TOP: CMP AX, 100, JGE DONE, ADD AX, BX, JMP TOP, DONE:. The body may run zero times. A do-while runs the body first and tests at the end: TOP: ADD AX, BX, CMP AX, 100, JL TOP. It always runs at least once and uses one jump per round instead of two, which is why compilers often turn while loops into this shape with one test before entry. Lesson 15 adds the special LOOP instruction for counted loops.

When to use which: Use JE and JNE for equality of anything. Use JA, JB family for unsigned values: ASCII codes, array indexes, addresses, marks that cannot be negative. Use JG, JL family for signed values: temperatures, balances that can go negative, differences. Use JC or JO right after arithmetic to catch overflow. When not to jump: if a few instructions can compute a result without branching, like using AND for a mask, the code is often shorter and faster, because taken jumps flush the queue.

Real-life example 1, SSC grading: A school in Rajshahi wants a program to turn marks into a letter grade. In Bangladesh, 80 or more is A+, 70 to 79 is A, 60 to 69 is A-, 50 to 59 is B, 40 to 49 is C, 33 to 39 is D, and below 33 is F. With marks in AL: CMP AL, 80, JAE GRADE_APLUS, CMP AL, 70, JAE GRADE_A, and so on down to CMP AL, 33, JAE GRADE_D, then JMP GRADE_F. Each check runs only if all the higher ones failed, so the first true condition wins, exactly like an if-else-if ladder. Marks are never negative, so the unsigned JAE is right.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet check: When you send money from a mobile wallet, the system must check that your balance is enough. In assembly terms: MOV AX, BALANCE, CMP AX, AMOUNT, JB NOT_ENOUGH, SUB AX, AMOUNT, MOV BALANCE, AX, JMP DONE, NOT_ENOUGH: show the message, DONE:. If someone used the signed JL here and the balance were a large value above 32,767, it would look negative and the check would wrongly fail. Real wallet systems are written in high-level languages, but the compiled code still ends in the same CMP and jump.

Common mistakes: Using JG for unsigned values or JA for signed ones. Forgetting the JMP after the then-part of an if-else. Testing the wrong direction, like writing JE when you meant to skip on not equal. Putting an instruction that changes flags, such as ADD or INC, between CMP and the jump. Note that MOV does not change flags, so a MOV in between is safe. Getting 'jump out of range' and not knowing the flip-and-JMP fix. Writing CMP 5, AX, which is illegal because the destination cannot be an immediate.

What exams ask: Classify JMP as short, near and far with their ranges. Calculate a short jump displacement. Give the flag conditions for JA, JG, JB and JL. Explain why signed comparisons test SF = OF. Translate an if-else or while from C into 8086 assembly. Predict which branch is taken after CMP with given signed or unsigned values.

Recap: Flow control works by changing IP. JMP always jumps: short (plus or minus about 128 bytes), near (same segment) or far (new CS and IP). Decisions use CMP followed by a conditional jump that reads the flags: JE and JNE for equality, JA and JB for unsigned, JG and JL for signed, plus single-flag jumps. On the 8086 conditional jumps are short only. If, else and while are built by jumping over or back to blocks of code, usually by testing the opposite condition. Next, we build counted loops and work through arrays.
key_points: A jump changes IP (and for far jumps CS), so the next instruction comes from a new place.
JMP can be short (-128 to +127 bytes), near (anywhere in the segment) or far (new CS:IP).
Short and near displacements are counted from the instruction after the jump.
CMP sets flags, then a conditional jump reads them; jumps never change flags.
Unsigned: JA/JAE/JB/JBE use CF and ZF. Signed: JG/JGE/JL/JLE use ZF, SF and OF.
8086 conditional jumps are short only; flip the condition and use JMP for far targets.
if/else and while are built by jumping over or back to code, usually testing the opposite condition.
lessons.tip: Before writing any decision in assembly, write the C-style if or while first, then mark each value as signed or unsigned. Picking the right jump family becomes automatic.
lessons.task: Write on paper the 8086 code for: if AL is a digit '0' to '9', set BL = 1, else set BL = 0. Then trace it for AL = '7', AL = 'A' and AL = '/' and check which jumps are taken.

quiz.q: AL = FFh, BL = 01h, then CMP AL, BL. Which jump is taken?
quiz.explain: As unsigned, 255 is above 1, so JA is taken; as signed it is -1, so JG would not be taken.

quiz.q: What is the reach of a short jump?
options: -128 to +127 bytes from the next instruction
quiz.explain: A short jump uses a signed 8-bit displacement.

quiz.q: Which flag condition makes JL (jump if less) taken?
options: SF is not equal to OF
quiz.explain: Signed less means the sign of the result, corrected by overflow, is negative.

quiz.q: A 2-byte short JMP is at offset 0200h and the target is 0210h. What is the displacement?
quiz.explain: Displacement = target - next instruction = 0210h - 0202h = 0Eh.

quiz.q: Why is a JMP placed at the end of the then-part of an if-else?
quiz.explain: Without it, the CPU would fall through and also run the else-part.

lessons.title: Loops and Arrays: LOOP, LOOPE, LOOPNE and Bubble Sort
lessons.content:
A bowler in a cricket match bowls six balls in an over. The umpire counts them on his fingers: six, five, four, three, two, one, over. He does not think about it; he just counts down and stops at zero. The 8086 has an instruction that does exactly this, called LOOP, with the CX register as the umpire's fingers. In this lesson we build counted loops, loops that stop early, nested loops, and we use them to walk through arrays: adding them, finding the largest value, searching, and even sorting.

What a loop is: A loop is a block of code that runs again and again. In the last lesson you built loops with CMP and conditional jumps. That works for any condition. But the most common loop of all is 'do this exactly N times', and for that the 8086 gives a ready-made tool: put N in CX, write the body, and end with LOOP label.

How LOOP works internally: LOOP label does two things in one instruction. First, CX = CX - 1. Second, if CX is not zero, jump to label; if CX is zero, fall through to the next line. It is the same as DEC CX followed by JNZ label, with one important difference: LOOP does not change any flags, while DEC does. Like conditional jumps on the 8086, LOOP is a short jump, so the body must fit within about 128 bytes back.

A first loop, traced: Print a star 5 times. MOV CX, 5, then STAR: MOV DL, '*', MOV AH, 2, INT 21h, LOOP STAR. Trace: CX = 5, print, LOOP makes CX = 4 and jumps. Print, CX = 3. Print, CX = 2. Print, CX = 1. Print, CX = 0, and now LOOP does not jump. Five stars, exactly. Notice CX is decreased before the test, so the body runs CX times, not CX + 1 times.

The CX = 0 trap: What if CX is 0 when the loop starts? The body runs once, then LOOP does CX = 0 - 1, which wraps around to FFFFh, not zero, so it jumps back. The loop runs 65,536 times in total. If CX comes from user input or a calculation, guard against this with JCXZ, which means 'jump if CX is zero'. Write JCXZ SKIP before the loop and SKIP: after it. JCXZ only tests CX; it does not change it and does not look at flags.

LOOPE and LOOPNE, loops that can stop early: Sometimes you want to repeat up to N times, but stop as soon as something happens. LOOPE (also called LOOPZ) decreases CX and jumps back only if CX is not zero and ZF = 1. So it keeps going while things are equal. LOOPNE (also LOOPNZ) decreases CX and jumps back only if CX is not zero and ZF = 0, so it keeps going while things are not equal. After the loop ends, you check ZF to learn why it ended: because of the condition, or because CX ran out.

Arrays in memory, from zero: An array is just several values stored side by side in memory. In the data segment you write MARKS DB 72, 85, 64, 91, 58. DB means each value is one byte. The assembler places 72 at the address of MARKS, 85 at MARKS + 1, and so on. A word array uses DW, and then each element takes 2 bytes, so element i is at MARKS + 2i. There is nothing special in memory telling where an array ends; you, the programmer, must remember the count.

Walking through an array: To visit each element, keep the address of the current one in a pointer register, usually SI, and move it forward each round. LEA SI, MARKS (or MOV SI, OFFSET MARKS) puts the starting offset in SI. Then MOV AL, [SI] reads the current byte. INC SI moves to the next byte. For a word array, use MOV AX, [SI] and ADD SI, 2. Forgetting to step by 2 for words is one of the most common array bugs.

Sum of an array, traced: Data: NUMS DB 4, 7, 1, 8, 5. Code: MOV CX, 5, LEA SI, NUMS, MOV AL, 0, then NEXT: ADD AL, [SI], INC SI, LOOP NEXT. Trace: AL = 0, add 4, AL = 4, CX becomes 4. Add 7, AL = 11, CX = 3. Add 1, AL = 12, CX = 2. Add 8, AL = 20, CX = 1. Add 5, AL = 25, CX = 0, loop ends. Sum = 25. If the sum could pass 255, keep the total in AX: start with AX = 0, and in the loop write ADD AL, [SI] then ADC AH, 0, so every carry out of AL moves into AH.

Finding the maximum: The idea is the same as finding the tallest student in a line. Assume the first one is tallest, then compare with each next one and update if you find taller. Code: LEA SI, NUMS, MOV AL, [SI], MOV CX, 4, then NEXT: INC SI, CMP AL, [SI], JAE NO_CHANGE, MOV AL, [SI], NO_CHANGE: LOOP NEXT. CX is 4, not 5, because the first element is already in AL. For 4, 7, 1, 8, 5, AL goes 4, 7, 7, 8, 8. Max = 8. Change JAE to JBE for the minimum, and use JGE or JLE if the values are signed.

Counting with a condition: How many marks are 80 or above? Keep a counter in BL. Inside the loop: CMP BYTE PTR [SI], 80, JB SKIP, INC BL, SKIP: INC SI, LOOP NEXT. For 72, 85, 64, 91, 58 you get BL = 2. The pattern 'compare, jump over the action, continue' is the core of most array programs.

Searching with LOOPNE: Find the position of the value 8 in NUMS. MOV AL, 8, MOV CX, 5, LEA SI, NUMS, DEC SI, then NEXT: INC SI, CMP [SI], AL, LOOPNE NEXT. Each round moves SI, compares, and continues only while not equal and CX is not zero. After the loop: if ZF = 1, the value was found and SI points at it; if ZF = 0, it is not in the array. Order matters here: INC SI comes before CMP, because INC changes ZF, while LOOPNE must see the ZF from CMP. For 4, 7, 1, 8, 5 the loop stops after 4 rounds with SI at the fourth element.

Nested loops: A loop inside a loop needs two counters, but LOOP always uses CX. The usual fix is to save the outer count on the stack. Outer: MOV CX, 3, ROW: PUSH CX, MOV CX, 4, COL: (print a star), LOOP COL, (print a newline), POP CX, LOOP ROW. This prints 3 rows of 4 stars. PUSH CX saves the outer count before the inner loop wipes CX to zero; POP CX brings it back for the outer LOOP. The stack itself is the topic of lesson 16; here just remember to keep PUSH and POP in pairs. Another option is to count the inner loop with a different register, like DEC BX and JNZ.

Bubble sort, the idea: Bubble sort compares each neighbouring pair and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After one full pass, the largest value has bubbled to the end. Repeat for N - 1 passes and the array is sorted. It is slow for big arrays, roughly N squared comparisons, but it is short and perfect for practising loops.

Bubble sort in 8086 assembly: For 5 bytes in NUMS: MOV CX, 4, OUTER: PUSH CX, LEA SI, NUMS, INNER: MOV AL, [SI], CMP AL, [SI+1], JBE NO_SWAP, XCHG AL, [SI+1], MOV [SI], AL, NO_SWAP: INC SI, LOOP INNER, POP CX, LOOP OUTER. Look at the swap: AL holds the left value. XCHG puts AL into the right slot and brings the right value into AL. MOV [SI], AL puts that value in the left slot. Two values swapped with three instructions.

Bubble sort traced, first pass: Start 4, 7, 1, 8, 5. Compare 4 and 7, fine. Compare 7 and 1, swap: 4, 1, 7, 8, 5. Compare 7 and 8, fine. Compare 8 and 5, swap: 4, 1, 7, 5, 8. The 8 has bubbled to the end. The inner loop ran 4 times because the outer CX was 4 when it was copied. On pass 2, the inner count is 3, so the already-placed 8 is not checked again, which is a free speed-up from reusing CX. After pass 2: 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, and the remaining passes change nothing.

Why use LOOP, and when not: LOOP is short (2 bytes), clear to read, and leaves the flags alone, which helps when the body sets flags for something else. But it only counts down in CX, only by 1, and only reaches short distances. When the loop count is not known in advance, like 'read keys until Enter', use CMP and conditional jumps instead. And on many later x86 processors, a separate DEC CX and JNZ runs as fast or faster than LOOP, so modern compilers rarely produce LOOP. For learning the 8086, LOOP is perfect.

Real-life example 1, an over in cricket: At a match in Mirpur, the scorer's computer stores the runs of each ball of an over in an array: OVER DB 1, 4, 0, 6, 2, 1. A loop with CX = 6 adds them: 1, 5, 5, 11, 13, 14. Total 14 runs in the over. A second loop with a counter counts the boundaries, values equal to 4 or 6, and finds 2. A third loop finds the maximum, 6. Every score display on TV is built from simple loops like these.

Real-life example 2, finding a phone number: A tiny phonebook device in a pharmacy in Khulna keeps the last digits of customer numbers in an array. When a customer calls, the program searches the array with LOOPNE for the matching value. If ZF = 1 after the loop, SI points to the matching record and the name is shown. If ZF = 0, it shows 'new customer'. The search stops the moment it finds a match, so it does not waste time on the rest of the list.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to set CX before LOOP, so it runs with whatever CX had, maybe 0 and thus 65,536 times. Changing CX inside the body, for example by a MUL or a DOS call that uses CX, without saving it. Stepping SI by 1 in a word array. Writing an off-by-one count, like CX = 5 for the maximum search when the first element was already loaded. Putting INC SI between CMP and LOOPNE. Forgetting PUSH CX and POP CX in nested loops, or popping in the wrong place.

What exams ask: Explain LOOP, LOOPE, LOOPNE and JCXZ with their conditions. Say what happens if CX = 0 before LOOP. Write programs for the sum, average, maximum, minimum or count of an array; search for an element; sort an array in ascending or descending order; print a triangle of stars with nested loops. Trace a given loop and give the final CX and AL.

Recap: LOOP decreases CX and jumps back while CX is not zero, without touching flags. LOOPE and LOOPNE also need ZF = 1 or ZF = 0 to continue, giving loops that stop early, and JCXZ protects against starting with CX = 0. Arrays are values side by side in memory, walked with a pointer in SI moving 1 byte or 2 bytes at a time. With these pieces you can sum, count, find max and min, search and sort. Nested loops save CX on the stack, which leads straight into the next lesson: how the stack really works.
key_points: LOOP label = DEC CX + jump if CX is not 0, but LOOP changes no flags.
The body runs CX times; starting with CX = 0 runs it 65,536 times, so guard with JCXZ.
LOOPE/LOOPZ continue while CX is not 0 and ZF = 1; LOOPNE/LOOPNZ while CX is not 0 and ZF = 0.
An array is values side by side; walk it with SI, step 1 for DB and 2 for DW.
Max/min: load the first element, compare with the rest, update; use unsigned or signed jumps to match the data.
Nested loops save the outer CX with PUSH CX / POP CX or use another counter register.
Bubble sort uses an outer and inner loop and swaps neighbours with XCHG.
lessons.tip: Trace every loop on paper with a small table: one column per register (CX, SI, AL) and one row per round. Off-by-one errors become obvious in the first two rows.
lessons.task: Write on paper an 8086 program that finds the minimum of the array 9, 3, 7, 2, 6 and counts how many values are greater than 5. Trace it with a table of CX, SI, AL and BL per round. Expected: minimum 2, count 3.

quiz.q: What does LOOP NEXT do?
options: Decreases CX and jumps to NEXT if CX is not zero
Increases CX and jumps to NEXT
Jumps to NEXT only if CX is zero
quiz.explain: LOOP decrements CX first, then jumps back while CX is not zero.

quiz.q: How many times does a LOOP body run if CX = 0 at the start?
quiz.explain: CX goes from 0 to FFFFh after the first round, so it runs 65,536 times in total.

quiz.q: LOOPNE continues looping when:
quiz.explain: LOOPNE keeps going while values are not equal and CX has not run out.

quiz.q: In a word array (DW), how should SI move to the next element?
quiz.explain: Each word takes 2 bytes.

quiz.q: Why is PUSH CX used before an inner loop?
options: To save the outer loop counter, since the inner LOOP also uses CX
quiz.explain: Both loops use CX, so the outer count is saved and restored with POP CX.

lessons.title: The Stack: PUSH, POP and LIFO
lessons.content:
Think about a wedding feast in a community centre in Dhaka. The waiters wash plates and stack them in one tall pile. When a guest needs a plate, the waiter takes the one on top. Nobody pulls a plate from the middle or the bottom, because the whole pile would fall. The last plate put on the pile is the first plate taken off. The CPU needs exactly this kind of pile for its own work, and in the 8086 it is called the stack.

What the stack is: The stack is an ordinary area of memory that the CPU uses in a special way. Data goes in and comes out only from one end, called the top. This rule is called LIFO, which means Last In, First Out. Putting a value on the top is called PUSH. Taking the top value off is called POP. There is no instruction to grab the fifth item from the top directly with push and pop; you can only reach the top.

The problem it solves: A CPU has only a handful of registers. The 8086 has AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI, BP and SP for general work. Very often a program needs a register for a new job while its old value is still important. Before stacks were common, programmers saved such values in fixed memory variables like TEMP1 and TEMP2. That works for one level, but it breaks as soon as a routine calls another routine that uses the same TEMP1. The stack solves this, because every new save goes on top of the old ones and nothing gets overwritten. It also gives the CPU a natural place to remember return addresses for procedures and interrupts, which you will see in the next lessons.

Where the stack lives: In the 8086, the stack sits in the stack segment. The segment register SS holds the segment base, and the stack pointer SP holds the offset of the current top. So the physical address of the top is SS times 16 plus SP, exactly like the segment:offset rule from the segmentation lesson. If SS = 2000h and SP = 0100h, the top of the stack is at 20000h + 0100h = 20100h. One stack segment can be at most 64 KB, because SP is a 16-bit register.

The stack grows downward: This surprises everyone the first time. In the 8086, when you push, SP gets smaller. When you pop, SP gets bigger. So the stack starts at a high offset and grows toward lower addresses. Picture the plate pile hanging from the ceiling and growing toward the floor. The empty stack has SP pointing just past the highest usable word. In a typical .EXE program written with .STACK 100h, the assembler reserves 256 bytes, and when the program starts the loader sets SP to 0100h, the end of that area.

PUSH step by step: PUSH AX does two things in this exact order. First, SP = SP minus 2. Second, the 16-bit value in AX is stored at SS:SP. Because the 8086 is little endian, the low byte goes to the lower address and the high byte goes to the next address. Let us trace it. SS = 2000h, SP = 0100h, AX = 1234h. After PUSH AX, SP = 00FEh. The byte 34h is stored at physical address 200FEh and the byte 12h at 200FFh. The value of AX itself does not change. PUSH copies; it does not empty the register.

POP step by step: POP BX does the opposite in the opposite order. First, the word at SS:SP is copied into BX. Second, SP = SP plus 2. Continuing our trace: SP = 00FEh, the word there is 1234h, so BX becomes 1234h and SP goes back to 0100h. The bytes 34h and 12h are still physically sitting in memory at 200FEh and 200FFh. POP does not erase anything. It only moves SP, and the old bytes are simply considered free space that the next PUSH will overwrite.

A small diagram in words: Imagine three pushes, PUSH AX with AX = 1111h, PUSH BX with BX = 2222h, PUSH CX with CX = 3333h, starting from SP = 0100h. After the first push SP = 00FEh and 1111h sits at offset 00FEh. After the second, SP = 00FCh and 2222h sits at 00FCh. After the third, SP = 00FAh and 3333h sits at 00FAh. Read the memory from low to high: 00FAh holds 3333h, 00FCh holds 2222h, 00FEh holds 1111h. The top, where SP points, holds the last value pushed. Now POP DX gives 3333h, the next POP gives 2222h, and the last gives 1111h. Reverse order, every time.

Word size only: On the 8086, PUSH and POP always move 16 bits. PUSH AL is not a valid instruction. If you want to save AL, push AX, which contains AL as its low half. Also, the original 8086 cannot push an immediate number like PUSH 5; that form arrived with the 80186. You can push registers, segment registers and memory words, like PUSH DS or PUSH WORD PTR [BX]. You can pop into registers and memory, but you cannot pop into CS, because changing CS alone would make the CPU jump to a strange place. Code addresses are changed by jumps, calls and returns instead.

PUSHF and POPF: The flags register holds the results of comparisons and settings like the direction flag and interrupt flag. PUSHF pushes the whole 16-bit flags register onto the stack, and POPF pops a word back into it. This is useful when a piece of code must not disturb the flags of the code around it. It is also a classic trick to change a flag that has no direct instruction, such as the trap flag TF: push the flags, pop them into AX, change the bit with OR or AND, push AX, and POPF. Interrupts use the same idea automatically, as you will see in the interrupt lesson.

Saving and restoring registers: The most common everyday use of the stack is protecting registers. Suppose your main code has a loop counter in CX, and in the middle you need CX for a different small loop. You write PUSH CX, do the inner work freely, then POP CX, and the outer counter is back as if nothing happened. When you save several registers, pop them in the reverse order: PUSH AX, PUSH BX, PUSH CX, then later POP CX, POP BX, POP AX. If you pop in the same order you pushed, AX and CX swap their values silently, which is a very hard bug to spot.

Swapping with the stack: PUSH AX, PUSH BX, POP AX, POP BX swaps AX and BX. Trace it: the stack top ends up with BX's value, which goes into AX first, then the older value of AX goes into BX. It works, but the XCHG AX, BX instruction does the same job in one instruction, so the stack trick is mainly a good exam exercise to test LIFO thinking.

Reversing a string: LIFO is exactly what you need to reverse anything. The plan: read characters one by one, push each one, then pop them all and print them. Because the last character pushed comes out first, the text comes out backwards. In assembly, the idea looks like this. Set CX = 0. Loop: read a key with INT 21h function 01h, which returns the character in AL. If AL is 0Dh, the Enter key, stop reading. Otherwise PUSH AX and INC CX. After reading, if CX is 0, there is nothing to print. Otherwise loop CX times: POP DX, then use INT 21h function 02h, which prints the character in DL. Type DHAKA and the program prints AKAHD.

Execution trace for the reversal: Typing C, A, T gives pushes of the words holding C, then A, then T, and CX becomes 3. SP has gone down by 6 bytes. The print loop pops T first, then A, then C, printing TAC, and SP is back where it started. That last point matters: a correct program leaves SP exactly where it found it. Pushes and pops must balance.

Stack overflow: What happens if you push too much? The 8086 has no hardware check for stack limits in real mode. SP just keeps decreasing. If SP passes 0000h it wraps around to FFFEh in the same segment, and pushes start overwriting whatever lives there. If the stack segment overlaps the data or code segment, as it often does in small programs and .COM files, the pushes silently destroy your variables or even your own instructions. The program then behaves strangely or crashes much later, far away from the real cause. Deep recursion and pushing inside a loop without popping are the usual reasons.

Stack underflow: Popping more than you pushed is the opposite mistake. POP then reads whatever happens to be above the real top, maybe old garbage or the return address that a procedure needs. The value you get is meaningless, and SP has moved past the data that belongs to someone else. The next RET may then jump into nowhere. A common real case: an early exit from a loop skips a POP, so one path through the code is balanced and the other is not.

How to size the stack: For student programs, .STACK 100h (256 bytes) is plenty, because each push is only 2 bytes. Deep recursion is different. If each level of a recursive procedure pushes a return address and two registers, that is 6 bytes per level, so 100 levels need 600 bytes. Estimating this kind of number before you write the code is a good engineering habit.

When to use the stack and when not: Use it for temporary saves, return addresses, passing parameters and short-lived local data. It is fast, needs no names, and naturally handles nesting. Do not use it for data that must live for the whole program, like a table of exam marks, because the stack area is constantly reused and SP moves all the time. Such data belongs in the data segment with a proper label. Also do not use the stack when a free register would do; a register move is faster than a memory push and pop.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz order box: A packer at a Dhaka warehouse fills a delivery box. Books go in first at the bottom, then a phone cover, then a small charger on top. At the customer's door the charger comes out first and the books last. The box is a stack. If the customer insists on the book first, everything above it must come out first. That is exactly why PUSH and POP order matters in a program.

Real-life example 2, interrupted homework: Rafi is solving a maths problem when his mother calls him to bring tea. He puts a bookmark on the page (push), goes to make the tea, and on the way his little sister asks for help with her drawing. He remembers where he was in the tea making (another push), helps her, then returns to the tea (pop), and finally back to maths (pop). Each interruption stacks on top of the previous one, and he unwinds them in reverse. The CPU handles nested procedure calls and interrupts in this same way.

Common mistakes: Thinking the stack grows upward; in the 8086 it grows downward, so PUSH decreases SP. Forgetting that SP changes by 2, not by 1. Writing PUSH AL, which is invalid. Popping in the same order as pushing instead of reverse. Leaving the stack unbalanced on one code path. Assuming POP clears memory. Forgetting that the stack top address is SS:SP, not just SP.

What exams ask: Given SS, SP and some register values, show SP and memory contents after a sequence of PUSH and POP instructions, including the byte order. Find the physical address of the stack top. Explain LIFO with a diagram. Write a program to reverse a string using the stack. Explain why PUSH and POP must be balanced, and what stack overflow and underflow mean. A quick self-check: SS = 3000h, SP = 0050h, AX = ABCDh, PUSH AX. Answer: SP = 004Eh, CDh at 3004Eh and ABh at 3004Fh.

Recap: The stack is memory at SS:SP used in LIFO order. PUSH first lowers SP by 2, then stores a word; POP first reads the word, then raises SP by 2. Only words move, data stays little endian, and nothing is erased by POP. Use it to save registers, reverse things and remember where to return, and always keep pushes and pops balanced. Next, procedures will show how CALL and RET use this same stack to jump into a routine and come back.
key_points: The stack is memory at SS:SP used Last In, First Out; PUSH adds on top, POP removes the top.
In the 8086 the stack grows downward: PUSH lowers SP, POP raises it.
PUSH: SP = SP - 2, then store the word at SS:SP (low byte at the lower address).
POP: read the word at SS:SP, then SP = SP + 2; memory is not erased.
Only 16-bit words: PUSH AL is invalid, and the 8086 cannot pop into CS or push an immediate.
PUSHF/POPF save and restore the whole flags register.
Pop saved registers in reverse order and keep pushes and pops balanced on every code path.
No stack-limit check in real mode: overflow silently overwrites other data, underflow reads garbage.
lessons.tip: Whenever you read stack code, draw a small vertical box with addresses and SP written beside it, and update it after every PUSH and POP. Two minutes of drawing saves an hour of debugging.
lessons.task: On paper, start with SS = 1000h, SP = 0020h, AX = 0A0Bh, BX = 0C0Dh. Apply PUSH AX, PUSH BX, POP AX, POP BX. After each step write SP and the bytes at each stack address. Then check: which values do AX and BX hold at the end, and why?

quiz.q: SS = 2000h, SP = 0100h, AX = 1234h. After PUSH AX, what is SP and where does the byte 34h go?
quiz.explain: PUSH first lowers SP by 2 to 00FEh, then stores the low byte 34h at the lower address 200FEh and 12h at 200FFh.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a valid 8086 instruction?
quiz.explain: The 8086 stack works in 16-bit words only, so 8-bit registers like AL cannot be pushed directly.

quiz.q: You run PUSH AX, PUSH BX, PUSH CX. Which order of pops restores all three correctly?
options: POP CX, POP BX, POP AX
POP AX, POP BX, POP CX
POP BX, POP CX, POP AX
POP AX, POP CX, POP BX
quiz.explain: LIFO: the last value pushed (CX) is on top, so it must be popped first.

quiz.q: What does POP BX do to the memory word it reads?
options: Leaves it in memory; only SP moves up by 2
Moves it to the bottom of the stack
quiz.explain: POP copies the word into BX and adds 2 to SP; the old bytes stay until a later push overwrites them.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of stack overflow in 8086 real mode?
options: The CPU raises an automatic stack-limit exception
SP stops at 0000h and further pushes are ignored
SP wraps around and pushes silently overwrite other data or code
quiz.explain: Real-mode 8086 has no stack limit check, so SP wraps within the segment and pushes overwrite whatever is there.

lessons.title: Procedures and Macros
lessons.content:
Imagine a tea stall owner in Old Dhaka who sends his helper boy to buy sugar many times a day. He does not explain the route every time. He just says "go get sugar", the boy goes, buys it, and comes back to exactly the stall he left. A procedure in assembly is that errand: one block of code written once, which any part of the program can send the CPU to run, and the CPU always comes back to the right place.

What a procedure is: A procedure, also called a subroutine or function, is a named block of instructions that does one job, such as printing a number or finding the largest value in an array. In MASM or TASM syntax you write it between NAME PROC and NAME ENDP. You run it with CALL NAME, and the procedure finishes with RET, which returns to the instruction right after the CALL.

The problem it solves: Without procedures you would copy the same 15 lines of "print a number" code everywhere you need it. That makes the program long, and if you find a bug you must fix every copy. You could try to use a plain JMP to go to shared code, but then how does that code know where to jump back? Different callers need different return points. The procedure mechanism answers that question automatically using the stack, which you learned in the previous lesson.

Why not just JMP back to a fixed label? Because a fixed label works for only one caller. If the print code is used from line 20 and from line 80, a hard-coded JMP BACK_TO_20 is wrong for the second caller. Early programmers sometimes stored the return address in a fixed memory variable before jumping, but that breaks the moment a procedure calls another procedure, or itself, because the second call overwrites the saved address. A stack, where each return address sits on top of the previous one, handles any depth of nesting.

How CALL works internally (near call): A near call jumps to a procedure in the same code segment, so only IP needs to change. CALL PRINT does this: first, it pushes the address of the next instruction (the current IP after fetching the CALL) onto the stack, which means SP = SP minus 2 and the return offset is stored at SS:SP. Second, it loads IP with the starting offset of PRINT. Execution continues inside the procedure.

How RET works internally (near return): RET pops the word on top of the stack into IP, and SP goes up by 2. If the stack is in the same state it was in just after the CALL, the top word is the return address, so the CPU continues right after the CALL. This is the key rule of procedures: when RET runs, the return address must be on top. Every PUSH inside the procedure must be matched by a POP before RET.

A tiny trace: Suppose CALL PRINT sits at offset 0100h and takes 3 bytes, so the next instruction is at 0103h. PRINT starts at 0200h. SP is 0100h before the call. After CALL: SP = 00FEh, the word 0103h is on the stack, IP = 0200h. The procedure runs. RET pops 0103h into IP and SP is back to 0100h. The caller continues at 0103h as if the procedure was one big instruction.

Far procedures: A far procedure lives in a different code segment, so both CS and IP must change. You declare it as NAME PROC FAR. A far CALL pushes CS first and then IP, which is 4 bytes in total, and then loads new values of both. The matching far return, written RET inside a FAR procedure or RETF explicitly, pops IP first and then CS. Mixing them up is a disaster: if a near call is answered by a far return, the CPU pops an extra word as CS and jumps to a random segment. The assembler chooses the right kind of RET when the PROC is labelled NEAR or FAR.

Passing parameters in registers: The simplest way to give a procedure its input is to put it in registers before the call. For example, a procedure PRINTNUM may expect the number in AX. The caller writes MOV AX, 345 then CALL PRINTNUM. Results usually come back in AX too. Register passing is fast and easy, but there are only a few registers, and the caller and procedure must agree exactly on which register means what. Writing that agreement as a comment above the procedure is a must.

Saving registers inside the procedure: A polite procedure does not destroy the caller's registers. If PRINTNUM uses BX, CX and DX internally, it starts with PUSH BX, PUSH CX, PUSH DX and ends with POP DX, POP CX, POP BX right before RET. Then the caller can trust that only the documented output register has changed. Forgetting this is one of the most common bugs in student programs: the main loop counter in CX suddenly becomes 0 because a procedure used CX for its own loop.

Passing parameters on the stack: When there are many parameters, or when you want the same style that compiled C code uses, the caller pushes the parameters and then calls. Example: PUSH AX (first value), PUSH BX (second value), CALL ADDTWO. Inside, the procedure cannot just POP them, because the return address is on top. Instead it uses BP as a fixed reference point. It starts with PUSH BP then MOV BP, SP. Now, for a near procedure, [BP] holds the old BP, [BP+2] holds the return address, [BP+4] holds the last pushed parameter (BX here) and [BP+6] holds the first pushed one (AX here). BP is a good choice because, by default, addresses formed with BP use the stack segment SS.

Stack picture for ADDTWO: Reading memory from low address to high: BP points at the saved old BP, then the return address, then the second parameter, then the first parameter. The procedure body can say MOV AX, [BP+6] and ADD AX, [BP+4] to get the sum in AX. At the end it does POP BP and returns. For a far procedure everything shifts by 2 because the return address is 4 bytes, so the first stack parameter is at [BP+6] counting from the last pushed one.

Cleaning the parameters with RET n: After the procedure returns, the two parameter words are still on the stack. Someone must remove them. Either the caller adds ADD SP, 4 after the call, or the procedure ends with RET 4. RET n first pops the return address and then adds n to SP. Both work; the important thing is that exactly one side cleans up. In real compilers this choice is part of the calling convention: the C convention has the caller clean, while the Pascal style has the procedure clean with RET n.

Local variables: Sometimes a procedure needs temporary memory of its own. After PUSH BP and MOV BP, SP, it can write SUB SP, 4 to reserve two words below BP. Those are the local variables, reached as [BP-2] and [BP-4]. At the end it writes MOV SP, BP to throw them away, then POP BP and RET. Because the space is on the stack, each call, even a recursive one, gets its own fresh copy. The block of stack used by one call, holding parameters, return address, old BP and locals, is called a stack frame.

Recursion, a procedure calling itself: Factorial is the classic example: n! = n times (n minus 1)!, and 1! = 1. Here is a register version that keeps n in CX and returns the answer in AX. FACT PROC: CMP CX, 1 then JBE BASE. Otherwise PUSH CX, DEC CX, CALL FACT, POP CX, MUL CX, RET. BASE: MOV AX, 1 then RET. FACT ENDP. The PUSH CX saves the current n, because the inner call will change CX. MUL CX multiplies AX by CX, putting the result in DX:AX, and for small n the answer fits in AX.

Trace for 3!: CX = 3. Not 1, so push 3, CX = 2, call. CX = 2, push 2, CX = 1, call. CX = 1, so AX = 1 and return. Pop CX = 2, AX = 1 times 2 = 2, return. Pop CX = 3, AX = 2 times 3 = 6, return. Answer 6. At the deepest point the stack held two saved CX values and three return addresses. That is why deep recursion needs a bigger stack, and why 8! = 40320 still fits in 16 bits but 9! = 362880 does not fit in AX alone.

Macros: A macro looks similar but works completely differently. You define it with NAME MACRO params and ENDM. For example PRINTMSG MACRO MSG, then LEA DX, MSG, MOV AH, 09h, INT 21h, then ENDM. When you write PRINTMSG HELLO in your code, the assembler copies those three instructions into that spot, replacing MSG with HELLO. This happens at assembly time, before the program ever runs. There is no CALL and no RET at run time.

Macro versus procedure: A procedure exists once in memory and is reached by CALL, so the program is smaller but every use pays the time for CALL, RET and stack work. A macro is pasted in at every use, so it runs slightly faster with no call overhead, but the program grows with each use. Rule of thumb: use a macro for very short code used often, like a two or three line print helper. Use a procedure for long code, for anything recursive (a macro cannot call itself into an infinite expansion), and when program size matters. One more trap: labels inside a macro would be duplicated on every expansion, so you declare them with the LOCAL directive to make the assembler generate unique names.

Real-life example 1, the bKash agent: A shop owner in a Gazipur market handles cash-in for many customers. The steps are always the same: check the number, enter the amount, confirm with PIN. That is a procedure. Each customer is a CALL with different parameters (number and amount), and when the transaction ends the owner returns to whatever he was doing before, like selling recharge cards. He also does not lose his own cash count while helping, which is like saving registers.

Real-life example 2, Russian dolls of errands: A teacher asks a student to fetch the attendance register. On the way the office clerk asks the student to also take a letter to the headmaster first. The student must remember two places to return to, the clerk and then the classroom, in reverse order. That is nested CALLs, and the student's memory works like the stack of return addresses.

Common mistakes: Leaving an extra PUSH inside the procedure, so RET pops data instead of the return address and jumps to garbage. Forgetting to save registers the caller depends on. Using a near RET for a far procedure or the reverse. Accessing stack parameters with the wrong offset, for example [BP+2] instead of [BP+4] in a near procedure. Cleaning parameters twice, with both RET 4 and ADD SP, 4. Forgetting LOCAL labels in a macro used twice, causing a duplicate-label error.

What exams ask: Explain what CALL and RET do to SP, IP and CS for near and far cases, often with a numerical trace. Draw the stack frame after PUSH BP and MOV BP, SP for a procedure with two parameters. Write a procedure to print a number or find the maximum of an array. Write recursive factorial and trace it. Compare macro and procedure in a table: expansion time, memory use, speed, parameter passing.

Recap: CALL pushes the return address and jumps; RET pops it back into IP (and CS for far procedures). Parameters can travel in registers or on the stack, where BP gives a steady view of them, and RET n or ADD SP, n removes them. Locals live below BP, and each call gets its own frame, which makes recursion possible. Macros are pasted in at assembly time, procedures are jumped to at run time. Next, string instructions will show how the 8086 moves and searches whole blocks of bytes with a single repeated instruction.
key_points: A procedure (PROC ... ENDP) is written once and run with CALL; RET returns right after the CALL.
Near CALL pushes IP and jumps; near RET pops IP. Far CALL pushes CS then IP; far RET pops IP then CS.
When RET runs, the return address must be on top, so every PUSH inside needs a POP first.
Parameters go in registers (fast, few) or on the stack, read via BP after PUSH BP / MOV BP, SP.
In a near procedure: [BP] old BP, [BP+2] return address, [BP+4] last pushed parameter.
RET n or ADD SP, n removes stack parameters; exactly one side must clean up.
Locals live below BP ([BP-2], ...); each call gets its own stack frame, which makes recursion work.
Macros are pasted in at assembly time (faster, bigger code, use LOCAL labels); procedures save space.
lessons.tip: Above every procedure, write a three-line comment: inputs (which registers or stack slots), outputs, and registers it changes. Your future self will thank you during debugging.
lessons.task: Draw the stack, word by word, for CALL FACT with CX = 4 using the register version of factorial from this lesson, at the deepest point of recursion. Count how many bytes of stack are used and check that the final AX is 24.

quiz.q: What does a near CALL PRINT do first?
options: Loads IP with PRINT and pushes nothing
Pushes the address of the next instruction, then loads IP with PRINT's offset
quiz.explain: A near call saves only the return offset (IP of the next instruction) on the stack and then jumps by loading IP.

quiz.q: In a near procedure that starts with PUSH BP and MOV BP, SP, where is the return address?
quiz.explain: [BP] holds the old BP, and the return offset pushed by CALL sits just above it at [BP+2].

quiz.q: What does RET 4 do?
options: Pops the return address, then adds 4 to SP to remove parameters
Adds 4 to SP, then pops the return address
quiz.explain: RET n first returns using the address on top, then discards n bytes of parameters by adding n to SP.

quiz.q: Which is true about a macro compared with a procedure?
options: A macro is expanded at assembly time and has no CALL/RET overhead
A macro uses less memory when used many times
A macro can easily be recursive
A macro pushes a return address
quiz.explain: The assembler pastes the macro body at each use, so there is no run-time call, but code size grows with each use.

quiz.q: A procedure has an extra PUSH AX with no matching POP before RET. What happens?
options: RET pops the value of AX into IP and execution jumps to a wrong address
SP is reset to its starting value
quiz.explain: RET always pops whatever word is on top; here that is AX's value, not the return address.

lessons.title: String Instructions: MOVS, CMPS, SCAS, LODS, STOS
lessons.content:
Picture a clerk at a Chattogram port office copying 500 container numbers from one register into another. Doing it one number at a time, with a fresh instruction from the boss for each line, would take forever. Much better if the boss says once: "copy from this page to that page, 500 lines, go". The 8086 has exactly this kind of shortcut for memory. They are called string instructions, and with a REP prefix one instruction can move, compare, search or fill a whole block of bytes.

What a string means here: In assembly, a string is not only text. It is any sequence of bytes or words lying next to each other in memory. A name like "RAHIM", an array of 100 exam marks, or a screen buffer are all strings to the CPU. String instructions are special instructions that work on such blocks, one element at a time, and update the pointers automatically after each element.

The problem they solve: To copy 100 bytes with ordinary instructions you would write a loop: MOV AL, [SI], MOV [DI], AL, INC SI, INC DI, DEC CX, JNZ back. That is six instructions per byte, and the CPU must fetch and decode all of them every time. String instructions pack the load, the store and both pointer updates into one instruction, and the REP prefix repeats it in hardware. The code is shorter, easier to read, and on the 8086 usually faster.

The fixed register roles: String instructions do not take normal operands; they use fixed registers. The source is always DS:SI, so SI is the Source Index. The destination is always ES:DI, so DI is the Destination Index. CX holds the count when a REP prefix is used. AL or AX holds the value for instructions that load, store or scan. You can override the source segment, for example with a CS: prefix, but the destination segment is always ES and cannot be overridden.

The ES trap: Because the destination uses ES, a program that copies inside its own data segment must set ES as well as DS. In an .EXE program the start usually looks like MOV AX, @DATA, MOV DS, AX, MOV ES, AX. Forgetting the last line is the number one reason a string copy writes to some unknown place in memory while the source looks perfectly fine.

The direction flag: After each element, SI and DI move automatically. Which way they move depends on DF, the direction flag. If DF = 0, they increase, so the operation goes forward through memory. If DF = 1, they decrease, so it goes backward. CLD clears DF to 0 and STD sets it to 1. The step size is 1 for byte versions, which end in B, and 2 for word versions, which end in W. Good practice is to write CLD or STD yourself before string work instead of trusting whatever DF happens to be.

MOVSB and MOVSW, move: MOVSB copies one byte from DS:SI to ES:DI, then moves SI and DI by 1. MOVSW copies a word and moves them by 2. No register in between is needed; this is the one common 8086 case where data goes from memory to memory directly. No flags are changed.

LODSB and LODSW, load: LODSB loads the byte at DS:SI into AL and moves SI. LODSW loads a word into AX and moves SI by 2. It is useful when you want to look at each element and do some work with it, such as converting a lowercase letter to uppercase.

STOSB and STOSW, store: STOSB stores AL into ES:DI and moves DI. STOSW stores AX. With REP it fills a block with one value. For example, to set a 200-byte buffer to zero: CLD, LEA DI, BUF, MOV CX, 200, MOV AL, 0, REP STOSB. LODS and STOS together also make a filter loop: load a character, change it, store it to a new place.

CMPSB and CMPSW, compare: CMPSB compares the byte at DS:SI with the byte at ES:DI by subtracting the destination byte from the source byte internally. It throws the result away but sets the flags, just like CMP. Then it moves both SI and DI. If the two bytes were equal, ZF = 1.

SCASB and SCASW, scan: SCASB compares AL with the byte at ES:DI (it computes AL minus that byte) and sets the flags, then moves DI. It is the search instruction: put the character you are looking for in AL and scan through memory until you find it.

The REP prefix: REP placed before MOVS or STOS means: while CX is not zero, do the instruction, then decrease CX by 1. So REP MOVSB with CX = 100 copies exactly 100 bytes. If CX is already 0 at the start, the instruction is not executed even once. REP does not test any flags. Inside the CPU, REP does not need a separate jump instruction: the repetition is handled by the CPU's own microcode, which is why it is compact and quick.

REPE and REPNE: For comparisons and searches you want to stop early. REPE, also written REPZ, means: repeat while CX is not zero and ZF = 1, that is, while things are equal. REPNE, also written REPNZ, means: repeat while CX is not zero and ZF = 0, that is, while things are not equal. So REPE CMPSB walks along two strings while they match and stops at the first difference. REPNE SCASB walks along memory while it has not found AL and stops at the first match.

Example 1, copying a name: Suppose SRC DB 'DHAKA' and DST DB 5 DUP(?). Code: CLD, LEA SI, SRC, LEA DI, DST, MOV CX, 5, REP MOVSB. Trace: CX = 5, copy D, SI and DI step forward, CX = 4; copy H, CX = 3; copy A, CX = 2; copy K, CX = 1; copy A, CX = 0, stop. DST now holds DHAKA, SI and DI point just past the ends of the two strings, and CX is 0.

Example 2, comparing two passwords: Let P1 and P2 be 6 bytes each. CLD, LEA SI, P1, LEA DI, P2, MOV CX, 6, REPE CMPSB. Then JNE DIFFERENT. Why does this work? If all six pairs match, ZF stays 1 the whole way and the loop ends because CX reaches 0, so ZF = 1 and JNE is not taken. If a pair differs, the CMPSB on that pair sets ZF = 0 and the repeat stops right there, and JNE is taken. After a mismatch, SI and DI already point one element past the differing position, a detail exam questions love.

Example 3, searching for a character: To find the first space in a 20-byte line: CLD, LEA DI, LINE, MOV CX, 20, MOV AL, ' ', REPNE SCASB, JNE NOTFOUND. If a space exists, the scan stops with ZF = 1 and DI pointing one byte after the space, so the space itself is at DI minus 1. Its position counted from the start is DI minus 1 minus the offset of LINE. If no space exists, CX runs out with ZF = 0 and we jump to NOTFOUND.

Example 4, converting to uppercase with LODSB and STOSB: Suppose NAME1 DB 'rahim' and we want the uppercase copy in NAME2. Code: CLD, LEA SI, NAME1, LEA DI, NAME2, MOV CX, 5. Loop: LODSB brings 'r' into AL and SI moves forward. In ASCII, a lowercase letter is exactly 20h more than its uppercase partner ('r' is 72h, 'R' is 52h), so SUB AL, 20h turns it into 'R'. STOSB writes AL to NAME2 and DI moves forward. LOOP repeats this for the remaining four letters. NAME2 ends as RAHIM. A real program would first check that AL is between 'a' and 'z', so digits and spaces are copied unchanged. This load-change-store pattern is the general tool whenever each element needs a small change on the way.

Overlapping blocks and STD: Suppose you want to shift a block 2 bytes to the right in memory, with the source and destination overlapping. Copying forward would overwrite source bytes before they are read, so the data gets smeared. The fix is to copy backward: STD, set SI and DI to the last bytes of source and destination, then REP MOVSB. The bytes are moved from the end, so nothing is overwritten too early. The C library function memmove makes exactly this choice, while memcpy assumes no overlap.

When to use string instructions and when not: Use them for copying blocks, filling buffers, comparing fixed-length records, searching for a byte, and walking through arrays with LODS and STOS. Do not use them when each step needs complicated logic that does not fit the load-change-store pattern, or when the data is not in consecutive memory. On modern x86 chips the speed picture is more complex; compilers and libraries choose between REP MOVSB and other methods depending on the processor and the size, so do not assume one is always the fastest there.

Real-life example 1, a SIM registration form: A mobile operator's shop in Sylhet saves customer forms. When a new record is created, the software first fills the 100-byte buffer with spaces (REP STOSB), then copies the customer's NID number in (REP MOVSB), and later checks whether the same NID already exists by comparing with stored records (REPE CMPSB). These are the same three building blocks you just learned, and low-level library code still does work like this.

Real-life example 2, finding a word in an SMS: Your old button phone shows "1 new message" and its tiny processor must find where the sender's number ends and the text begins, often marked by a separator byte. A scan for that byte, exactly like REPNE SCASB, finds the position quickly. Then the text part is copied into the display buffer with a block move.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to set ES, so the destination is wrong. Not setting DF with CLD, so a leftover DF = 1 makes the copy run backward. Putting the count in the wrong register; it must be CX. Confusing which side REPE stops on: REPE stops at the first difference, REPNE at the first match. Forgetting that after the stop, DI and SI have already moved one step past. Expecting MOVS to set flags, which it never does. Using REP with CMPS when you meant REPE.

What exams ask: State which registers and segments each string instruction uses. Explain DF, CLD and STD. Write a program to copy a string, reverse a string, compare two strings or count occurrences of a character. Trace REP MOVSB for a small count and give final SI, DI and CX. Explain the difference between REP, REPE and REPNE, and why overlapping copies need STD.

Recap: String instructions work on blocks of consecutive memory using fixed registers: source DS:SI, destination ES:DI, count CX, value in AL or AX. MOVS copies, LODS loads, STOS stores, CMPS compares two blocks, SCAS searches for AL. After each element SI and DI step by 1 or 2, forward when DF = 0 and backward when DF = 1. REP repeats CX times, REPE repeats while equal, REPNE while not equal. Next, DOS and BIOS services will show how your program talks to the keyboard and screen through INT 21h and friends.
key_points: A string is any run of consecutive bytes or words; string instructions process it element by element.
Fixed roles: source DS:SI, destination ES:DI (ES cannot be overridden), count CX, value AL/AX.
DF decides direction: CLD (DF = 0) forward, STD (DF = 1) backward; step 1 for B, 2 for W.
MOVS copies memory to memory, LODS loads into AL/AX, STOS stores AL/AX, CMPS compares, SCAS searches for AL.
REP repeats CX times; REPE/REPZ repeats while equal; REPNE/REPNZ repeats while not equal.
After a stop, SI and DI already point one element past the matching or differing item.
Set ES as well as DS before string work, and copy backward with STD when blocks overlap upward.
lessons.tip: Before writing any string instruction, say out loud the five things it needs: source, destination, count, direction and (if any) value in AL. If one is missing, the bug is already written.
lessons.task: On paper, trace REPE CMPSB for the strings 'DHAKA' and 'DHAMA' with CX = 5 and DF = 0. Write SI offset, DI offset, CX and ZF after each step, and say where it stops and what the final CX tells you.

quiz.q: Which registers does MOVSB use for source and destination?
quiz.explain: The source is always DS:SI and the destination is always ES:DI.

quiz.q: With DF = 1, what happens to SI and DI after each MOVSW?
quiz.explain: DF = 1 means backward, and word versions step by 2.

quiz.q: REPNE SCASB stops early when:
options: The byte at ES:DI equals AL (ZF = 1)
The byte at ES:DI differs from AL
quiz.explain: REPNE repeats while not equal, so it stops at the first match (or when CX reaches 0).

quiz.q: A REP MOVSB copy writes to the wrong place even though SI and DI look correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: ES was never set to the data segment
quiz.explain: The destination is ES:DI, so a wrong ES sends the bytes to another segment.

quiz.q: Why copy backward with STD when source and destination overlap and the destination is higher in memory?
options: So source bytes are read before they are overwritten
quiz.explain: Copying from the end means each source byte is read before the moving destination reaches it.

lessons.title: DOS and BIOS Services: Talking to Keyboard and Screen
lessons.content:
When you want a parcel delivered from Dhaka to Rajshahi, you do not drive the truck yourself. You go to a courier counter, fill in a slip, and the courier company handles the roads, trucks and drivers. Your assembly program is in the same position with the keyboard and the screen. Talking to that hardware directly is hard work, so the program goes to a service counter and asks. On an 8086 PC the counters are DOS services, reached with INT 21h, and BIOS services, reached with INT 10h, INT 16h and others.

What these services are: DOS (the Disk Operating System, such as MS-DOS) and the BIOS (Basic Input Output System, firmware stored in ROM on the motherboard) contain ready-made routines for common jobs: read a key, print a character, print a line of text, move the cursor, end the program. Your program calls them with a software interrupt instruction, INT n. You pick which job you want by putting a function number in AH, and you pass other inputs in registers such as AL, DX or BX. How INT itself works inside the CPU is the topic of the next lesson; here we use it as a service call.

The problem they solve: Showing one letter on screen by hand means knowing the video card's memory address, the colour attribute byte, the cursor position and the scrolling rules. Reading a key by hand means talking to the keyboard controller through I/O ports and translating scan codes. Every program would repeat this, and it would break on a machine with different hardware. Services hide these details behind a small, stable interface. Before such services existed, early programs really did contain their own hardware routines for each machine.

The layers: Think of a three-storey building. Your program is on the top floor. Below it is DOS, which offers higher-level jobs like printing a whole string or reading a line with editing. Below DOS is the BIOS, which offers lower-level jobs like printing one character at the cursor or waiting for one key. At the bottom is the hardware: ports, video memory and the keyboard controller. DOS functions often call BIOS functions, and BIOS functions talk to the hardware. You can call DOS or BIOS directly, depending on how much control you need.

An important reality check: INT 21h only works when DOS, or something that imitates it, is running. Modern 64-bit Windows cannot run 16-bit DOS programs directly, so students use DOSBox or emu8086, which provide these services. On a modern operating system, programs ask the OS for services through system calls instead, which is the same idea with a different mechanism.

INT 21h function 01h, read a key with echo: MOV AH, 01h then INT 21h. The program waits until a key is pressed, the character is shown on screen (that is the echo), and its ASCII code comes back in AL. If the user presses 7, AL = 37h, not 7. Remember this, because it is the source of the most common bug in number input. Function 08h does the same without echo, which is useful for passwords.

INT 21h function 02h, print one character: Put the character in DL, then MOV AH, 02h and INT 21h. To print the letter A: MOV DL, 'A', MOV AH, 02h, INT 21h. To go to a new line, print two characters: carriage return 0Dh, which moves the cursor to the start of the line, and line feed 0Ah, which moves it down one line. Many students print only one of them and get a staircase effect or overwritten text.

INT 21h function 09h, print a string: Put the offset of the string in DX (DS must point to its segment), then MOV AH, 09h and INT 21h. The string must end with a dollar sign. For example MSG DB 'Assalamu Alaikum', 0Dh, 0Ah, '$'. Then LEA DX, MSG, MOV AH, 09h, INT 21h prints the greeting and a new line. If you forget the dollar sign, DOS keeps printing whatever bytes follow in memory until it happens to find a dollar sign, so the screen fills with junk.

INT 21h function 0Ah, read a whole line: This buffered input lets the user type, use Backspace, and press Enter. You prepare a buffer: the first byte is the maximum number of characters, including the Enter; the second byte will be filled by DOS with how many characters were actually typed, not counting the Enter; then come the characters, followed by 0Dh. Example: BUF DB 21, ?, 21 DUP(?). After LEA DX, BUF, MOV AH, 0Ah, INT 21h, if the user typed Karim and pressed Enter, BUF+1 holds 5 and BUF+2 to BUF+6 hold K, a, r, i, m, with 0Dh at BUF+7.

INT 21h function 4Ch, end the program: MOV AH, 4Ch then INT 21h ends the program and returns control to DOS. AL holds an exit code; 0 normally means success. Usually written as MOV AX, 4C00h, INT 21h. Without this, the CPU keeps executing whatever bytes come after your code, which may be data, and the machine may hang.

BIOS INT 10h, video services: Function 0Eh prints the character in AL at the cursor and moves the cursor forward, like a typewriter; this is called teletype output. Function 02h sets the cursor position: BH is the page (usually 0), DH is the row, DL is the column. For example MOV AH, 02h, MOV BH, 0, MOV DH, 12, MOV DL, 35, INT 10h puts the cursor near the middle of an 80 by 25 text screen. Function 00h sets the video mode; MOV AX, 0003h then INT 10h selects the normal 80 by 25 colour text mode and clears the screen as a side effect.

BIOS INT 16h, keyboard services: Function 00h waits for a key and returns the ASCII code in AL and the keyboard scan code in AH. Keys like the arrows have no ASCII character, so AL is 0 (or E0h on some keyboards) and you must look at the scan code in AH to tell them apart. Function 01h checks whether a key is waiting without stopping the program: ZF = 1 means no key, ZF = 0 means a key is ready. That lets a simple game keep moving while still reacting to keys.

DOS or BIOS, which one: DOS functions are higher level and easier, especially for strings and line input, and they respect features like redirection of output to a file. BIOS functions give finer control, such as cursor positioning and reading special keys, but do less work for you. For simple console programs in this course, DOS functions are enough. For a menu screen or a small game, you will mix in BIOS calls.

Printing a number, the idea: The CPU stores 345 as a binary value, 0159h. The screen needs three characters: '3', '4', '5'. So we must split the number into decimal digits and convert each digit to ASCII by adding 30h. Repeated division by 10 gives the digits, but from right to left: 345 divided by 10 is 34 remainder 5, 34 divided by 10 is 3 remainder 4, 3 divided by 10 is 0 remainder 3. The digits come out as 5, 4, 3, reversed. The stack fixes the order, because popping reverses it.

Printing a number, the code: AX holds the number, MOV BX, 10, XOR CX, CX. Loop1: XOR DX, DX, DIV BX (now AX is the quotient and DX the remainder), PUSH DX, INC CX, TEST AX, AX, JNZ Loop1. Loop2: POP DX, ADD DL, 30h, MOV AH, 02h, INT 21h, LOOP Loop2. Clearing DX before each DIV is essential, because DIV BX divides the 32-bit value DX:AX; leftover DX makes the quotient wrong or causes a divide overflow. Using TEST AX, AX before the jump also handles the number 0 correctly: it prints one digit, 0.

Reading a number, the idea: When the user types 345, the program receives three separate ASCII characters, 33h, 34h and 35h. To build the value, keep a running total: start at 0, and for each digit, total = total times 10 plus the digit. Trace: total 0; read '3', digit 3, total = 0 times 10 + 3 = 3; read '4', total = 3 times 10 + 4 = 34; read '5', total = 34 times 10 + 5 = 345; read Enter (0Dh), stop. This is the same way you read a number on paper from left to right.

Reading a number, the code: XOR BX, BX holds the total. Read: MOV AH, 01h, INT 21h, CMP AL, 0Dh, JE Done. Then SUB AL, 30h, MOV AH, 0, MOV CX, AX to keep the digit, MOV AX, BX, MOV DX, 10, MUL DX, ADD AX, CX, MOV BX, AX, JMP Read. Done: BX holds the value. Note that MUL DX overwrites DX with the high half of the product, which is why the digit is kept in CX. A careful program also checks that AL is between '0' and '9' before subtracting, and rejects other keys.

Real-life example 1, a mudi shop bill calculator: Imagine a simple DOS-style program on an old PC in a grocery shop in Mymensingh. It prints "Enter price:" with function 09h, reads the price with the number-reading routine, reads the quantity the same way, multiplies them, prints "Total:" and then the result with the number-printing routine. Every piece you learned in this lesson appears in that one small tool.

Real-life example 2, a quiz game at a school science fair: A student builds a quiz in emu8086. INT 10h clears the screen and places the question in the middle. INT 16h function 00h waits for A, B, C or D. The program compares the answer, prints "Correct!" or "Try again" with function 09h, and moves the cursor with INT 10h function 02h for the next question. Visitors think it is a real game, and it is built only from service calls.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the dollar sign in a function 09h string. Forgetting to load DS with the data segment before printing, so DX points into the wrong segment. Treating the ASCII code in AL as the digit value. Printing only 0Ah or only 0Dh for a new line. Not clearing DX before DIV in number printing. Forgetting MOV AH, 4Ch and INT 21h at the end, so the program runs into data. Forgetting that function 0Ah's count byte excludes the Enter key.

What exams ask: List INT 21h functions 01h, 02h, 09h, 0Ah and 4Ch with their inputs and outputs. Write a program that reads two single-digit numbers and prints their sum. Write procedures to read and print multi-digit decimal numbers. Explain the format of the 0Ah input buffer. Explain the difference between DOS and BIOS services and give one example of each.

Recap: Programs ask DOS (INT 21h) and the BIOS (INT 10h for video, INT 16h for keyboard) to do I/O, choosing the function in AH. 01h reads a key into AL, 02h prints DL, 09h prints a dollar-terminated string at DS:DX, 0Ah reads a line into a buffer, 4Ch exits. Characters are ASCII, so digits need plus or minus 30h. Print numbers by dividing by 10 and reversing with the stack; read numbers with total = total times 10 plus digit. Next, we look inside INT itself: what an interrupt is and what the CPU does step by step when one arrives.
key_points: Programs ask DOS (INT 21h) and BIOS (INT 10h video, INT 16h keyboard) for I/O; AH picks the function.
INT 21h: 01h read key into AL (ASCII), 02h print DL, 09h print '$'-ended string at DS:DX, 0Ah read a line, 4Ch exit.
New line = 0Dh (carriage return) + 0Ah (line feed).
0Ah buffer: byte 0 = max chars incl. Enter, byte 1 = chars typed excl. Enter, then the text and 0Dh.
INT 10h: 0Eh teletype output, 02h set cursor (BH page, DH row, DL column), 00h set video mode.
INT 16h: 00h waits for a key (AL ASCII, AH scan code), 01h checks without waiting (ZF = 1 means none).
Print a number: divide by 10, push remainders, pop and add 30h. Read one: total = total x 10 + (char - 30h).
DOS services need DOS or an emulator such as DOSBox or emu8086.
lessons.tip: Build a small personal library early: a PRINTSTR macro, a NEWLINE macro, and READNUM/PRINTNUM procedures. Almost every lab task reuses them.
lessons.task: Write out on paper (or in emu8086) a program that asks "Your age?", reads a two-digit number, adds 1 and prints "Next year you will be" followed by the result. Trace it by hand for input 19.

quiz.q: The user presses the key 7 after MOV AH, 01h / INT 21h. What is in AL?
quiz.explain: Function 01h returns the ASCII code; the character '7' is 37h, so subtract 30h to get the value 7.

quiz.q: Which string is correctly prepared for INT 21h function 09h?
quiz.explain: Function 09h prints until it finds a dollar sign, so the string must end with '$'.

quiz.q: In the 0Ah input buffer BUF DB 21, ?, 21 DUP(?), the user types ABC and presses Enter. What is at BUF+1?
quiz.explain: DOS stores the number of characters typed, not counting the Enter key.

quiz.q: Why must DX be cleared before DIV BX when printing a number digit by digit?
options: DIV BX divides the 32-bit value DX:AX, so leftover DX gives a wrong result or overflow
quiz.explain: A 16-bit DIV uses DX as the high half of the dividend.

quiz.q: Which BIOS service waits for a key and returns both the ASCII code and the scan code?
quiz.explain: INT 16h function 00h returns ASCII in AL and the scan code in AH.

lessons.title: Interrupts I: How the 8086 Responds
lessons.content:
Imagine you are studying for your SSC exam and waiting for a friend to bring notes. You could get up every two minutes, open the door and check whether he is there. You would waste your whole evening walking to the door. Or you could keep studying and let the doorbell ring when he arrives. The doorbell is an interrupt. The CPU faces the same choice with keyboards, timers and disks, and the interrupt is how it avoids wasting its time.

What an interrupt is: An interrupt is a signal that makes the CPU pause the program it is running, run a special routine to handle the event, and then return to the paused program exactly where it left off, as if nothing had happened. The special routine is called an interrupt service routine, or ISR, also called an interrupt handler.

Before interrupts, polling: The simple way to find out whether a device needs attention is polling: the CPU reads the device's status port again and again in a loop, asking "are you ready?" Polling is easy to write and works well when the event is expected very soon or the CPU has nothing else to do. But it wastes CPU time when events are rare, and if the CPU is busy elsewhere and does not poll in time, it may miss an event, such as a key press being overwritten by the next one.

The solution: With interrupts, the device itself tells the CPU when it needs attention. The CPU does useful work in between, and responds only when something actually happens. The cost is extra hardware (an interrupt pin and usually a controller chip) and a small delay to save and restore the state for each interrupt. For rare or unpredictable events, this is a huge win.
